(c) *Hölder exponential-weights converse* (`thermal_exp_weights`; `card_ge_laplace` is the case
`p = 1/2`, `v = π`): for `p ∈ (0,1)`, `t = β(1−p)/p` and every `v ≥ 0`,

    Σ_y π(y)^{1−p} v(y)^p  ≤  (|A| · max_a Σ_y v(y) e^{−t s(a,y)})^p · e^{(1−p)ε}.

So the evaluated set is a quantizer of the Gibbs ensemble for the distortion `e^{βs}`, and its
size is at least `exp(entropy)` up to the partition sum of a slack ball.  As `β → ∞` with `ε/β`
fixed, (c) becomes Theorem 11.6(b) (with the weights `v e^{−t·gap}`).

**Theorem 11.14 (transport–entropy duality at fixed `β`) [V + K].**  For every reference `μ`,
every admissible `g` and every `β ≥ 0`, with the tilted measure `ν ∝ μ e^{βg}` and **any**
coupling `γ` of `(ν, μ)`,

    ln E_μ e^{β(g − E_μ g)} = β (E_ν g − E_μ g) − KL(ν‖μ) ≤ β Σ_{x,y} γ(x,y) d(x,y) − KL(ν‖μ)

(`logMGF_eq_tilt`; `transport_le` is weak Kantorovich duality, `E_ν g − E_μ g ≤ Σ γ d`;
`logMGF_le_transport_entropy`).  Minimising over couplings gives
`≤ β W_d(ν,μ) − KL(ν‖μ)` with `W_d` the transport cost, which by Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality
for quasi-metrics **[K]** equals `sup_{g admissible} (E_ν g − E_μ g)`.  Consequently a transport
inequality `Σ γ d ≤ √(2C·KL(ν‖μ))` for the coupling gives the sub-Gaussian bound `β²C/2`
(`gap_le_of_T1`).
Conversely every `ν` is matched by its Kantorovich potential (Donsker–Varadhan), so
`sup_g ln E_μ e^{β(g−E_μ g)} = sup_ν [β W_d(ν,μ) − KL(ν‖μ)]` **[K]** (Gozlan–Léonard 2007,
Cor. 7.11; Bobkov–Houdré–Tetali 2006).  This is the fixed-`β` statement that replaces the
Bobkov–Götze equivalence of §3.2; the orientation matters for asymmetric envelopes (for the
Boltzmann factor `e^{−βΔ}` the roles of `ν` and `μ` in `W_d` are exchanged).  It unifies the
passive bounds: the zero-evaluation free-energy gap of §3.2 is the transport–entropy conjugate
of the envelope, product references give `Σ c_i²` (Marton, McDiarmid), dependent references the
Wasserstein-matrix constants — and the extremal residual is then no longer additive
(`DEAD_ENDS.md` D25).  Harness XI.9.

**Theorem 11.15 (exact exponent at finite temperature) [V lower bound; P upper bound].**  For
`n` identical independent sites with single-site Gibbs measure `π`, slack `s` (positive off the
diagonal: `κ < 1`, `c > 0`) and accuracies `ε_n` that are neither extensive nor exponentially
small — `ε_n = o(n)` **and** `ln(1/ε_n) = o(n)`, e.g. `ε_n ≥ n^{−m}` — the least number of
evaluations in a certificate of `ln Z` to within `ε_n` satisfies

    n⁻¹ ln N_Z → R_β = max_Q R(Q; s, KL(Q‖π)/β)
               = max_{t ≥ 0, v ≥ 0} { ((β+t)/β) ln Σ_s π(s)^{t/(β+t)} v(s)^{β/(β+t)} − ln max_a Σ_s v(s) e^{−t s(a,s)} }.

The distortion allowed to a macrostate (type) `Q` is `KL(Q‖π)/β = F_β[Q] − F_β`, **its
free-energy gap**; as `β → ∞` it becomes the energy gap `Σ_s Q(s) gap(s)` and `R_β → R*`
(Theorem 11.9).  Always `R_β ≥ H(π)` (take `Q = π`): at finite temperature and sub-extensive
accuracy the number of evaluations is exponential in the thermodynamic entropy even when every
site is sharp.  Example (`thermal_binary_exponential`): two-state sites with excitation energy
`2`, envelope constants `1` — one evaluation certifies the ground state exactly
(`thermal_binary_sharp`) — at `β = ln 2`: every certificate of `ln Z` to within `ε` has at least
`e^{−ε} (6/5)ⁿ` evaluations.  (The hypothesis actually used, `Z(f+L_A) ≤ e^ε Z`, holds with
equality for the single evaluation of the ground state at `ε = n ln(6/5)`,
`thermal_binary_single_tight`; it involves the true `Z` and is not computable from the
evaluations — as a two-sided certificate that single evaluation has width `n ln(4/3)`.)

*Proof.*  Lower bound: Theorem 11.13(c) with product weights (`thermal_product_exp_weights`),
valid for every `n`; the maximum over `p` and `v` equals `max_Q R(Q; s, KL(Q‖π)/β)` by the dual
formula for `R(Q, D)` and the Gibbs variational principle in `Q` (the distortion level
`KL(Q‖π)/β` is linear in `ln π` and `ln Q`).  Upper bound: cover every type class `T_Q` at the
per-site distortion `D_Q = max(0, KL(Q‖π)/β − a_n)`,
`a_n = [(k+1) ln(n+1) + ln(4/ε_n)]/(nβ)` (type covering, which is uniform in the type and in the
level; a class with `D_Q = 0` is evaluated entirely, because the slack is positive off the
diagonal).  Here `a_n → 0` is exactly the hypothesis `ln(1/ε_n) = o(n)`.  Every `y ∈ T_Q` has
`e^{β s(A,y)} ≤ e^{nβD_Q}`, `π(T_Q) ≤ e^{−n KL(Q‖π)}`, and there are at most `(n+1)^k` types, so
the classes with `D_Q > 0` contribute at most `(n+1)^k e^{−nβ a_n} ≤ ε_n/4` to
`Z(f+L_A)/Z = Σ_Q π(T_Q) E[e^{βs} | T_Q]` and have total mass at most `ε_n/4`; hence
`Z(f+L_A)/Z ≤ 1 + ε_n/4` and `Z(f+U_A)/Z = E_π e^{−βs(Y,A)} ≥ π(A) ≥ 1 − ε_n/4`, and the two ends
differ by at most `ε_n` in logarithm (for `ε_n ≤ 1`).  The rate is
`max_Q R(Q; s, D_Q) + o(1) = R_β + o(1)` by continuity of the rate–distortion function. ∎

*The restriction on the accuracy is necessary* (second referee report, C1; `DEAD_ENDS.md` D29).
For `ε = 0` every certificate of `ln Z` is the whole space, `N_Z(0) = kⁿ`
(`exact_free_energy_certificate_eq_univ`), whereas `R_β < ln k` unless `π` is uniform.  More
generally a two-sided certificate forces `π(Aᶜ) ≤ ε/(1 − e^{−β s_min})`, so for `ε_n = e^{−λn}`
the evaluated set contains at least half of every type class with `KL(Q‖π) < λ` and the exponent
is at least `max{H(Q) : KL(Q‖π) < λ}`, which reaches `ln k` once `λ > KL(uniform‖π)`.  The
construction above with `a_n → λ/β` gives the upper bound
`max_Q R(Q; s, (KL(Q‖π) − λ)₊/β)` in that regime; whether it is attained is open.  (Theorem 11.9
has no such restriction: `ε = 0` is allowed there.)

The single-letter identity and the lower bound were checked
numerically (the two sides agree to `10⁻³` on a grid; `R_β = 0.666, 0.482, 0.216` at
`β = 1, 4, 40` for `e/c = 1/2`, approaching `R* = 0.188`, benchmark B8; harness XI.8 tests the
one-shot converse on every evaluated set of small instances).  For the sharp site of the
example above the exponent is `R_β = 0.514` (entropy `0.500`); the verified one-shot bound with
uniform weights gives `ln(6/5) = 0.182`.

*Attribution.*  The upper bound is an instance of a known source-coding theorem.  Merhav
("On optimum strategies for minimizing the exponential moments of a given cost function",
arXiv:1103.2882, 2011) shows that for fixed-rate lossy coding of a memoryless source `P` the
optimum exponential rate of `E exp(α n d)` is `max_Q [α D_Q(R) − D(Q‖P)]`, `D_Q(R)` the
distortion–rate function of `Q`, by type covering; the formula for `R_β` is the rate at which
this exponent vanishes for `P = π`, `α = β`, `d = s`.  (The guessing exponent
`max_Q [ρ R(D;Q) − D(Q‖P)]` of Arikan–Merhav 1998 is the same kind of object.)  We read the
general theorem and its variational identity in the paper; the rate–distortion example was
available to us only through an automatic summary.  The science division has since read the
section in full (`SCI-REV-0006` W7): the statement is an *example* of a general observation of
Merhav's §4 — if a strategy attains `n[λ(Q) + o(1)]` on every type class and no strategy does
better on a non-negligible fraction of it, then "it is then a straightforward exercise to
show, using the method of types" that the optimum exponent is `max_Q [αλ(Q) − D(Q‖P)]` (his
eq. (37)) — for memoryless finite-alphabet sources and additive distortion, with
`λ(Q) = D_Q(R)` by type covering.  So the formula for `R_β` is a corollary of an example, not
of a numbered theorem, and the attribution stands **[K, the relevant section read in full by
the science division]**.  What was not found is the identification — the complexity of
certifying a free energy under an envelope *is* this exponent, with the distortion budget of a
macrostate equal to its free-energy gap — and the one-shot converse of Theorem 11.13
(`prior_art/L4` C9, `prior_art/L6` T6).

*The contrast with linear information.*  For a product reference, one reference average `⟨Δ⟩₀`
— a single *linear*
functional of the residual — pins `ln Z` to within `β² Σ c_i²/8` (Theorem 3.1(c); the product
hypothesis cannot be dropped, §3.2), and `N` random
evaluations at independent samples of that reference estimate it to
`±(Σc_i² ln(2/δ)/(2N))^{1/2}` with confidence `1−δ`, independently of
the size of the state space **[K]**.  Deterministic point-wise certification to an extensive accuracy
`ε = nε₁` still costs exponentially many evaluations whenever `ε₁` is below a threshold — by
Theorem 11.13(b), `n⁻¹ ln |A| ≥ H(π) − ln(1 + (k−1)e^{−t(1−κ)c}) − tε₁/β` for every `t` — which
includes the accuracy `β²c²/8` per site of the sandwich when `βc` is small and the Gibbs entropy
is not (for a cold sharp site, `e^{−βe} ≲ βc/8`, the single evaluation of the ground state
already reaches that accuracy).  So at the accuracy of the sandwich the exponential price is
the price of *deterministic* information; Theorem 11.21 (§11.9) is the machine-checked
randomised statement.  Randomisation does not rescue at every accuracy: on the uniform cube
class, below the accuracy `n ln cosh(βc/2)` — which is strictly smaller than the width
`β²Σc_i²/8` of Theorem 11.21 — every algorithm needs exponentially many evaluations on the zero
residual, with a smaller exponent (Theorem 11.25, §11.10); for other product references this is
proved only below an instance-dependent accuracy (`ε₁^crit`, §11.10).

### 11.7 Second-order envelopes: a way out under weak coupling

A residual class with bounded *mixed* differences,

    |g(x^{i→a, j→b}) − g(x^{i→a}) − g(x^{j→b}) + g(x)| ≤ c_ij        (all x, i ≠ j, a, b),

bounds the non-additive part of the residual only.  In such a class information from different
evaluations *does* combine.

**Theorem 11.16 (star sandwich) [V] (`SecondOrderEnvelope.lean`).**  Let `x₀` be a reference
configuration and let `g` be evaluated on its star (`x₀` and its `Σ_i (k_i − 1)` single-site
neighbours).  With the additive interpolant `g_star(x) = g(x₀) + Σ_i [g(x₀^{i→x_i}) − g(x₀)]` and
symmetric `c`,

    |g(x) − g_star(x)| ≤ Σ_{i<j, both changed} c_ij        (`secondOrder_remainder`),

so `E₀ + g` lies between two *pairwise* models whose one-body tables contain the star
evaluations and whose pair tables are shifted by `∓ c_ij/2` on changed pairs
(`pairwise_sandwich`); a certificate of the lower model accepted by the tropical kernel bounds
the true energy (`verify_sound_secondOrder`).  If `c ≡ 0` the residual is determined by its star
(`starPart_eq_of_additive`).

**Theorem 11.17 (the sandwich is the exact envelope) [V].**  For symmetric nonnegative `c` the
two functions `g_star ∓ Σ_{i<j changed} c_ij` belong to the class and agree with `g` on the star
(`secondOrder_lower_attained`, `secondOrder_upper_attained`); so they are the least and greatest
elements of the set of residuals consistent with the star data
(`secondOrder_envelope_exact`) — a McShane–Whitney theorem for the second-order class, in which
the extremal extensions are pairwise models.  Consequently the robust problem is *exactly* a
pairwise problem (`secondOrder_robust_min_exact`), and `x₀` is a minimiser for every consistent
residual of the class iff it minimises its own lower pairwise model
(`secondOrder_certified_minimizer_iff`): a second-order sharp-minimum condition, in which the
*measured* single-site excitation energies of the full energy compete with the pair constants
`c_ij` only.  Harness XI.11 confirms exactness against a linear program over the whole class.

**Theorem 11.18 (order `m`) [V] (`HigherOrderEnvelope.lean`; harness XI.10).**  If all mixed
differences of order `m` over a set `T` of sites are bounded by `c_T` (`HigherDiffBound`), then
the anchored interpolant `I_{m−1} g` of order `m−1` (`anchoredInterp`: the truncated cut-HDMR /
many-body expansion at `x₀`, which uses `g` on the Hamming ball of radius `m−1` and is exact
there, `anchoredInterp_eq_of_card_lt`, by the Möbius identity `anchored_decomposition`)
satisfies `|g(x) − I_{m−1}g(x)| ≤ Σ_{T ⊆ changed sites, |T| = m} c_T` (`higherOrder_remainder`),
and for nonnegative constants the bound is attained at every configuration by a member of the
class with the same ball data.  (Machine-checked for zero ball data, where the member is the
remainder function itself, `higherOrder_remainder_sharp`, and for `m = 2` with arbitrary data,
`secondOrder_lower_attained`; for `m ≥ 3` with arbitrary data it is **[P]** — the interpolant has
no differences of order `m` — and was confirmed by linear programming for `m = 3`.)  For `m = 2`
it is Theorem 11.16
(`secondOrder_remainder_of_higherOrder`); a three-site instance of order three is
`higherOrder_witness`.  *Proof.*  `h = g − I_{m−1}g`
vanishes on the ball and has the same order-`m` differences.  Induct on `m` and on the number
`w` of changed sites: for a changed site `j`, `|h(x)| ≤ |h(x with j reset)| + |D_j h|`, and
`D_j h`, as a function of the other sites, vanishes on the ball of radius `m−2` and has
order-`(m−1)` differences bounded by `c_{T∪{j}}`. ∎  The anchored decomposition and its
remainder estimates are classical (Kuo–Sloan–Wasilkowski–Woźniakowski 2010; Griebel–Holtz 2010);
its use as a certified residual class with an exact reduction to a kernel was not found
(`prior_art/L5`, P9).

**Theorem 11.18a (third-order classes reduce to pairwise lower models) [V; (d) P]
(`ThirdOrderModel.lean`; harness XI.16; requested by the Scientific Discovery Division,
SCI-MSG-0015 P2-T1, with the site form of (c)).**  Let every third mixed difference of the
residual `g` over a triple `T` of sites be bounded by `c_T ≥ 0` (Theorem 11.18 with `m = 3`), and
let `I₂g` be the interpolant of order two around `x₀` — it uses `g` on the Hamming ball of
radius two, `1 + Σ_i(k_i − 1) + Σ_{i<j}(k_i − 1)(k_j − 1)` evaluations.
(a) `I₂g` is a pairwise function: the star part of Theorem 11.16 plus, for every pair of
changed sites, the second mixed difference of `g` at the reference (`anchoredInterp_three`).
(b) Let site penalties `γ_i` and pair penalties `γ_ij` *cover the triples*:
`Σ_{T ⊆ S, |T| = 3} c_T ≤ Σ_{i∈S} γ_i + Σ_{i<j∈S} γ_ij` for every set `S` of sites.  Then for every
configuration `x`

    E₀(x) + g(x)  ≥  E₀(x) + I₂g(x) − Σ_{i changed} γ_i − Σ_{i<j both changed} γ_ij

(`thirdOrder_pairwise_lower`).  The right-hand side is a pairwise model (`thirdOrderLowerModel`),
and a certificate of it accepted by the tropical kernel bounds the true energy
(`verify_sound_thirdOrder`).
(c) Two coverings.  The **site form** `γ_i = ⅓Σ_{T∋i}c_T` — more generally any nonnegative shares
of each triple among its three sites (`cover_of_site_shares`,
`thirdOrder_pairwise_lower_thirds`) — and the **pair form** `γ_ij = ⅓Σ_{T⊇{i,j}}c_T`
(`cover_of_pair_thirds`, `thirdOrder_pairwise_lower_pair_thirds`).  The pair form is the tighter
one: a triple with one changed site costs `c_T/3` in the site form and nothing in the pair
form, with two changed sites `2c_T/3` against `c_T/3`, with three `c_T` in both — where all three
sites of a triple are changed both forms charge what the exact envelope charges (that is what
`thirdOrder_witness` states); with one changed site the site form overcharges (`c_T/3` against
nothing) and the pair form does not, with two both do (`2c_T/3` and `c_T/3` against nothing): the
envelope charges nothing there.  (The first version said "at a single triple both are
exact", without the restriction: Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0012; the second said
"with one or two of them changed neither does", which is wrong for the pair form with one
changed site — the division's own slip, found by it: SCI-REV-0014, m6.)  The two forms cost the same
evaluations but not the same interaction graph: the pair form adds a pair term wherever a
triple has `c_T > 0`.  Where the lower model must stay banded — the division's sandwich of
transfer-matrix models, SCI-MSG-0020 — a *banded* variant keeps the share of every pair within
the band and gives the share of every other pair in halves to its two sites; it lies pointwise
between the two forms (its §6).
(d) **[P]** Neither is the exact envelope.  By Theorem 11.18 the least member of the class
with the given ball data is `I₂g − Σ_{T ⊆ changed sites}c_T`, a three-body function; the
pairwise models are relaxations of it, and the best shares are a linear programme for the
producer, which the checker need not trust — a covering *by shares* is checked triple by triple
(nonnegative shares that add up to at least one).  Two remarks of the division's review
(SCI-REV-0012, P4-T4; both re-derived).  Among the shares of one triple the pure pair shares are
pointwise best: a share moved from a site to a pair that contains it never increases the
penalty of a configuration.  And the coverings of (b) are more than shares: on four sites with
`c_{012} = c_{013} = 1` the penalties `γ₀₁ = γ₂₃ = 1` cover every set of sites and are dominated by no
allocation of shares (the pair `{2, 3}` lies in neither triple, so both triples would have to be
charged to `{0, 1}`); a covering that does not come from shares has to be checked on all sets
of sites.
*Proof.*  (a) Raising the order of the interpolant by one adds the mixed differences over
the pairs of changed sites, and a second mixed difference with an unchanged site
vanishes.  (b) Theorem 11.18, then the covering inequality at `S` = the changed sites.
(c) `Σ_{i∈S}γ_i = ⅓Σ_Tc_T·|T ∩ S|` and `Σ_{i<j∈S}γ_ij = ⅓Σ_Tc_T·#{`pairs of `T` inside `S}`; a triple
inside `S` is counted three times in each.  ∎
*The split between known part and residual* (an observation of the Scientific Discovery
Division, SCI-MSG-0015 §2; its request P2-T4).  Moving a pairwise function `p` from the known
part to the residual, or back, changes neither the constants `c_T` (the third mixed
differences of a pairwise function vanish) nor the lower models of this theorem (the
interpolant of order two reproduces a pairwise function exactly, `I₂(g + p) = I₂g + p`).  It
does change the first- and second-order constants of the residual, and with them the
star envelope of Theorems 11.16–11.17 and its row-sum condition.  **The cost of the star
depends on how the energy is split; that of the ball does not.**  In the division's
measurement this is what defeats the star for polar and charged side chains — pair
terms of the solvent part that nearly cancel pair terms of the vacuum part — while the
ball certifies those instances.
*Measured input* (the division's, on fixed synthetic model peptides with rigid ideal
backbones; exact maxima over enumerated domains, **not certified constants**, and lower
bounds for the same constants on larger domains): in rotamer variables on a fixed
backbone the third-order constants of a generalized-Born solvent term are `0.003`–`0.2`
kcal/mol for neutral side chains — on a hexamer of serines `γ_i ≤ 0.011` against
single-site excitation energies of `1.0`–`1.1` — and up to `2.4` for charged ones.  What is
missing for a guarantee is unchanged: an a-priori bound on `c_T`, obtained without
enumerating the domain.
*Site form against pair form on those instances* (**[M]**, the division's workstream P4,
SCI-REV-0012 §2, at our request; measured constants; not re-computed by us).  On all 136
instances with at least three multi-state sites the pair form is the larger lower bound at
every state; the reference minimises the model in 132 instances with the pair form against
113 with the site form (the three-body envelope: 133), and `ln Z(model) − ln Z(E)` is smaller by
a median factor `6.8` (range `1.0`–`137`).  The largest gap `max(E − model)` is the same for both
forms in 129 of the 136 — where every site is changed both charge `Σc_T`, and that is where the
largest gap is: it is the wrong quantity for comparing them.  For the division's sandwich at
order `m` the pair form `γ_ij = Σ_{T⊇{i,j}}ĉ_T/C(m, 2)` turns a useless floor into a usable one
(its cost number for a hexamer of valines on a strand at `m = 3`: `16.4` with site penalties,
`0.064` with pair penalties, `0.157` with the banded variant; its §6).

**Proposition 11.18b (share certificates: the row-sum condition completed) [(a) V; (b) P
from K; (c) V for the covering, P for the rest; (d) V; (e) V for soundness, P for the
duality; N for the frequencies; M for the division's instances]
(`ShareCertificates.lean`, `StateShares.lean`; harness XI.17, XI.21; an answer to request P2-T2
of the Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-MSG-0015: "is there a condition of maximum-density
type?"; reviewed and tested on its instances by that division, SCI-REV-0012, whose
state-dependent form is part (e)).**
Setting of Theorems 11.16–11.18a; `Δ_i` denotes the least single-site excitation energy of
the full energy at site `i` (measured on the star).
(a) *Soundness* **[V]**.  Let the known part be additive.  If every pair constant can be split
between its two sites, `c_ij ≤ s_ij + s_ji` with shares `s ≥ 0`, so that every site carries at
most its excitation energy, `Σ_{j≠i} s_ij ≤ Δ_i`, then `x₀` minimises `E₀ + g′` for every residual
`g′` of the class (`pairSum_le_of_shares`, `secondOrder_certified_of_shares`).  The split in
halves is the row-sum condition of the paragraph below, which is thereby machine-checked
(`secondOrder_certified_of_rowSum`).
(b) *Completeness* **[P from K]**.  For an additive known part the exact criterion of Theorem
11.17 reads: no set `S` of sites is *over-dense*, `Σ_{i<j∈S} c_ij ≤ Σ_{i∈S} Δ_i` for every `S` (the
constants do not depend on the states, so the worst state of a site is its cheapest
one — **on a product domain**, where the cheapest states of all sites of `S` are admissible
together; on domains with exclusions this step fails, Proposition 11.18c(a)).  That holds
**iff shares as in (a) exist**: in the network source → pairs (capacity
`c_ij`) → the two sites of a pair → sink (capacity `Δ_i`) a flow saturating all pair arcs
exists iff no cut is too small, and the cuts are the sets `S` (max-flow min-cut; the
fractional form of Hakimi's orientation theorem; deciding it is the weighted
densest-subgraph, or maximum-closure, problem of Goldberg and Picard — cited from memory).
So **the exact second-order sharp-minimum condition is decided by one maximum flow and has
a certificate of `n(n−1)` numbers that is checked by additions**; the row-sum condition is
the special flow that splits every pair in halves, and it is strictly weaker.
(c) *Third order.*  The lower models of Theorem 11.18a are pairwise functions whose pair
tables contain the *measured* second mixed differences `D_ij` of the residual at the
reference; so (d) below applies to them, with the deficits
`w_ij := max[γ_ij − T_ij(a, b) − D_ij(a, b)]₊` and the excitation energies reduced by the site
penalties `γ_i`.  The purely combinatorial part has the same form as (a), (b): shares of
each `c_T` among its three sites cover every set of sites (`cover_of_site_shares` **[V]**), the
rule of thirds is the equal split, and shares with loads at most `Δ_i` exist iff no set of
sites is over-dense with respect to the triples, `Σ_{T⊆S} c_T ≤ Σ_{i∈S} Δ_i` (**[P]**, the same
flow argument with triples in place of pairs) — which is the exact criterion for the
ball data when the measured and the known pair terms vanish, given the attainment
statement of Theorem 11.18 (**[P]** for `m = 3`).
(d) *A pairwise known part* **[V]** (`energy_sub_eq_excitations_add_secondDiff`,
`secondOrder_certified_of_deficit_shares`; on paper at the sixteenth checkpoint).  The lower
model is pairwise, so
`L(x) − L(x₀) = Σ_{i∈S}A_i(x_i) + Σ_{i<j∈S}[T_ij(x_i, x_j) − c_ij]` with `S` the changed sites, `A_i` the
single-site excitation energies of the full energy and `T_ij` the second difference of the
known part's pair table at the reference.  With the *deficits*
`w_ij := max_{a ≠ x₀_i, b ≠ x₀_j}[c_ij − T_ij(a, b)]₊`, shares of the `w_ij` with loads at most `Δ_i` are
sufficient for `x₀` to minimise `L`.  They are not necessary, for three reasons: the worst
states of different pairs need not be compatible; pair terms of the known part that help
are discarded; and within a single pair the pair of states that realises the deficit need
not consist of the cheapest states of its two sites — the certificate compares
`max_{a,b}[c_ij − T_ij(a, b)]₊` with `min_aA_i(a) + min_bA_j(b)`.  (The third reason is the division's,
SCI-REV-0012 §1: it is the mechanism of all four failures on its instances.)
Computing the deficits costs `O(n²k²)` operations and no evaluation of the residual beyond
the star.
(e) *Shares that depend on the state* **[soundness V: `secondOrder_certified_of_state_shares`,
with the witness `stateShare_witness`; the duality P; proposed, with the measurements, by the
Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0012 §4].**  Let every site `i` in every changed state `a`
take a share `s_ij(a) ≥ 0` of each pair `{i, j}`, with

    s_ij(a) + s_ji(b)  ≥  c_ij − T_ij(a, b)      (all changed states a of i, b of j),            Σ_{j≠i} s_ij(a)  ≤  A_i(a) .

Then `x₀` minimises `L`, hence `E₀ + g′` for every residual of the class: for a configuration
with changed sites `S`,
`Σ_{i<j∈S}[c_ij − T_ij(x_i, x_j)] ≤ Σ_{i∈S}Σ_{j∈S, j≠i}s_ij(x_i) ≤ Σ_{i∈S}Σ_{j≠i}s_ij(x_i) ≤ Σ_{i∈S}A_i(x_i)`.  Constant
shares are the special case (d), and it is a proper one: two sites with states `{0, 1, 2}`,
excitation energies `(1, 10)`, `c₁₂ = 3` and a known pair term that raises the pair of states
`(1, 1)` by `2` have the shares `s(1) = ½`, `s(2) = 5/2`, while the deficit `3` of the pair of states
`(1, 2)` exceeds `Δ₁ + Δ₂ = 2` (the Lean witness).  **Such shares exist iff `x₀` is an optimal
solution of the pairwise linear relaxation** (the local polytope: one-site marginals and
consistent pair marginals) of the minimisation of `L`: with `θ_i(a) = A_i(a)`,
`θ_ij(a, b) = T_ij(a, b) − c_ij` for changed states and zero otherwise, the reparametrisation
`θ′_i(a) = θ_i(a) − Σ_js_ij(a)`, `θ′_ij(a, b) = θ_ij(a, b) + s_ij(a) + s_ji(b)` leaves every `L(x)` unchanged, and the
three conditions say exactly that every one-site and every pair term of `θ′` is minimised
at the reference (for a pair with one changed state that is `s_ij(a) ≥ 0`); a dual solution of
the relaxation can be normalised to this form, and strong duality gives the converse.  So
state-dependent shares are **the dual certificate of the linear relaxation**, and they fail
exactly where the relaxation has an integrality gap at `x₀` — three binary sites with
`A = (1, 1, 1)`, `c₁₂ = c₁₃ = 2` and a known pair term `T₂₃ = 10`: `x₀` minimises `L`, the relaxation
has the value `−½` (every site changed with weight ½, sites 1 and 2 always together, sites 1
and 3 always together, sites 2 and 3 never: consistent pair marginals of no distribution),
and no shares exist, `4 > 3` (harness XI.21).  The mathematics is the linear-programming
duality of pairwise energy minimisation, which is **known** (Schlesinger's dual and its
reparametrisations — "equivalent transformations" — in the literature on MAP inference; cited
from memory by both divisions, no source opened); what is used here is its direction for a
checker: `O(n²k²)` additions and comparisons on tables on the ball, the constants and the
shares, with no enumeration on either side.  The pair shares of the triples of Theorem 11.18a
enter the same constraints linearly, so one linear programme with `O(n²k + n³)` variables
searches for a whole third-order certificate (the division's observation).
*Proof of (a).*  `Σ_{i<j∈S}c_ij ≤ Σ_{i<j∈S}(s_ij + s_ji) = Σ_{i∈S}Σ_{j∈S, j≠i}s_ij ≤ Σ_{i∈S}Σ_{j≠i}s_ij ≤ Σ_{i∈S}Δ_i`, and
for an additive known part the lower model at `x` exceeds its value at `x₀` by the sum of
the excitation energies of the changed sites minus the pair constants of the changed
pairs; Theorem 11.17 concludes.  ∎
*How much is gained* (**[N]**, harness XI.17 in its full mode, random instances with 3 to 7
sites).  Additive known part: the exact criterion held in 29 of 100 instances; a share
certificate existed in exactly those 29; the row-sum condition held in 9.  Triples: 58,
58 and 19 (rule of thirds).  Pairwise known part with two or three states per site: the
reference minimised the lower model in 41 of 100 instances; shares of the deficits
existed in 40 of them and in no other; the row-sum condition for the deficits held in
17.  State-dependent shares (harness XI.21, full mode, 200 random instances with 2 to 4
sites): they exist in 146, constant shares of the deficits in 138 of those, the reference
minimises the model in 148 — two integrality gaps — and in every instance they exist exactly
when the relaxation is solved by the reference.  (These are the numbers of the stored
harness output; earlier versions of this paragraph quoted those of a draft of the test —
Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0014, m3.)
*On the division's instances* (**[M]**: its workstream P4, SCI-REV-0012 §1, §4, at our request;
its *measured* constants — exact maxima over enumerated domains, not certified ones; flows
in exact rational arithmetic; not re-computed by us).  Of the 13 analyses in which its
row-sum condition fails and the exact criterion holds, the share certificate of (d)
certifies **11** (the split in halves 2); of the 110 analyses of the generalised-Born term in
which the criterion holds, **106** (halves: 91; never where the criterion fails).  The two
failures are at a single pair of sites, by `0.036` and `0.034` kcal/mol, by the third reason
of (d).  State-dependent shares certify all 13 and all 110, and every third-order model
that the pair and site forms certify; one linear programme over pair shares and state
shares, with inputs from the ball only, gives an exactly verified certificate in 133 of
136 instances — every instance in which the three-body envelope certifies.  For an exactly
additive residual the constants vanish and the certificate of (d) still fails in 55 of 180
analyses: it is a statement about the known part too, whose negative pair terms are
charged at the worst pair of states to the cheapest states.  And the division's own plain
row-sum condition (without deficits) is *not* sufficient for a pairwise known part: it
holds while the criterion fails in seven of its analyses; the deficit version never does.
*Where the relaxation has a gap: shares at the leaves* (**[M]**: the division's workstream P7,
SCI-RES-0014, at our request — exact certificates in integers of `2⁻⁴⁰` kcal/mol on its
measured constants, accepted by our `verify` when Lean's evaluator runs it, which is an
execution of the function and not a theorem; not re-computed by us).  The five analyses
with an integrality gap are four models.  Branching on one site certifies four of the
five (9, 21 and 13 leaves, or 2, 2 and 3 leaf certificates if children may share a leaf);
the fifth is certified by no single site and by a tree of depth two with three leaves.
One triplet constraint closes the gap in three of the five, two triplets in the others.
Over 1 732 pairwise models on its enumerated instances 18 have a gap (1.0 %), 17 of them
certified at depth one.  So "shares at the leaves" is a term of the certificate algebra
that exists — `branch` and `leaf`; a triplet certificate is a `sum` over three-site
instances — and one `branch` on a site with pairwise leaves certifies exactly what the
relaxation with the triplet constraints of all triples through that site certifies (the
division's Proposition P7.3, the first step of a lift-and-project hierarchy; its paper
proof, not re-derived by us).  Two things the format lacked are machine-checked now.
(i) **A domain-split rule** (`SCert`, `verifyS`, `verifyS_sound` **[V]**, `SplitRule.lean`, a layer
above the kernel that leaves `Cert` unchanged): a node with two children, one checked on
the box in which a site keeps the states of a list and one on the box in which it keeps
the others.  A leaf certificate for a box is one for every sub-box (`leafOK_mono`), so a
split of two leaves is accepted exactly when the `branch` with the two leaves repeated is
(`split_leaves_iff_branch`): the rule adds no proving power and saves checks — the division
measures a factor `3.8` to `6.7` on its instances.  On a frustrated triangle with three states
per site no single leaf is accepted for any bound above `0`, and a split of two leaves
certifies the minimum `1` (`splitTriangle_verified`, `splitTriangle_no_leaf`).
(ii) **Soundness for instances that store each pair table once** (`verify_sound_real_symm`,
`verify_sound_secondOrder_symm` **[V]**, `SymmetricPairHypothesis.lean`; the division's Lemma
P7.7): the published rational instance need only satisfy
`I.J i j a b + I.J j i b a ≤ M.J i j a b + M.J j i b a` for `i ≠ j` — the energy and the leaf check see the
two orientations only through their sum — whereas the termwise hypothesis of
`verify_sound_secondOrder` fails for such an instance against the lower model wherever a
constant is positive (`symm_hypothesis_witness`).  What is still missing is evaluation:
inside the Lean kernel the function `verify` as written does not reach these sizes (the
division: 512 table entries exhausted 11.9 GB), but that is a property of its encoding,
not of the kernel.  An integer re-implementation of one leaf check, written for kernel
evaluation — tables packed into natural numbers and read hierarchically — is evaluated
by `decide +kernel` on `147 456` table entries in `13.5` seconds and `1.6` GB, without any axiom,
while arrays with indexed reads exceed `5` GB at `1 024` entries (**[M]**: a measurement,
`experiments/coordinator_checks/kernel_eval/`, five encodings, negative controls).  The
theorem that such an integer checker implies the leaf check of the kernel for the decoded
instance has not been written; until it is, an accepted certificate is the output of a
compiled checker with `verify_sound` as its specification, not a kernel theorem (§12, item 7).

**Proposition 11.18c (domains with pairwise exclusions: what replaces the product) [P; N,
harness XI.18; an answer to request P2-T3 of the Scientific Discovery Division,
SCI-MSG-0015].**  Let `D ⊆ Π_iS_i` be a domain — for instance a product minus forbidden pairs
of states (clashes) — with `x₀ ∈ D`.  Call `D` *reset-closed at `x₀`* if with every configuration
it contains every configuration obtained from it by resetting some of its changed sites
to the reference.
(a) *On a reset-closed domain the bounds and the sufficient conditions survive; the
completeness of shares does not.*  Theorems 11.16, 11.17, 11.18, 11.18a and the sufficient
directions of Proposition 11.18b — (a), (d), (e): shares imply that `x₀` minimises the lower
model, now over `D` — hold for functions that are defined on `D` only, with constants that
bound the mixed differences over those rectangles (boxes) only that lie inside `D`: their
proofs evaluate `g` at configurations "`x` on a set of its changed sites, the reference
elsewhere" and nowhere else, and the least member of the class on a product restricts to a
member of the class on `D`.  (The Lean statements are for full products; this extension
is on paper.)  **The completeness part (b) of Proposition 11.18b fails on `D`** — *found by the
Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0012 §3; our first version claimed Proposition 11.18b
here without restriction.*  Two sites with states `{0, 1, 2}`, `x₀ = (0, 0)`, `D` the product minus
the pair of states `(1, 1)`; an additive known part with excitation energies `(1, 10)` at both
sites, zero star data, `c₁₂ = 3`.  The least member of the class on `D` is `−3` where both sites
are changed, so the lower model lies `8, 8, 17` above its value at `x₀` at `(1, 2)`, `(2, 1)`,
`(2, 2)`: `x₀` is certified for every member.  But `Δ₁ + Δ₂ = 2 < 3`: the set of both sites is
over-dense and no shares exist.  "The worst state of a site is its cheapest one" needs the
cheapest states of several sites to be admissible together.  (Harness XI.21, with the class
on `D` as a linear programme; on random domains of three sites the criterion held without
shares in 10 of 100.)
(b) *The largest reset-closed part.*  For pairwise exclusions,
`D′ := {x ∈ D : every changed state of x is compatible with the reference state of every other site}`
is reset-closed, and every reset-closed subset of `D` lies in it (a reset-closed set
contains with `x` the star points of its changed states).  Every product of site sets
that contains `x₀` and lies in `D` is reset-closed.
(c) *Connectivity is not the right condition.*  `D = {00, 01, 11}` is connected by
single-site moves and contains no rectangle; so the second-order class on `D`, with any
constants, contains every function, and the value at `11` is not constrained by the
values on the star `{00, 01}`.  What star and ball data at `x₀` can certify is the minimum
over `D′`.  A configuration of `D ∖ D′` contains a state that clashes with the reference at
another site, which must change with it; no configuration of `D′` contains that state, so
adding any multiple of its indicator — a function of one site — to `g` changes no value on
`D′` and no mixed difference of order two or more: at every point of `D ∖ D′` the class with all
values on `D′` fixed is unbounded below, for every order and all constants (the division's
strengthening, SCI-REV-0012 §3).  For these configurations there are two remedies, neither
free: **merge** the two sites into one — the pair of states becomes a single-site state,
alphabets multiply, and the constants must be bounded for the merged variables — or use
**further references**, a cover of `D` by reset-closed pieces `D′(x₀^{(r)})`, each with its own
data and its own lower model, the certified bound being the least of the pieces' bounds.
*Proof.*  (a) For `x ∈ D` with changed sites `i₁, …, i_m` put `y_k := x` on `{i₁, …, i_k}`, reference
elsewhere.  Then `g(x) − g(x₀) − Σ_k[g(x₀^{i_k → x}) − g(x₀)] = Σ_{l<k}`(second mixed difference over
`i_l, i_k` at the base `y_{l−1}`), and the four corners of each of these rectangles are
resets of `x`; this is the proof of Theorem 11.16, and the induction of Theorem 11.18 uses
resets of `x` in the same way.  (b) Two sites of a reset of `x` carry two states of `x`, or a
state of `x` and a reference state, or two reference states; each pair is allowed.  ∎
*Numbers* (**[N]**, harness XI.18, full mode): 66 random domains with 3 to 5 sites and 2 or 3
states; `D` itself failed to be reset-closed in 43 of them; on `D′` the second- and
third-order remainder bounds held at all 1226 points, with equality attained.  In the
division's measurement the theorems were applied "on greedily pruned clash-free products"
— covered by (b), as products.  Our first version added "and what the pruning discards is
the set that (c) is about"; that was wrong as a description, and the division has since
measured it (SCI-REV-0012 §5, a correction of its own SCI-MSG-0015): the pruned product is
strictly smaller than `D′` in 34 of its 40 analyses with a non-product domain (a median of
79 % of it), and **in 14 of the 40 the minimum of the clash-free domain is not in the
pruned product** — for phenylalanine on a strand it lies 2 to 13 kcal/mol lower.  A
certificate over a pruned product is a certificate of the minimum over that product and of
nothing else.  The better choice is the reference first, then the domain: at the minimiser
`x*` of the clash-free domain, on `D′(x*)`, the star certifies in 13 of the 40 analyses and
the pair form of Theorem 11.18a in 30 of 34.

**Theorem 11.18d (the remainder of the anchored expansion as an identity; anchored
constants; shares of every level) [V] (`AnchoredRemainder.lean`, `DownClosedRemainder.lean`,
`ShareLevels.lean`, `TermOrders.lean`; harness XI.19, XI.23, XI.24).**
*Parts (a) and (b) are Proposition 1 of the Scientific Discovery Division's workstream P3
and its "Consequently", part (c) its allocation lemma, part (d) in the site-penalty form
the bracketed option of its Theorem 5 (SCI-MSG-0020); parts (a′) and (b′) are Propositions
10 and 11 of its workstream P5 (SCI-MSG-0024); the pair and triple forms of (c′) with a band
are Lemmas A, A′ and B of its workstream P6 (SCI-MSG-0025).  All are machine-checked here
at its requests P3-T1, P5-T2, P6-T1; the Lean proofs are ours and follow the induction of
Theorem 11.18.  (The first version of this sentence named (a) and (c) only — its review
SCI-REV-0013, m9.)*  Order the sites linearly, in
any way.  For a configuration `y` with changed sites `S` and for `T ⊆ S` let `z_T(y)` be the
configuration that equals `y` at the changed sites before the first site of `T` and the
reference `x₀` everywhere else, and let `Δ_T g(z; y_T)` be the mixed difference of `g` over
`T` at the base point `z` with target states `y`.
(a) *Identity* (`anchored_remainder_identity`).  For every function `g`, reference, `y` and
order `m ≥ 0`:

    g(y) − I_{m−1}g(y)  =  Σ_{T ⊆ S, |T| = m}  Δ_T g(z_T(y); y_T).

The base point equals the reference on `T` and at every site after the first site of `T`
(`remainderBase_on`, `remainderBase_of_not_before`).  (By symmetry the identity also holds
with "after the last site of `T`" — a mutation of the harness that we first took for a
false statement.)
(a′) *Any down-closed family of evaluated subsets* (`downClosed_remainder_identity`,
`downClosed_remainder_bound`; the division's Proposition 10).  Let `𝒟` be a family of sets
of sites that contains every subset of each of its members, and call `T` a *threshold set*
of `𝒟` if `T ∉ 𝒟` and `T` without its first site is in `𝒟`.  Then

    g(y) − Σ_{U ∈ 𝒟, U ⊆ S} Δ_U g(x₀; y_U)  =  Σ_{T ⊆ S, T a threshold set}  Δ_T g(z_T(y); y_T),

with the same base points, and the left side is bounded by the anchored constants of the
threshold sets.  For `𝒟 = {|U| < m}` the threshold sets are the `m`-subsets and this is (a)
(`isThreshold_card_lt_iff`, `downClosed_remainder_card_lt`).  So different orders may be
used for near and for far sites.  The division built the lemma for a certificate "exact
inside a window, bounds outside", found that for its solvent model the many-body terms
are too long-ranged for that (triples spanning sixteen residues still carry bounds of
0.01–0.2 kcal/mol each), and reports it as correct and so far unused.
(a″) *Every term in its own order* (`anchored_remainder_identity_orders`,
`anchored_remainder_bound_orders`, `anchored_remainder_bound_hosts`, `term_orders_sharp`,
`term_orders_sharp_host_moves` in `TermOrders.lean`; the statement is Theorem AH of the
division's workstream P8, SCI-MSG-0027, with the hypothesis as its coordinator sharpened
it; machine-checked here at its request P8-T1, the Lean proofs ours).  The order enters
the identity through the base points only, and the interpolant is additive in the
function.  So if `g = Σ_τ g_τ` and every term is given its own linear order of the sites,

    g(y) − I_{m−1}g(y)  =  Σ_τ Σ_{T ⊆ S, |T| = m}  Δ_T g_τ(z^τ_T(y); y_T),

`z^τ_T` the base point of the order of `τ`.  If a term has a set `H_τ` of at most `m` *hosts*
— sites on whose states its constants depend strongly — and its order puts them last,
then every host outside `T` is at the reference in every configuration that enters the
mixed difference over `T` (`remainderBase_host_anchor`, `card_after_lt_of_hosts_last`: fewer
than `m = |T|` sites follow a host, so it cannot precede all of `T`).  Hence
`|g(y) − I_{m−1}g(y)| ≤ Σ_τ Σ_{T ⊆ S, |T| = m} c_{τ,T}` for constants that bound the mixed
differences of `g_τ` over `T` at the base points that agree with the reference on `T` **and
at the hosts of `τ` outside `T`**: no maximum over the states of a host outside `T`.  In
the form without an order: for terms with at most `m` hosts each
(`anchored_remainder_bound_hosts`; every set of sites can be put last).  **`m` hosts cannot
be replaced by `m + 1`**: for the triple coupling on three binary sites with all three
sites as hosts and `m = 2` the host-anchored constants are `0` and the remainder is `1`,
and whatever the order a host outside some pair leaves the reference (harness XI.24
tests the identity with random orders, the bound, and three false variants — the anchor
context alone, `m + 1` hosts, hosts and non-hosts exchanged — on functions built to break
them).  *What it is for* (the division's finding and numbers, SCI-MSG-0027 §1): a pair
term of its solvent model moves with the side chains that host its atoms, and bounding
each ingredient by its maximum over all host states separately lost factors of 12 to 313
on head-to-head pairs of a charged sequence; with the maximum taken after the bound is
assembled, and hosts kept at the anchor, its order-`m` constants for a twelve-residue
lysine sequence fall from `689, 145, 23` to `34.0, 2.40, 0.136` `k_BT` at orders 4, 5, 6 —
most of it from the state-wise maximum, 4 to 7 per cent from this identity.
(b) *Anchored constants* (`anchored_remainder_bound`).  Hence
`|g(y) − I_{m−1}g(y)| ≤ Σ_{T ⊆ S, |T| = m} c_T` as soon as `c_T` bounds the mixed differences over
`T` at the base points that agree with the reference on `T` — not at all base points, as
Theorem 11.18 asks.  For two states per site the two kinds of constants coincide (a
one-line argument on paper, and **[N]**); for three or more the anchored ones can be
strictly smaller (**[N]**: for 85 of the sets `T` met in harness XI.19, full mode — all of
them with three states per site, the largest alphabet that test uses).
(b′) *A mixed difference in an arbitrary context* (`mixedDiff_context_identity`,
`mixedDiff_context_bound`; the division's Proposition 11).  For a context `z` that agrees
with the reference on `T`, the difference `Δ_T g(z; y_T) − Δ_T g(x₀; y_T)` is a sum over the
changed sites `j` of `z` of mixed differences over `T ∪ {j}` at base points that agree with
the reference on `T ∪ {j}`; hence

    sup_z |Δ_T g(z; y_T)|   ≤   |Δ_T g(x₀; y_T)|  +  Σ_{j ∉ T} c_{T ∪ {j}}

with anchored constants on the right.  The first term is the signed value at the
reference and costs the evaluations of the next order; the second is paid with the
constants of the next order, once for each of the `m + 1` sites after summing over `T`.  It
is why the division concludes that a certificate "signed at the reference, bounds for the
rest" is dominated by the plain recipe one order higher (§12 item 13(a)).
(c) *Allocation at order `m`* (`cover_of_site_shares_order`, `cover_of_equal_shares`).  If
every constant `c_T ≥ 0` is split among the sites of `T`, the constants of the `m`-subsets of
any set of sites add up to at most the shares carried by its sites.  With equal shares,
`γ_i = (1/m)·Σ_{T ∋ i, |T| = m} c_T`: `Σ_{T ⊆ S, |T| = m} c_T ≤ Σ_{i∈S} γ_i`, with equality for the set
of all sites (the case `k = 1`, `S` everything, of the counting form below).
(c′) *Shares of every level* (`sum_levelShare_eq`, `cover_of_level_shares`,
`level_shares_antitone`, `level_window_cover`, `level_window_le`, `cover_of_subset_shares`).
Charge each constant in equal parts to the `k`-subsets of `T` instead of its sites,
`γ^{(k)}_K = Σ_{T ⊇ K} c_T / C(m, k)`.  By counting,

    pen_k(S) := Σ_{K ⊆ S, |K| = k} γ^{(k)}_K  =  Σ_T c_T · C(|T ∩ S|, k) / C(m, k) :

a subset with `t` of its `m` sites changed is charged the fraction `C(t, k)/C(m, k)` of its
constant, and for constants that are nonnegative on the `m`-subsets

    Σ_{T ⊆ S} c_T  =  pen_m(S)  ≤  pen_{m−1}(S)  ≤  …  ≤  pen_2(S)  ≤  pen_1(S)  ≤  pen_0  =  Σ_T c_T

pointwise in `S` (`C(t, k+1)·C(m, k) ≤ C(t, k)·C(m, k+1)` for `t ≤ m`): level `m` is the envelope
itself, level 1 the site penalties of (c), level 0 the constant bound.  The shares of
level `k + 1` outside any window may be pushed down in equal parts to their `k`-subsets;
the result lies between the two levels (double counting,
`sum_superset_levelShare_succ`: the shares of the `(k+1)`-sets that contain `K` add up to
`k + 1` times the share of `K`).  And the shares need not be equal: any nonnegative `λ_{T,K}`
with `Σ_{K ⊆ T} λ_{T,K} ≥ c_T` cover — the allocation is free, and Proposition 11.18f says how
to choose it.  The pair form at `m = 3` is Theorem 11.18a(c); pairs and triples at order `m`
with a band along the chain are the division's Lemmas A, A′ and B, with which its
certificate at twenty residues needs order 4 where the site form needed 5 (SCI-MSG-0025:
`0.055` nats from 9 921 evaluations with triples, where sites give `1.74`).
(d) *A sandwich from the Hamming ball* (`anchored_remainder_site_penalties`).

    I_{m−1}g(y) − Σ_{i∈S} γ_i   ≤   g(y)   ≤   I_{m−1}g(y) + Σ_{i∈S} γ_i :

two functions that use `g` on the Hamming ball of radius `m − 1` only; the same holds with
the shares of any level, with a window, and with any allocation in place of the site
penalties (`anchored_remainder_level_shares`, `anchored_remainder_window_shares`,
`anchored_remainder_subset_shares`).  For `m = 3` the lower
one is the site form of Theorem 11.18a with anchored constants.  For `m ≥ 4` the two
functions are not pairwise — they contain the evaluated terms of orders `3, …, m − 1`; the
division's certificate replaces those, and the pairs beyond a band along the chain, by
pointwise minorants and majorants and so obtains two banded pairwise models with exact
partition functions (its Theorem 5: its own paper proof, not checked here).
(d′) *The anchored split of a pair table* (`anchoredSplit_row`, `anchoredSplit_col`,
`anchoredSplit_sandwich`, `anchoredSplit_sandwich_extrema`, `anchoredSplit_exact_at_anchor`
in `TermOrders.lean`; the division's, SCI-MSG-0027 §3, request A18-T1; two lines).  A pair
table `P(x_i, x_j)` that a banded model cannot keep has to be replaced by one-site
functions.  With the anchor states `x⁰_i`, `x⁰_j` put `A(x_i) = P(x_i, x⁰_j)`,
`B(x_j) = P(x⁰_i, x_j) − P(x⁰_i, x⁰_j)` and `D = P − A − B`.  Then `D` vanishes on the anchor
row and on the anchor column, and

    A(x_i) + B(x_j) + min_{x_j} D(x_i, ·)   ≤   P(x_i, x_j)   ≤   A(x_i) + B(x_j) + max_{x_j} D(x_i, ·),

**exact whenever `x_i = x⁰_i`**.  By Proposition 11.113b(a) the pair then costs the bracket
about `P(x_i ≠ x⁰_i)·range(D)`: keep the site that moves less.  A split by column means is
exact nowhere — the non-additive part of a far pair is then paid in the anchor state
itself.  (The division: on its charged twelve-residue instance this takes the certified
bracket from `0.19` to `0.057` nats, three quarters of the old bracket having been ten
pairs of charged side chains beyond the band; an apolar sequence gains nothing.  The
first-order-optimal split against given site marginals is a transport problem — its
remark, not built.)
*Not machine-checked and not checked by us:* how constants `c_T` are obtained for a given
energy term — the division's chain rule for mixed differences, its term-by-term bound
for a generalised-Born term with interval enclosures of derivatives, and its closed form
for the sum over all `m`-subsets.

**Proposition 11.18e (the Hamming ball is necessary for a deterministic certificate) [P;
the core of (b) V; (b′)(ii) C; harness XI.20, XI.22] (an answer to the division's question
P3-T4; part (b) corrected, and (c) sharpened, by its review SCI-REV-0013).**  Let `k_i` be
the number of states of site `i`, and call a function *of order below `m`* if it is a sum
of functions of fewer than `m` sites each.  These functions form a space of dimension
`N_ball = Σ_{|U| < m} Π_{i∈U}(k_i − 1)` — the number of configurations with fewer than `m` changed
sites — and the evaluations on the Hamming ball of radius `m − 1` around any reference are
unisolvent for it.  Let `𝒢` be a class of residuals that is closed under adding functions
of order below `m`: the class of all functions with given order-`m` constants, uniform or
anchored, and no a-priori bound on the terms of lower order is one.
(a) Every deterministic algorithm, adaptive or not, that returns a finite lower bound for
`min(E₀ + g)` or a bracket of finite width for `ln Z`, valid for every `g ∈ 𝒢`, evaluates `g` at
no fewer than `N_ball` configurations — on every input.  (If on some `g` it evaluates fewer,
some function `h ≢ 0` of order below `m` vanishes at all the configurations it evaluated;
`g + th ∈ 𝒢` for every real `t`, the algorithm sees the same values and returns the same
answer, and `min(E₀ + g + th) → −∞` as `t → +∞` or as `t → −∞`.)  The ball attains the count,
and so does every other unisolvent set: what is necessary is the number, not the shape.
(b) *Randomised algorithms without a hint: what is asked decides* (**corrected at the
nineteenth checkpoint; the correction, the counter-algorithm and its machine-checked core
are the Scientific Discovery Division's, review SCI-REV-0013, finding M1**).  The first
version claimed the count of (a) for randomised algorithms as well,
`sup_{g∈𝒢} E|Q(g)| ≥ (1 − δ)·N_ball − o(1)`, with a sketch: under a Gaussian prior of large
variance the target keeps a spread that grows with the variance.  **For the task of (a)
that is false.**  Let `ρ` be the least support fraction of (c).  There is
`c = c(k₁, …, k_n; m) > 0` such that every function `h` of order below `m` satisfies
`|h(x)| ≥ c·‖h‖_∞` on at least the fraction `ρ` of the configurations (compactness on the
unit sphere of a finite-dimensional space).  Write `g = h + R` with `h = I_{m−1}g` and
`|R| ≤ C := Σ_T c_T` (Theorem 11.18d), draw `q = ⌈ln(1/δ)/−ln(1 − ρ)⌉` uniformly random
configurations and put `B = (max_j |g(x^j)| + C)/c + C`.  With probability at least `1 − δ`
one of them has `|h| ≥ c‖h‖_∞`, and then `‖g‖_∞ ≤ B`: `min E₀ − B` bounds the minimum from
below and `|ln Z(E₀ + g) − ln Z(E₀)| ≤ B` — finite, valid with probability `1 − δ` on every
member, from at most `⌈k^{m−1} ln(1/δ)⌉` evaluations **whatever the number of sites**.  On the
cube with `m = 2`: `c = 1/(n + 1)` and `ρ = ½` — the largest of the `n + 1` coefficients of an
affine function is at least `‖h‖_∞/(n + 1)`, and flipping its site (all sites, if it is the
constant) pairs the points so that one point of every pair is at least that large
(**[V]** `ScienceR12.affine_half_large`, the division's file, adopted as `AffineHalf.lean`) —
so **five random evaluations at `δ = 0.05` do what costs a deterministic algorithm `n + 1`**
(harness XI.22: the half is attained by `1 + s₁`, `n + 1` cannot be replaced by `n`, the
bound `B` is attained, and at a point where `h` is small it fails).  The sketch failed
because a growing spread does not prevent a valid bound that scales with the observed
values: in (a) the adversary chooses the hidden direction after the evaluation set, and a
random set defeats every fixed direction with probability `ρ` per point.  The bound is
valid and useless — `c` is small — so **the count `N_ball` is a statement about
deterministic certificates**, and nothing here makes a useful certificate cheaper
(`DEAD_ENDS.md` D60).
(b′) *What remains true, and what is open.*  (i) **[P]** (**reviewed by the Scientific
Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0015: correct; the weaker hypothesis, the conditions on
"attained" and the last paragraph are its findings m1–m3.**)  Where, for every `g ∈ 𝒢`
and every state `a`, the class contains `g − D·1_a` for arbitrarily large `D` — in
particular where it is closed under adding *every* function, `m > n` (one site with `k`
states and `m ≥ 2` is the case `n = 1`); a box class without a floor is another such class
— the count holds for randomised algorithms on every instance, even for a bracket of
unspecified width: if a state `a` is not evaluated, the run is the same on `g` and on `g`
with a needle of depth `D` at `a`, for which the returned bracket is invalid once `D`
exceeds its upper end (this uses that the returned upper end of the bracket of `ln Z`, or
the returned lower bound of the minimum, is finite; a run that returns no finite bound
counts as a failure); so `P_g(a` is not evaluated`) ≤ δ` for every `a` and every `g`, and
`E|Q(g)| ≥ (1 − δ)·|X|`, `|Q(g)|` the number of distinct states evaluated.  The bound is
attained on every instance, for every width and every `δ`, by the trivial mixture "with
probability `δ` evaluate nothing, otherwise everything".  For `kδ ≤ 1` it is also attained
by skipping one uniformly random state with probability `kδ`, provided the bracket
returned after a skip is wrong for at most one skipped state — the failure probability
of that algorithm is `δ` times the number of states whose omission makes the returned
bracket wrong.  For the minimum, the lower bound "least evaluated value minus `w`" does
it with any slack `w ≥ 0`.  For `ln Z` the bracket `[ln Σ_{x≠a}e^{−g(x)}, the same + W]` needs
`W ≥ ln 2`: it is wrong iff `a` carries more than the fraction `1 − e^{−W}` of `Z`, which at most
`min(k, ⌈1/(1 − e^{−W})⌉ − 1)` states can do — one when `W ≥ ln 2`; with two equally deep
states and a smaller width both skips fail and the failure probability is `2δ`, and with
`k` equal states and `W < ln(k/(k − 1))` it is `kδ` (the division's remark on a first reading,
SCI-RES-0016 §3, and the general count of its review — conditions on the attaining
algorithm, not on the count, since the task leaves the width free; harness XI.22(d)).
*With needles of finitely many depths* (the division's addition A1, re-derived): if the
class contains, with `g`, needles at `a` of `L` depths such that no output is valid for two
of the `L + 1` instances, then `P_g(a` is not evaluated`) ≤ δ(L + 1)/L` — on that event the run
and its output are the same on all `L + 1` instances, the output is valid for at most one
of them and invalid with probability at most `δ` on each.
*The saving of (b) on more than one site comes from evaluations outside the ball* — a
consequence of the proof of (i), not of its statement (on several sites with `m ≤ n` the
class does not contain the needles).  An algorithm that evaluates only inside a fixed
unisolvent set `B` — the ball, say — has `P_g(a` is not evaluated`) ≤ δ` for every `a ∈ B`,
hence `E|Q(g)| ≥ (1 − δ)·N_ball`: let `h_a` be the function of order below `m` that is `1` at `a`
and `0` on the rest of `B` (it exists because `B` is unisolvent); if `a` is not evaluated the
run is the same on `g` and on `g + t·h_a`, and `min(E₀ + g + t·h_a) → −∞` as `t → −∞`.  A function
of order below `m` cannot hide from a random point; inside a unisolvent set it can, as a
needle does.  (ii) **[C]** For a bracket of *prescribed* width we conjecture
`sup_{g∈𝒢} E|Q(g)| ≥ (1 − δ)·N_ball − o(1)` (the division's formulation).  A Gaussian prior
does not prove it: for one site with two states and independent Gaussian values, stopping
after one evaluation whenever its value is so low that the other state is higher with
posterior probability near one fails with average probability `Φ(−a)²/2` while stopping
early with probability `Φ(−a)` — an average count of `2 − √(2δ)`, below `2(1 − δ)`, which
(i) forbids instance by instance.  A proof needs the argument of (i) for hidden
directions that are not needles, or a prior under which no transcript with a hidden
direction is confident.  (On two binary sites with `m = 2`, any two evaluation points
contain the minimiser for two of the four sign patterns of large coefficients and miss
it for the other two: a hidden direction should halve the probability of being right.)
*An outline for `n` binary sites at order two, which would give
`sup_g E|Q(g)| ≥ (1 − 2δ)(n + 1) − o(1)`* (the coordinator's; its combinatorial steps are
verified exactly, its measure-theoretic steps are not written out).  `h = α + β·s`; for
large coefficients `ln Z ≈ −min h`, attained at `x* = −sign β`.  *Prior:* independent
symmetric coefficients whose magnitudes are log-uniform over a range `e^Λ` above a cutoff
far beyond the prescribed width, and a constant term spread far wider; with probability
`1 − o(1)` the magnitudes are pairwise separated by any fixed factor.  An algorithm that
stops with fewer than `n + 1` affinely independent evaluations may be given further ones
until exactly one direction `ν` is hidden (`ν` orthogonal to the differences `x^j − x¹`); then
`min h` is a known combination of the observed values iff `ν·x* = ν·x¹` — call this event
`S`.  *Pairing:* let `k` minimise `|β_k/ν_k|` over the support of `ν`, `t = −2β_k/ν_k`,
`β′ = β + tν`, `α′ = α − tν·x¹`.  Then `(α′, β′)` has the same transcript; `β′` has the signs of
`β` except at `k`; the map is an involution — a reflection of the hidden coordinate — that
changes the other magnitudes, hence the prior density, by a factor `1 + o(1)`; and it maps
`S` into its complement, because `ν·x*` changes by `2ν_k x*_k ≠ 0`.  Hence
`P(S | transcript) ≤ ½ + o(1)`; off `S` the minimum moves along the hidden direction with a
non-zero slope, so one output is right there with vanishing posterior probability; and
an algorithm that is right with probability `1 − δ` stops early with probability at most
`2δ + o(1)` under this prior.  The combinatorial steps — same transcript, involution, `S`
into its complement, different minima on `S` — hold in all 41 786 cases with separated
magnitudes among 72 000 exact random cases on cubes with two to seven sites, and the
frequency of `S` is at most `½` within noise for each of 180 evaluation sets
(`experiments/coordinator_checks/random_ball/pairing_check.py`).  Not written out: the
cutoffs of the prior, the "lucky" outputs off `S`, the passage from `ln Z` to the minimum,
any order above two, any alphabet beyond two states.  **Until they are, (ii) is a
conjecture.**
(c) With a hint the count does not apply.  A function of order below `m` that is not
identically zero is non-zero on a fraction at least `1/Π(m − 1 largest k_i)` of the
configurations — `k^{−(m−1)}` for `k` states at every site — and this is attained by the
indicator of a cylinder on the `m − 1` largest sites.  (Induction on the number of sites,
as for the Schwartz–Zippel lemma: if no slice in the last site vanishes identically, each
slice has the bound of the remaining sites; if one does, the differences of the other
slices with it have order below `m − 1` on the remaining sites.  The form for unequal
alphabets and its proof are the division's, review SCI-REV-0013, m8; `k_max^{−(m−1)}` is
valid and then not attained.  Exhaustively verified on eight small grids, harness
XI.22(c).)  So if the order-`m` constants
vanish — the residual *is* of order below `m` — a hinted residual of order below `m` is
refuted, if it is wrong, with probability `1 − δ` by `⌈k^{m−1} ln(1/δ)⌉` evaluations at
uniformly random configurations, whatever the number of sites.  With non-zero constants
the comparison needs a tolerance, and the hinted count is open.
For `m = 2`, (a) says that the star of Theorem 11.16 — the reference and one evaluation per
site and non-reference state — cannot be undercut by any deterministic algorithm on a
second-order class without a-priori bounds on the first-order terms.  A-priori bounds on
the lower orders change the picture: then fewer evaluations may do, at the price of the
exponents of §§11.9–11.20.

**Proposition 11.18f (which shares: the allocation for a law) [P; harness XI.23] (an answer
to the division's question P5-T3, SCI-MSG-0024; elementary convexity, nothing claimed
new).**  Fix constants `c_T ≥ 0` on the `m`-subsets, a level `k`, and a law `P` of the changed
set `S` — for a certificate, the law of `S` under the Gibbs measure of the evaluated model
`A`, which is known.  An *allocation* is a family `λ_{T,K} ≥ 0` (`K ⊆ T`, `|K| = k`) with
`Σ_K λ_{T,K} = c_T`; its penalty `pen_λ(S) = Σ_{K ⊆ S} Σ_{T ⊇ K} λ_{T,K}` covers (Theorem
11.18d(c′)) and is linear in `λ`.  With `m_∓ = A ∓ pen_λ` the two ends of the bracket of `ln Z`
are `ln Z(A) + U(λ)` and `ln Z(A) − L(λ)`,

    U(λ) = ln E_P e^{pen_λ(S)},          L(λ) = −ln E_P e^{−pen_λ(S)}.

(a) *The cost depends on the changed set only.*  The cost number of Theorem 11.110(e) at
the model is `E_P e^{pen(S)} − 1 = Σ_S P(S)(e^{pen(S)} − 1)`; for independent sites and site
penalties it is `Π_i (1 + p_i(e^{γ_i} − 1)) − 1`, the division's formula.  A penalty of level
`k` vanishes on sets with fewer than `k` changed sites, so in a nearly frozen ensemble — `p`
the probability that a site is off its anchor — the cost is of order `p^k`: the division's
observation that sites, pairs and triples cost about `Γp`, `Γp²`, `Γp³`.  For independent
sites with a common `p` and equal shares the mean penalty of level `k` is exactly `p^k·Γ`
(by the counting form of Theorem 11.18d(c′) and the `k`-th factorial moment of a binomial
variable), so a narrow bracket is about `2p^kΓ` wide — the law the division then measured
on its enumerated instances, within 0.97 to 1.09 wherever the site bracket is below half
a nat (its addendum A17 (15), read by us in part), with the design rule "level `k` at
order `m` reaches `ε` when `2p^kΓ_m ≲ ε`".
(b) *The upper end is convex and the lower end concave* in `λ`, with
`∂U/∂λ_{T,K} = P⁺_λ(K ⊆ S)`, the probability that `K` is changed under the tilted law
`P⁺_λ ∝ P·e^{pen_λ}` (for `L`: under `P·e^{−pen_λ}`).  Hence an allocation minimises `U` iff every
constant sits on those `k`-subsets of its `T` that are least often changed under `P⁺_λ` — on
an exchangeable instance: equal shares, the choice of Theorem 11.18a and of the division
— while **the minimum of `L` is attained at a vertex — at an ordering vertex: every
constant charged to the first `k`-subset of its `T` in one linear order of the
`k`-subsets** (`pen_λ` depends on `λ` only through the charges `μ_K = Σ_{T ⊇ K} λ_{T,K}`; the
achievable charge vectors form a sum of simplices — the base polytope of a polymatroid —
whose vertices are given by the linear orders; and `L` is concave in `μ`.  The precision
"an ordering vertex" is the Scientific Discovery Division's, review SCI-REV-0015, m6).
Not every vertex is a local minimum — up to ties a vertex is one iff every constant sits
on the `k`-subset of its `T` that is least often changed under the tilted law `P·e^{−pen}` of
the vertex itself — and there can be many local minima (the division counted between 1
and 60 among the 59 049 vertices of small instances).  For independent sites and
exchangeable constants the order "most frozen first" is the global minimiser of `L`; in
general finding the best order is a search — it contains a minimum-weight hitting-set
problem (the division's two statements, not re-derived by us).  The two ends want
different allocations, and each may have its own.
(c) *First order.*  To first order in the constants both ends are
`Σ_T Σ_K λ_{T,K}·P(K ⊆ S)`: **charge every constant to its least probable sub-pattern.**  For
independent sites and `k = 1` that is the most frozen site of `T`, and the penalties are
differences of one function on nested sets of sites: with the sites in a linear order
by `p_i` (ties broken in any fixed way) and `R_i` consisting of `i` and the sites after it
— the sites at least as mobile — `γ_i = Γ(R_i) − Γ(R_i ∖ {i})`, `Γ(R) = Σ_{T ⊆ R} c_T` — no subset
is enumerated wherever `Γ(R)` has a closed form (the division's Lemma B gives `Γ` with
sites excluded).  (Read with ties as `R_i = {j : p_j ≥ p_i}`, the formula charges a shared
constant to every tied site: a valid cover, not an allocation — in the first instance
of the numbers below `γ = (1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0)`, sum `4` against `Γ = 2`.  Where sites are tied
the first-order optimum is not unique and the two ends already disagree: the upper end
is least when the tied sites share a constant — `0.0259` against the vertex's `0.0298` in
that instance — the lower end when one of them takes it.  The division's review
SCI-REV-0015, m4.)
(c′) *The site allocations are the core of a convex game, and the rule of (c) is its
greedy vertex* (the Scientific Discovery Division's, SCI-RES-0017 §3 (iii); the
game-theoretic facts are classical — Shapley 1971 on the cores of convex games, Edmonds
1970 on the greedy rule — and are cited from memory by both divisions, opened by
neither).  `Γ(R) = Σ_{T ⊆ R} c_T` is supermodular; the level-one allocations
`γ_i = Σ_{T ∋ i} λ_{T,i}` are exactly the vectors with `Σ_i γ_i = Γ` and `Σ_{i∈R} γ_i ≥ Γ(R)` for
every `R` — the core of the game `Γ` — whose vertices are the marginal vectors of the
orderings, the formula of (c); equal shares are the Shapley value.  **Among all vectors
that cover the nested sets `R_j` of an ordering by nondecreasing `p`, the marginal vector
has the least first-order cost `Σ_i p_i γ_i`** — **[V]** `ScienceA17.greedy_optimal` (Abel
summation; written and machine-checked by the division, adopted unchanged as
`proofs/Frontiers/CoreGreedy.lean`; it uses the covering property on the nested sets
only).  Since `U` is convex in the penalties with the tilted site marginals as gradient,
the best upper end over the core is a convex programme whose linear oracle is the rule
of (c) applied to the tilted marginals (Frank–Wolfe: every step is a sort and `n + 1`
closed-form sums, so it runs beyond enumeration, and the duality gap bounds what any
site allocation can still gain), and the best lower end is an ordering.  The
floating-point allowance of the evaluated terms is a game of the same kind and is
allocated by the same rule (the division's §3 (v)).
*The pair level* (an answer to its question A17-T3; harness XI.23).  For a product law
the least probable pair of `T` is its two most frozen sites, and the pair penalties of
that vertex are second differences of the same function on sets of sites: with the sites
in the order of `p`, `i` before `j`, and `A_j` the sites after `j`,
`μ_{ij} = Γ(A_j ∪ {i, j}) − Γ(A_j ∪ {i}) − Γ(A_j ∪ {j}) + Γ(A_j)` — four closed-form sums per pair, no
subset enumerated.  For a law that is not a product — the tilted law of a pair model is
not — the linear oracle is the least probable pair of `T` in an arbitrary order of the
pairs, and the penalty of a pair is then a sum over the `m`-sets that contain it and are
independent in the graph of the earlier pairs: no closed form in general.  A vertex
induced by an order of the *sites* is always an allocation with the closed form above, so
a step that uses it keeps every bracket valid, and gives up only the duality gap.
(c″) *Beyond first order: the range of validity of "the most frozen site"* (the
division's review SCI-REV-0015, m5, and its measurement SCI-RES-0017 §3; the formulas
re-derived here).  For independent sites and level 1, with `f_i = ln((1 − p_i)/p_i)` the
free-energy cost of changing site `i` and `sp(z) = ln(1 + e^z)`:

    U = Σ_i [ sp(γ_i − f_i) − sp(−f_i) ],          L = Σ_i [ sp(−f_i) − sp(−f_i − γ_i) ] :

**the upper end sees the net cost `f_i − γ_i`, the lower end `f_i + γ_i`.**  A site with
penalty `γ_i` costs between `max(p_iγ_i, γ_i − ln(1/p_i))` and `p_i(e^{γ_i} − 1)` at the upper end —
beyond `ln(1/p_i)` a penalty is paid nat for nat — and at most `min(p_iγ_i, −ln(1 − p_i))` at the
lower end.  By (b), the vertex of (c) minimises `U` iff in every `T` the charged site still
has the largest `f_i − γ_i` of its `T`; the minimiser of `U` equalises `f − γ` over the sites
that share constants.  There is no bound of `U` at the vertex by a multiple of `U` at equal
shares (a tied pair with one constant `2 ln(1/p)`: about `ln(1/p)` against `2 ln 2`), while
at the lower end every allocation of level `k` is within the factor `C(m, k)` of equal
shares, for any law (`pen_λ ≤ C(m, k)·pen_equal` pointwise, and
`E e^{−C·pen} ≥ (E e^{−pen})^C`).  So **the rule is safe for the lower end and, for the upper
end, only while each charged site's penalty stays below its cost.**  On the division's
enumerated twelve-residue leucine helix (its numbers) the rule brings the lower end from
`0.5` nats to `2·10⁻⁵` at every order from 4 on and, at order 5, raises the upper end from
`3.2` nats to `8.6` — `20.2 k_BT` charged to a site whose cheapest change costs `14.1` — where
the convex optimum over the core gives `0.0075`.
*A bound that no site allocation can beat* (the division's, SCI-RES-0017 §3 (iv);
re-derived).  For any law of the changed set with site marginals `p_i`, and any site
penalties `γ ≥ 0`: `e^{Σ_{i∈S} γ_i} = Π_{i∈S}(1 + (e^{γ_i} − 1)) ≥ 1 + Σ_{i∈S}(e^{γ_i} − 1)`, so
`U ≥ ln(1 + Σ_i p_i(e^{γ_i} − 1))`; a covering vector has `Σ_i γ_i ≥ Γ`; and the minimum of the
right-hand side under that constraint is water-filling, `γ_i = ln(λ/p_i)⁺` with `λ` fixed by
`Σ_i ln(λ/p_i)⁺ = Γ` — each site is charged what its rarity can pay:

    U(γ)  ≥  ln( 1 + Σ_i (λ − p_i)⁺ )          for every covering vector of site penalties.

The site level can work only if `Γ` fits under the depths `ln(1/p_i)`; where it does, the
water-filling vector is the optimum to first order (it need not cover; on the division's
instance it does, and the bound, the closed-form vector and 2 000 Frank–Wolfe steps give
`0.00742`, `0.00744`, `0.00752` nats at order 5; harness XI.23).
*Numbers* (harness XI.23; exact enumeration; six sites, triples, equal constants).  Four
nearly frozen sites (`p = 0.01`) and two mobile ones (`p = 0.3`), constants `0.1`: equal site
shares give `(U, L) = (0.240, 0.189)`; charging every triple to its most frozen site
`(0.030, 0.014)` — the upper end 8 times and the lower end 13 times smaller, about what
equal *pair* shares give, `(0.016, 0.014)`; the envelope itself has `(0.0004, 0.0004)`.  A
homogeneous instance (`p = 0.05`, constants `0.5`): the vertex allocation raises the upper
end (`2.99` against `1.17`) and lowers the lower one (`0.159` against `0.248`), as (b) says.
**The level is the stronger lever; within a level the allocation matters where the sites
differ; and in evaluations neither matters — Proposition 11.113a.**

*Limitation: the remainder is quadratic in the distance* (second referee, M3; `DEAD_ENDS.md`
D32; harness `DEAD.13`).  The half-width of the star envelope, `Σ_{i<j changed} c_ij`, grows with
the square of the Hamming distance from the centre, and further evaluations of the same kind do
not remove this.  For `n` two-state sites with dense constants `c_ij = c`, the function
`−c·C(|x| − 1, 2)` belongs to the class, vanishes on the *whole Hamming ball of radius 2* around
`x₀ = 0` and equals `−c(w−1)(w−2)/2` at weight `w`; so with `f(x) = e|x|` and zero true residual
not even the `1 + n + C(n,2)` evaluations of that ball certify the minimiser once
`n ≥ 2e/c + 3`, and two stars at opposite corners do not once `n ≥ 6e/c + 6` (an explicit
member vanishing on both is given in the referee report).  A star certifies exactly when the
second-order sharp-minimum condition of Theorem 11.17 holds; for an additive known part a
sufficient condition is the **row-sum condition**
`½ Σ_{j ≠ i} c_ij ≤` (measured single-site excitation energy at site `i`, for every state)
**[V]** (`secondOrder_certified_of_rowSum`; on paper until the sixteenth checkpoint of cycle
10) — then `Σ_{i ∈ S} Δ_i ≥ ½ Σ_{i ∈ S} Σ_{j ∈ S, j ≠ i} c_ij = Σ_{i<j ∈ S} c_ij` for every set
`S` of changed sites.  It is the special case "equal shares" of the exact condition of
Proposition 11.18b, which is decidable by one maximum flow.  With non-sparse constants, star-type data lead back to a covering
problem, now with radius of order `(2·gap/c)^{1/2}`; other evaluation sets do not escape it —
around a residual whose second differences vanish, the uncertainty left by any set of
evaluations grows quadratically with the distance to the set (Theorem 11.31(a); §11.12,
with the remark after Theorem 11.32 on residuals that are not additive).

*The resulting picture.*  First-order envelope: uncertainty is a distance to the evaluated set,
information is tropical (a minimum over evaluations), certification is covering, and on product
landscapes (independent sites of fixed types, an additive residual with `κ < 1`) the price is
exponential unless the known part is sharp (Theorems 11.4, 11.9) — for every algorithm
(§11.10) — and for certificates of `ln Z` at sub-extensive accuracy also when it is sharp
(Theorem 11.15); with another envelope geometry the price can be lower (the RMSD envelope at
the zero residual, Theorem 11.38).
Second-order envelope with weak coupling (row sums of the constants below the
measured excitation energies): `n(k−1)+1` evaluations determine the additive part exactly, the
remainder is a pairwise function, and certification returns to the pairwise kernel, whose own
cost is governed by the proof-complexity results of §6.  Away from that regime the star is
re-centred at the incumbent — a trust-region scheme without a guarantee of termination by
itself (blueprint §6.6).  What dense constants cost, exactly, is the subject of §11.12: no set
of evaluations escapes the quadratic law, the price is exponential unless the excitation
energies are of the order of `c·n`, and the star is not the best choice of `n+1` evaluations.

### 11.8 A partition-function kernel with decomposition rules

The referee's fourth major point (§3.4) is repaired in `PartitionProduct.lean` by extending the
certificate type to `ZCert2` with two rules.

**Theorem 11.19 (cut rule) [V].**  For a set `S` of sites and bounds `lo ≤ W_ij ≤ hi`,
`lo ≥ 0`, on the pair factors across the cut,
`Λ · Z_S · Z_{Sᶜ} ≤ Z ≤ Υ · Z_S · Z_{Sᶜ}` with `Λ, Υ` the products of the bounds
(`WInstance.Z_cut`), with equality when the cut factors are identically one
(`WInstance.Z_cut_eq`).  The extended checker is sound (`zverify2_sound`, `zverify2Top_sound`).
On two disjoint frustrated triangles one cut and 16 leaves give the exact value `169/16`
(`twoTriangles_cut_exact`), while every certificate without decomposition rules whose lower end
is exact has at least `64` leaves (`cut_rule_separation`; in general at least the number of
configurations of the box for positive rigid instances, `zverify2_elementary_exact_leaves`).

**Theorem 11.20 (elimination rule) [V].**  A site with at most two neighbours can be summed out
exactly into a one-body factor of its neighbour or a pair factor between its two neighbours
(`WInstance.Z_elim1`, `WInstance.Z_elim2`).  For **every** chain-structured instance on `m+1`
sites with nonnegative factors the explicit transfer-matrix certificate — `m` eliminations and
one leaf — is accepted by the kernel with the exact partition sum (`zverify2Top_chainCert`,
`chainCert_leaves`).  If the factors are positive and the instance is rigid, every certificate
built from the elementary rules (leaf, branch, thermal prune) whose lower end is exact has at
least `k^{m+1}` leaves (`chain_separation`); for the two-state ferromagnetic chain this is
`1` against `2^{m+1}` for every length (`ferroChain_separation`; `elimination_separation` is
the kernel-evaluated case of six sites).  Trees and cycles reduce in the same way
(`tree_elim_exact`, `ring_elim_exact`); in general the rule is exact on every interaction graph
reducible by removing sites of degree at most two (treewidth at most two) **[P]**.

`chain_separation` is the finite-temperature counterpart of the tropical separation of §6.3,
proved on a *connected* family, with two reservations (second referee, M4; `DEAD_ENDS.md` D33).
*It concerns exact lower endpoints only*: a certificate whose lower end is `(1 − 10⁻⁹) Z` is
outside the theorem, although approximate enclosures are the normal case at finite
temperature; a robust version is open.  *Its hypothesis `WInstance.Rigid` is a property of the
representation, not of the model*: it asks that one of the two ordered factors `W_ij`, `W_ji`
distinguishes the states of a site, and the instance with `W₀₁(a,b) = 2^{a+2b}`,
`W₁₀(b,a) = 2^{−(a+2b)}` — two independent uniform sites, every configuration of weight one —
satisfies it, so that the theorem requires four leaves for it (`gauge_trivial_separation`).
What is measured in such a case is that the leaf rule bounds the two orientations of a pair
separately; a normalisation of the instance would remove it.  For the ferromagnetic chain the
interaction is genuine and the statement is as intended.  The tropical kernel's `sum` rule and
these two rules are the same idea in two semirings; what remains open is a lower bound for
certificates that *do* use decomposition rules on frustrated connected families, an
approximate version of the separation, and a comparison with proof systems for model counting.
Harness XI.12.

### 11.9 Probabilistic certificates: the sampled sandwich

The lower bounds of §11.6 concern deterministic certificates built from pointwise evaluations.
