`f(d) = d(1 + d)/((d(a − h) + a)(d + 2))` increasing in `d` with limit `1/(a − h)` (the gain itself is
a sawtooth in `d`, because of the ceiling in `J`); so more than
`κ = h·f(h/(a − h)) = h²a/((a−h)(a+h)(2a−h))` per level, the value at the start `d = h/(a − h)`.
Hence, for every `k ≥ 1`,

    τ_k − h  ≤  c₁/(k + c₂),      c₁ = h(1 + κ)/κ,    c₂ = (a + h)(2a − h)/(ha) − 2,      limsup_k k·(τ_k − h) ≤ a.

*Step II with numbers.*  For `0 < g < ε*` let `m_k = sup_{0<y≤g} (T_k − θ_hint)(y)` and `s = g + θ_hint(g)`.
For `y ≤ g`, (iii) gives `T_{k+1}(y) − θ_hint(y) ≤ (1 − y/s)·m_k`, and `θ_hint(y) ≥ h − y` gives
`T_{k+1}(y) − θ_hint(y) ≤ τ_{k+1} − h + y`; the smaller of the two lines is largest where they cross, so
`m_{k+1} ≤ max{0, m_k(τ_{k+1} − h + s)/(m_k + s)}`, and by induction, for every `k ≥ 1`,

    T_k(g) − θ_hint(g)  ≤  A(g)/(k + c₂),      A(g) = max{ c₁ + g + θ_hint(g) ,  (1 + c₂)(a − h + g) }.

At `u = 1`: `κ = 0.0427`, `c₁ = 0.712 = 6.4a`, `c₂ = 6.35`.  So the exponent `θ_hint(g) + η` needs at most
`⌈A(g)/η⌉` levels: the number of levels behind Theorems 11.54 and 11.58 is explicit.  The bound is
a rate, not the rate — the rate is `2π²h²θ_hint″(0)/k²`, that is `(τ_k − h)/a → 0.641/k²` at `u = 1`
(Theorem 11.53b below; "`≈ 0.65/k²`" numerically in §11.19, remark (1)), and over the class of all
convex pairs `1/k` cannot be improved (remark (2) there) —, and a one-sided
evaluation of the recursion of the cube on a grid, an upper bound of every `T_k`, stays below it
at all `40` levels computed, for `u = ½, 1, 2` (`experiments/coordinator_checks/nested_review_R6/t4_rate.py`,
which has the proof in full).  By itself the rate does not make the `o(n)` of Theorems 11.54
and 11.58 explicit: for that the sub-exponential factors of a family with `k` nested levels
have to be bounded uniformly in `k`.  The first version of this remark said that they are
not.  **For an explicit schedule built on the epochs of this proof they are, and the
`o(n)` of Theorem 11.58 is `O(√(n ln n))` — Theorem 11.58a.**  With convex families of lines in
place of single-line epochs it is `O(n^{1/3}(ln n)^{2/3})`, and at extensive accuracies the term
of Theorem 11.54 is `O((ln n)²)` — Theorem 11.58e.

**Theorem 11.53a (the recursion at the level of lines: the slope map, and a saddle-node at the hinted exponent) [V for (a), (b′), (d) and for the iteration in (c): `LineDynamics.lean`; P for (b), (c), (e): the coordinator's proofs, `docs/workstreams/R_REPORT.md` §§1–5, **refereed internally by two independent referees with their own code** (`docs/workstreams/R_REVIEW_B.md`: the slope map, the lower bound, the passage time; `docs/workstreams/R_REVIEW_A.md`: one level for convex families, the sub-solutions, the range condition, the upper bound) — **no error of substance in either half**; a brute force on the operator `R` itself, the chain on six pairs and the recursion iterated to 61 levels on pairs the author had not used confirm the statements and the constant to `0.1` per cent; their minor findings (two wrong expository sentences, a remark valid only for an infinite slope at zero, an over-statement of a numerical check, routine steps left unwritten) are applied in the report; internal reviews are not external peer review].**
*Everything here is a statement about the non-adaptive exponent function alone: nothing of
the cube is used beyond it.*  Let `θ = θ_na ≥ 0` be convex and nonincreasing on `(0, ∞)` with
`θ(0+) = a < ∞`, let `h` be its fixed point (`θ(h) = h`, by (11.18.1)), assume `h < a`, and put

    J(t)  =  inf_{e > 0} [ (1 − t)·θ(e) + t·e ],        0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

`J` is concave, `J ≤ h`, and `J(t) = h` exactly when `−t/(1 − t)` is a subgradient of `θ` at `h`; so `max J = h`,
attained at a single point `L` when `θ` is differentiable at `h`.  Geometrically `J(t)` is the largest
intercept of a line of slope `−t` below the graph of `θ_hint`, continued along the shear of
(11.18.1) to negative arguments: `θ_hint(x) = sup_t [J(t) − tx]`, `θ_hint′(0) = −L`, `θ_hint″(0) = −1/J″(L)`.
For the cube `J(t) = Λ(tu) − tΛ(u)` with `Λ(v) = ln(2/(1 + e^{−v}))`; for the Gaussian pair `J(t) = t − t²`.

(a) **Lemma L (a line below `T` stays below one more level) [V: `line_le_Rstep`, `line_le_min_Rstep`].**
Let `0 ≤ σ ≤ σ′`, let `T` be bounded above with `T(x) ≥ B − σx` for all `x > 0`, and let
`(1 − σ)·θ(e) + σ′·e ≥ B` for every `e > 0`.  Then `R[T](g) ≥ B − σ′g` for every `g > 0`, hence
`min(T, R[T])(g) ≥ B − σ′g`.
*Proof.*  For any `φ, β` let `e′ = (g − β)/φ`, `μ = φθ(e′)` and evaluate the bracket of (11.18.2) at
`γ₀ = max(β, μ)`: it is `μ + (1−φ)T(γ₀/(1−φ)) ≥ μ + (1−φ)B − σγ₀`.  If `μ ≥ β` this is
`(1−φ)B + (1−σ)φθ(e′) ≥ B − σ′φe′ ≥ B − σ′g`; if `μ < β` it is at least
`(1−σ)φθ(e′) + (1−φ)B − σβ ≥ B − σ′(g − β) − σβ ≥ B − σ′g`.  ∎

(b) **The slope map [P].**  The least admissible `σ′` in (a) is

    Σ(B, σ)  =  sup_{e > 0} [B − (1 − σ)·θ(e)]/e,

finite if `B < (1 − σ)·a` and infinite if `B > (1 − σ)·a`.  It is a supremum of functions that are
*affine in `(B, σ)`* with nonnegative coefficients: **`Σ` is jointly convex and nondecreasing in
both arguments.**  Through `J`: `Σ(B, σ) − σ` is the least `w` with `(1 + w)·J((σ + w)/(1 + w)) ≥ B`.  Hence
`Σ(B, σ) ≥ σ` iff `B ≥ J(σ)`; the fixed points of `σ ↦ Σ(B, σ)` are the solutions of `J(σ) = B` — for `B < h`
a stable one below `L` (the tangent lines of `θ_hint`) and an unstable one above, for `B = h` only `L`,
for `B > h` none — and `Σ(B, σ) − σ ≥ (B − h)/h` for all `σ` when `B ≥ h`.  **The hinted exponent is the
saddle-node value of the slope map.**  If `J` is twice differentiable at `L` with
`J″(L) = −1/θ_hint″(0) < 0`, then for `B = h + δ`, uniformly as `δ → 0` and `σ → L`,

    Σ(B, σ) − σ  =  [ δ + (σ − L)²/(2θ_hint″(0)) ]/h · (1 + o(1)).

(b′) **The Gaussian pair [V: `gauss_slope_map`, `gauss_slope_map_least`].**  `Σ(B, σ) = B(1 − σ)/(1 − σ − B)`, a
Möbius map of `1 − σ` with trace `1 − 2B` and determinant `B²`: parabolic at `B = ¼ = h` with the fixed
point `σ = ½ = L`, elliptic for `B > ¼` — a rotation by the angle `arctan(√(4B − 1)/(1 − 2B)) ≈ 4√(B − ¼)`
per level in the angular coordinate of the projective line.

(c) **A lower bound for every level [V for the iteration: `lines_le_exactRec`, `le_sSup_exactRec`; P
for the rest].**  Let `p_0 ≡ 0` and `p_{j+1}(B) = Σ(B, p_j(B))` (the *orbit curves*: the slopes of the
flat line with intercept `B` after `j` levels; `p_1(B)` is the slope of the tangent line of `θ` with
intercept `B`).  Every curve `p_j(B)` is convex and nondecreasing in `B` (composition of the jointly
convex `Σ` with a convex function), and `p_j ≤ p_{j+1}`.  If `p_k(B) < ∞` then `T_k(x) ≥ B − p_k(B)·x` for all
`x > 0`; in particular

    τ_k  ≥  sup{ B : p_k(B) < ∞ }.

For the Gaussian pair the orbit curves have a closed form — with `B = 1/(4cos²α)`:
`p_j(B) = 1 − B·[1 + sin((2j + 3)α)/sin((2j + 1)α)]` as long as `(2j + 1)α < π`, by Cayley–Hamilton for
the matrix of (b′) — so that

    τ_k  ≥  1/(4·cos²(π/(2k + 1))),        τ_k − ¼  ≥  ¼·tan²(π/(2k + 1))  =  (π²/16)/(k + ½)²·(1 + O(k⁻²))

(`(3 − √5)/2 = 0.381966` at `k = 2`; the closed form is the referee's, `R_REPORT.md` §10; checked
against the orbit in exact rational arithmetic and in harness XVI.6, XVI.8); machine-checked
instances: `T_2(0+) ≥ 3/8`, `T_3(0+) ≥ 3/10` (`gauss_level_two_ge`, `gauss_level_three_ge`).

(d) **Lemma M (a majorant with nondecreasing `x + M(x)`, one level) [V: `StepLE.monotoneS_step`,
`StepLE.line_step`, `StepLE.line_step_rate`].**  Let `T` be nonincreasing and `T ≤ M` on `(0, R]` with `x + M(x)`
nondecreasing there.  For `g > 0`, `0 < φ < 1`, `e = g/φ`, `μ = φθ(e) > 0` and `X = μ/(1 − φ) ≤ R`:
`R[T](g) ≤ (1 − φ)(X + M(X))`.  For a line `M(x) = B − σx`, `σ ≤ 1`: `R[T](g) ≤ B − σ′g` with
`σ′ = [B − (1 − σ)θ(e)]/e`, for `g ≤ Re/(θ(e) + R)` — the slope step of Theorem 11.58a at a general outer
rate (`e = h` there).

(e) **One level for a convex family of lines [P: Lemma M and Sion's minimax theorem].**  Let `b > 0`,
let `W : [0, b] → [0, 1]` be convex, nondecreasing and continuous, and let `T` be nonincreasing and
below the upper envelope `max_{B ≤ b} (B − W(B)x)` of the lines with intercept `B` and slope `−W(B)`.
Then for every `g > 0`

    R[T](g)  ≤  sup{ B − Σ(B, W(B))·g  :  0 ≤ B ≤ b,  Σ(B, W(B)) < ∞ }:

**on a convex family of lines the level operator acts line by line, through the slope
map**, and the lines whose image slope is infinite — those with `B > (1 − W(B))·a` — drop out.
*Proof.*  By (d) with `R = ∞`, `R[T](g) ≤ inf_{e > g} max_𝓔 Φ`, where `Φ(e; B, s) = B − (g/e)(B − (1 − s)θ(e))` and
`𝓔 = {(B, s) : B ≤ b, W(B) ≤ s ≤ 1}` is compact and — because `W` is convex — convex.  `Φ` is affine in
`(B, s)` and, because `θ` is convex and `s ≤ 1`, quasi-convex in `e` (the set where it is at most `c`
is `{e : g(1 − s)θ(e) + (B − c)e − gB ≤ 0}`).  By Sion's minimax theorem the infimum and the maximum
commute, and for a single line `inf_{e > g} Φ` is `B − Σ(B, s)g` if the line `x ↦ B − Σ(B, s)x` touches
`(1 − s)θ` beyond `g`, and `(1 − s)θ(g)` otherwise — the value at `g` of the tangent line of `(1 − s)θ` at
`g`, which is the image of a line `(B″, s)` with `B″ ≤ B`, again in `𝓔` because `W` is nondecreasing.  ∎
(Details and the cases: `R_REPORT.md` §5.)  The minimax identity is exact — the infimum over the
outer rate of the bound of (d) equals the right side (harness XVI.8: 240 random convex
families; referee A: 2 700 cases to `10⁻¹²`) —, while `R[T]` itself can be smaller, since also
`R[T](g) ≤ T(g−)`; referee A's brute force on `R` in 480 cases never exceeded the bound.
**Convexity of the family cannot be dropped**: for a family that is not convex the value is
that of its convex hull, which exceeds the line-by-line value (by up to `0.07·a` in the
harness; referee A, on `R` itself, in 17 cases), and propagating the lines of a majorant one
by one gave `τ₃ ≤ ⅓` for the Gaussian pair, where `τ₃ ≥ 1/(2√2)` (`DEAD_ENDS.md` D64, harness XVI.7).
Nor can "nondecreasing".

**Theorem 11.53b (the rate of the level recursion) [P: the coordinator's proof, `docs/workstreams/R_REPORT.md`, **refereed internally by two independent referees with their own code** (`docs/workstreams/R_REVIEW_B.md`: the slope map, the lower bound, the passage time; `docs/workstreams/R_REVIEW_A.md`: one level for convex families, the sub-solutions, the range condition, the upper bound) — **no error of substance in either half**; a brute force on the operator `R` itself, the chain on six pairs and the recursion iterated to 61 levels on pairs the author had not used confirm the statements and the constant to `0.1` per cent; their minor findings (two wrong expository sentences, a remark valid only for an infinite slope at zero, an over-statement of a numerical check, routine steps left unwritten) are applied in the report; internal reviews are not external peer review; numerical checks: harness XVI.8 (thirteen mutations), `experiments/workstreams/R`].**
*In the setting of Theorem 11.53a let `J` have a unique maximiser `L ∈ (0, 1)` and be twice
differentiable there, `J(t) = h − (t − L)²/(2ϑ) + o((t − L)²)` with `0 < ϑ < ∞` (so `ϑ = θ_hint″(0)`; if `θ` is `C²`
near `h` with `θ″(h) > 0` this holds with `ϑ = θ″(h)/(1 + |θ′(h)|)³`).  Then*

    lim_{k → ∞} k²·(τ_k − h)  =  2π²·h²·θ_hint″(0).

For the cube the constant is `2π²h²/(u²ρ_h(1 − ρ_h))`, `ρ_h = Λ₁/u` (`0.0711473 = 0.64129·a` at `u = 1`, `0.70193·a`
at `u = 2`); for the Gaussian pair `π²/16`.  The "`0.65/k²`" of §11.19, remark (1), is this number.

*Proof in outline* (in full: `R_REPORT.md` §§6–8).  *The passage time.*  By Theorem 11.53a(b), for
`B = h + δ` the map `σ ↦ Σ(B, σ)` has no fixed point but a bottleneck at `L` of width `√δ`, and the
number `N(δ)` of steps that the orbit of the flat line needs to exceed a slope level `L + η`
satisfies `√δ·N(δ) → π·h·√(2θ_hint″(0))` (comparison with `∫ dσ/(δ + (σ − L)²/(2θ_hint″(0)))`; outside a
window around `L` the steps are bounded below).  *Lower bound.*  By Theorem 11.53a(c), `τ_k ≥ h + δ`
as long as `k < N(δ)`.  *Upper bound.*  By Theorem 11.53a(e) an upper bound for the next level
is a **convex sub-solution of the slope map**: a convex `W′ ≤ Σ(·, W(·))` with values in `[0, 1]` on
the intercepts that are left.  The orbit curves, cut at the level `L + η` and continued by
their tangent lines, are convex, and the cut curve of level `j + 1` lies below the image of
the cut curve of level `j` — because `B ↦ Σ(B, W(B))` is convex for convex `W`, and a tangent line
of a convex function is a global minorant.  What remains is that the cut curve stays
below slope one where it is used (the *range condition*).  Started from the flat majorant
at a level `k₁` with `τ_{k₁} ≤ h + ε₁` — which exists by the remark above, `τ_k − h ≤ c₁/(k + c₂)` — it holds at
every later level if `η` and `ε₁` are small: the slope of the cut curve at most multiplies by
the derivative `∂Σ/∂σ` near the fixed point, which is close to one there (the multiplier of
the saddle-node is `θ(h)/h = 1`), while the room below slope one exceeds what is needed by
the margin `h/a`.  This gives `τ_{k₁+j+1} ≤ B_t(j) + (1 − L − η)/m_j`, with `B_t(j)` the intercept at which
the `j`-th orbit curve reaches the level and `m_j = p_j′(B_t(j))` its slope there; `B_t(j) − h` is determined by
`N(δ) = j`, and `1/m_j` is of smaller order.  ∎

*Remarks.*
(1) *A sandwich between two points of one family of curves.*  For every `k`, `τ_k` is at least the
intercept at which the `k`-th orbit curve blows up, and for large `k` at most the intercept
at which a curve `k₁ + 1` levels earlier reaches the slope `L + η`, plus a term of relative
order `1/k`.  Numerically (floating point, not certified): with `c_*² = 2π²h²θ_hint″(0)`, the
lower bound behaves like `c_*²/(k + ½)²` (ratio `0.9902, 0.9938, 0.9969` at `k = 100, 160, 320`,
Gaussian pair; `0.9918` at `k = 120`, cube `u = 1`), the recursion itself on a grid like
`c_*²/(k + c)²` with `c ≈ 0.15`–`0.25` (`0.9982` at `k = 160`; `0.9959` at `k = 120`), the exact dynamics of
convex majorants like `c_*²/(k + c′)²` with `c′ ≈ 0`–`0.08` (`1.00006` at `k = 160`; `0.99903`), and the chain
of the proof, restarted at `h + 0.02`, gives `1.031·c_*²/j²` after `j = 1000` further levels
(`experiments/coordinator_checks/level_rate`, `experiments/workstreams/R`).  The restart is
needed: from `h + 0.15` the range condition fails for the Gaussian pair.
(2) *Where the law changes.*  The structural part — Lemma L, Lemma M, the convexity of `Σ`,
(c), (e), the sub-solutions — holds for every convex nonincreasing `θ` with `h < a`.  The
twice differentiable maximum of `J` enters through the passage time and the multiplier.
**If `θ` has a kink at its fixed point** — one-sided slopes `−r₂ < −r₁` at `h` — then `J = h` on
`[L₁, L₂]`, `L_i = r_i/(1 + r_i)`, the slope map moves by exactly `δ/h` per level across this interval, and
`τ_k − h ≥ (L₂ − L₁)·h/(k + 2)` for every `k` (Proposition K of the report; example
`θ(e) = max(1 − 3e, ½ − e, 0)`): together with the general bound `c₁/(k + c₂)` the rate is `Θ(1/k)`.
So over all convex pairs the rate `O(1/k)` of the remark above cannot be improved, and
the `1/k²` of the cube is a consequence of the smoothness and strict convexity of `θ_na` at
its fixed point.  Heuristically, `h − J(t) ≍ |t − L|^p` gives `τ_k − h ≍ k^{−p/(p−1)}` for `p > 1`, and
convergence that is geometric or faster for a corner of `J` (`θ` affine near `h`); only the
lower halves of these follow from (c) as it stands.  If `J` is differentiable at `L` with
one-sided second derivatives `−1/ϑ_∓`, the limit is `(π²h²/4)(√(2ϑ_−) + √(2ϑ_+))²`.  **If `|θ′(0+)| ≤ 1`
the recursion is solved exactly by the orbit curves**: image slopes are at most `1 − σ`, no
line ever leaves the family, (c) and (e) coincide, and `T_k(x) = sup{B − p_k(B)x : p_k(B) < ∞}` for
every `k` and `x` (Corollary E of the report; the cube and the Gaussian pair have infinite
slope at zero and are not of this kind).
(3) *What it means, and what it does not.*  The theorem is about the operator `R` — the
analysis of the nested algorithms at the level of exponents: `k` nested levels, *analysed by
`R`*, have the exponent `h + (c_*² + o(1))/k²` at accuracy zero.  It is not a statement about
algorithms that are not nested in this way, the `o(1)` has no rate (no certified constants at
finite `k`), and by itself it gives no cost at finite `n`: with `k ≍ n^{1/3}` levels and a loss of `O(ln n)` per
level one would expect `n·h + O(n^{1/3}(ln n)^{2/3})`, which needs the sub-exponential factors
of `k` levels uniformly in `k` (the schedule of Theorem 11.58a, built
on single lines, is confined to `O(√(n ln n))` because single-line epochs have the rate `1/k`
only: `DEAD_ENDS.md` D64).  **Both gaps have since been closed by Theorem 11.58e**: the cost
`n·h + O(n^{1/3}(ln n)^{2/3})` for a schedule of convex families, and certified upper bounds for the
exponent at every finite `k` (which are not the exponents themselves from the third level on).
(4) *Not machine-checked:* (b), the passage time, (e) (it needs a minimax theorem), the
sub-solution argument and the range condition.  Machine-checked: Lemmas L and M, the
iteration of (c), the Gaussian slope map, three numerical instances.
(5) *The profile at positive accuracy* **[a sketch and numerics: `R_REPORT.md` §8a]**.  Both
bounds are envelopes of lines over the same orbit curves, and at accuracies `x = ζh/k` they
give

    k²·[ T_k(ζh/k) − θ_hint(ζh/k) ]  →  h²·θ_hint″(0)·f(ζ),      f(ζ) = sup{ 2z² + 2ζ·z·cot z : z ∈ (0, π) or z ∈ i(0, ∞) } − ζ²/2,

`f(0) = 2π²`, `f(3) = 3/2`; `f` solves `ζf′²/2 + ζf′ + (ζ − 2)f = 0`, the similarity equation of a
continuum caricature of the recursion (`∂_kD = −x[D/h + (∂_xD)²/(2hθ_hint″(0))]` for the defect
`D = T_k − θ_hint`), through its folded saddle.  The uniform estimate that the limit needs is
not written out; numerically the envelope of the minorant lines increases to `f` for the
Gaussian pair and for the cube alike (`5.61, 5.79, 5.89, 5.94` at `ζ = 1`, `k = 20, 40, 80, 160`, against
`f(1) = 5.992`), and the recursion on a grid has `11.74, 9.07, 5.98, 2.93, 1.50, 0.40` at
`ζ = ¼, ½, 1, 2, 3, 5`, `k = 160`, against `11.77, 9.09, 5.99, 2.93, 1.50, 0.39`.

**Theorem 11.54 (the adaptive exponent without a hint) [P: Theorems 11.25(a), 11.44, 11.52, 11.53].**
For every `u > 0`, `0 < ε₁ < ε*` and `0 < δ < ½`, the least number of evaluations with which a
randomised adaptive algorithm without a hint is correct on all of `L_u`, in the worst case
over the class, is

    exp( n·θ_hint(ε₁) + o(n) ),        θ_hint(ε₁) = KL( (Λ₁ + ε₁)/u ‖ ½ ),

the same exponent as with a hint at the hardest instance, while non-adaptive algorithms need
`exp(n·θ_na(ε₁) + o(n))` with `θ_na > θ_hint`.  *At the exponential scale, and in the worst case
over this class, a hint is worth nothing
to an adaptive algorithm, and everything that it is worth is lost by a non-adaptive one.*
*Proof.*  Lower bound: Theorem 11.25(a) at the zero function (an algorithm without a hint is
an algorithm with one); it bounds the expected number of evaluations at one instance, hence
the worst case, with the same convention for the accuracy.  Upper bound.  Fix `η > 0`; choose
`g < ε₁` with `θ_hint(g) ≤ θ_hint(ε₁) + η`, then `k` with `T_k(g) < θ_hint(g) + η` (Theorem 11.53(d)), then the
parameters of the `k − 1` levels, then let `n → ∞`.  *Base:* the two-sample brackets form a family
with exponent function `T₁ = θ_na` (`K = 24 ln(4/δ′) = O(d)`; cost `e^{dθ_na(ξ)+o(d)}` for `ξ < ε*` and `e^{o(d)}`
from `ε*` on).  *Assembly:* for a family with nonincreasing exponent function `T` and a tuple
`(φ, β, g, η₀)`, Theorem 11.52 gives procedures of accuracy `gd + ln(4eJ + 3)` in every dimension
`d ≥ d₀`, where `d₀` depends on the tuple: the failure probability of that theorem is proved from
a dimension `n₀(η₀)` on, and the logarithm of the ratio of its bracket, in general at most
`max(gd, b) + ln(4eJ + 3)`, is at most `gd + ln(4eJ + 3)` only once `b ≤ gd`, which holds for
`d ≥ β/((1−φ)(g−β))`.  Enumerate a countable dense set of tuples and
let the new procedure for `(d, x, δ′)` be the cheapest among the old one and those of the first `d`
tuples that have `d₀ ≤ d` and accuracy at most `x`.  Its cost is nonincreasing in `x` and `δ′`, and for
fixed `ξ` every tuple with `g < ξ` is eventually admissible.  The passage from the dense set to the
infimum over all `(φ, β)` needs an approximation from one side, because `T` is only nonincreasing:
for `φ′ ≥ φ`, `β′ ≥ β` and every `γ ≥ β′`, `(1−φ′)T(γ/(1−φ′)) ≤ (1−φ)T(γ/(1−φ))`, so the bracket of
(11.18.2) at `(φ′, β′, g′)` exceeds the one at `(φ, β, g)` by at most
`|φ′θ_na((g′−β′)/φ′) − φθ_na((g−β)/φ)|`, which tends to zero along tuples of the dense set with `φ′ ↓ φ`,
`β′ ↓ β`, `g′ → g`, since `θ_na` is continuous.  So the new family has the exponent function
`T′ ≤ min(T, R[T])(·⁻) + η₀`, with a **left limit** in the accuracy — nothing shows that the `T_k`
are continuous.  (The restriction to `d ≥ d₀` and the one-sided approximation were missing in the
first version: Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0007.  Proposition E of `K_REPORT.md` §3.3
needs neither: it uses finitely many tuples chosen in advance instead of a dense set, and
Theorem 11.56 with `θ` chosen so that the accuracy is exactly `Gn`, whose failure probability is
bounded for every `n` — see the remark after Theorem 11.56.)  *Shift:* if `T̃ ≤ T(·⁻) + η′` then
`R[T̃](g) ≤ R[T](g − ε) + ε + η′` for `0 < ε < g` (replace `β` by `β + ε` and `γ` by `γ − ε`; the outer exponent
is unchanged).  *Induction:* if the level-`k` family has `T̃_k ≤ T_k(·⁻) + η_k`, the level-`(k+1)` family
has `T̃_{k+1} ≤ T_{k+1}(·⁻) + η_k + 2η₀`.  So at accuracy `ε₁n` the level-`k` family costs
`exp(n(T_k(g) + kη′) + o(n))` for every `g < ε₁`, which suffices because `θ_hint` is continuous; and
the midpoint of a bracket of accuracy at most `ε₁n` is a correct output.  The `o(n)` at level
`k + 1` consists of polynomial factors and of the finitely many `o(n_i)` of level `k`; the
failure probability handed down is `δ/(2^{n+6}n³)` per level, still `e^{−O(kn)}` at the bottom.  (The
induction in this form is the referee's.)  ∎

*What this does and does not say.*
(1) It is a statement about exponents, with `o(n)` terms that come from `k` nested levels,
each with its own ladder and union bounds; `k → ∞` as the exponent approaches `θ_hint`.  An
earlier variant of the two-level algorithm was simulated by the workstream at `n = 32`: of 32
runs, 12 closed within the budget, with valid brackets, and on the three instances where
the comparison was made it needed far more evaluations than plain Monte Carlo for a wider
bracket.  The referee evaluated the corrected algorithm in expectation with exact binomial
arithmetic on 30 radial outer profiles and by adversarial search over profiles: the excess
of `n^{−1} ln(cost)` over `τ` falls from `0.029` at `n = 10³` to `0.0002` at `n = 10⁶`, never above the
explicit finite-`n` bound of the proof; and simulated the outer loop with adversarial inner
oracles in about 17 000 runs without a violation (with the closure rule of the first draft,
2 940 of 2 940 runs in the affected parameter range return a false bracket).  At small
sizes no level is ever left as negligible — that branch needs roughly `n_o h ≳ ln(2Je²)` — so a
small simulation must say which branches it exercised (harness XV.3 reaches it with a steep
slope and reports the counts).  **Nothing here is an algorithm one would run.**  With the constants of the proof
(and expectations in place of counts) the two-level algorithm overtakes the two-sample
bracket of Proposition 11.46 on the zero function, at `u = 1` and the accuracy rate `ε*/4`,
between `n = 2000` and `n = 5000` — where either needs more than `e^{70}` evaluations (benchmark
B13).  Numerically, at `u = 1` and a small accuracy, `T_k/θ_na = 0.50, 0.36, 0.32, 0.29, 0.28, 0.274,
0.271` for `k = 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 14` levels, against `θ_hint/θ_na = 0.268` (B13; at half the threshold
two levels already give `0.76` against `0.74`).
(2) Extensive accuracies only (`ε = ε₁n`, `0 < ε₁ < ε*`): the brackets have accuracy `gn + O(log n)`.
At a bounded accuracy the non-adaptive exponent is `a` (Theorem 11.44) and the hinted one `h`;
the adaptive exponent at accuracy `ε₁n` tends to `h` as `ε₁ → 0`, but at `ε = O(1)` it is only
known to lie between `h` and `a`.
(3) The cube, with the uniform reference measure and a class defined by one constant.  The
proof uses three things: the tail lemma (Harper's theorem) on subcubes; the fact that fibre
averages of a Lipschitz function are Lipschitz; and the **additivity of the Hamming distance
over blocks of coordinates**, by which a block of `φn` coordinates carries a problem of the
same kind and of size `φn` — this is what makes the outer sample cheap.  The analysis of the
recursion (Theorem 11.53) is abstract and would apply to any pair of exponent functions with
the identity (11.18.1), which only says that the hardest pair of instances for a
non-adaptive sample has all its mass on the set the sample has not seen.  But the third
ingredient is special, and so is the fact that on the cube every query point is a typical
point.  The small-slope limit of the two exponent functions, `(1 − √e)²` and `(1 − e)²/4`, looks
like a statement about Lipschitz functions on Gaussian space, and it is **not** one: there
a block of coordinates has the same Euclidean Lipschitz constant as the whole space, so
the two-level construction gains nothing — now a proposition, for every fixed split of
the coordinates: Theorem 11.120(b).  The extremal sets of the isoperimetric inequality
are half-spaces, which an algorithm can detect with a few evaluations far from the
bulk; but dips on large *balls* are not detected that way, and the hinted lower bound
does hold in high dimension (Theorem 11.120(c); the first version of this remark said
that it does not transfer).  With the sum of the coordinate distances as metric, Gauss
space is an exact instance of the abstract level theorem (Theorem 11.118).  Product
reference measures and larger alphabets with a weighted Hamming distance are worked out
at the exponential scale in §§11.20 and 11.26; what the level theorem uses, in general,
is §11.33.
(4) Worst case over the class.  One consequence concerns algorithms *with* a hint: an
algorithm with a hint may ignore it, so by Theorem 11.54 no instance of the class costs a
hinted algorithm more than `exp(nθ_hint(ε₁) + o(n))` — **the zero function is the hardest
instance with a hint**, at the exponential scale (for additive instances this also follows
from the game formula of Theorem 11.27: workstream H).  What remains open is the comparison
instance by instance in the other direction: at an instance that is cheap with a hint — a
cone costs two evaluations — the nested algorithm is not shown to be cheap, and whether
some adaptive algorithm without a hint matches the hinted cost at *every* instance, up to
`e^{o(n)}`, is not known.
(5) The time-honoured relatives of the algorithm — nested sampling, multilevel splitting,
nested simulation with adaptive allocation — estimate the same layer-cake decomposition
with a constrained sampler or with mean-square criteria.  What was not found in print
(abstracts only): a certified one-sided version, the use of an isoperimetric tail lemma to
close the ladder, and a recursion for worst-case exponents.  In information-based complexity
adaption is known not to help for linear problems on convex symmetric classes and to help
by polynomial factors in some randomised linear settings (Heinrich 2024; Kunsch–Novak–Wnuk
2024).  *Where our problem sits* (Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0004, observation
(b); our earlier note in `prior_art/L7` — "`ln Z` is not linear, so 'adaption does not help'
does not apply" — was not the accurate explanation): in the weights `w = e^{−ψ}` the solution
operator `A(w) = E_π w` **is linear** and the class is a **convex cone**; what takes the
problem out of the reach of those theorems is that the class is **not symmetric**, the
error is **relative**, and the information is standard (function values).  For such
problems adaption is known to help by factors polynomial in the cardinality (Novak 1995,
as quoted by Krieg–Novak–Ullrich 2025; not read by us), and in these units the shear law of
§11.21 says how much here: the error factor of the best non-adaptive method with `N`
evaluations is `N^{1+o(1)}` times that of the best adaptive one, for `N ≤ e^{nh}` — **the adaption
gain equals the cardinality**.  The pattern "learn where to look, then verify" of §11.10
and of this section is the explore–verify scheme of Karnin (2016) and the
identification-as-cheap-as-verification phenomenon of Garivier–Kaufmann (2016), in
another regime (theirs: noisy observations, confidence `δ → 0`; here: exact evaluations,
fixed `δ`, exponents in `n`).  **That adaption can remove an exponential barrier of non-adaptive randomised methods
is not new**: Mathé–Novak (2007) — whose method gives the lower bound of §11.16 — show it for
integration against an unknown log-concave density with Lipschitz logarithm, by a
Metropolis walk ("the curse of dimension (for nonadaptive methods) can be broken by
adaption"), and zero finding (Sikorski 1982) is the textbook example for a nonlinear
problem.  What was not found: the exact exponents on a Hamming–Lipschitz class without
concavity and without a Markov chain, their coincidence with the hinted exponent, and the
recursion.  All of this is at the level of abstracts and search summaries; see
`prior_art/L7_query_complexity.md`.

*What the referee checked* (`reviews/R7_referee_report.md`).  Re-derived every line of Theorem
11.52 (good event and its probability, validity, width, termination, sample sizes, the
count, the cost sum); found the closure gap independently; closed the abort rule and the
induction on paper; compiled the Lean file and printed its axioms; verified by hand that
the functions of the cube satisfy the hypotheses of the abstract theorem, and the "≥" half
of Theorem 11.53(b) — both have since been machine-checked (`CubeHintPair.lean`); iterated the
recursion with own code to 64 levels (the excess over `θ_hint` halves with the grid spacing: a
discretisation artefact); ran the radial algorithm on full cubes.  *Not checked:* the algorithm end to end with real inner brackets, or with
three nested levels; non-radial outer landscapes in the evaluation of the cost (the referee
argues that only the law of the fibre averages matters); the uniformity of the `o(n)` terms
through `k` levels other than on paper; Theorems 11.25(a), 11.44, 11.45 and Proposition 11.46
beyond their statements; prior art beyond abstracts.  **The number of evaluations of the
algorithm therefore rests on a paper proof read by two parties and on numerical evidence
up to `n = 10⁶`, not on a machine check.**

### 11.19 Every bounded accuracy: the adaptive exponent without a hint is the hinted one

Theorem 11.54 is a statement about extensive accuracies `ε = ε₁n`.  The two-level algorithm
behind it loses a factor `4eJ + 3 = O(n)` in the ratio of its bracket at every level —
invisible at an extensive accuracy, fatal at a bounded one — and its closure test compares the
tail with the mass certified at *one* level.  What happens at a fixed accuracy `ε` was open
(§12 item 2(d) of the previous checkpoint): with a hint the exponent is
`h = θ_hint(0) = KL(Λ₁/u‖½)` (Theorem 11.25(d)); non-adaptive algorithms have
`a = KL(p_u‖½) > h` (Theorem 11.45); adaptive ones without a hint were only known to lie between.
Workstream K (`docs/workstreams/K_REPORT.md`) settles it: **the exponent is `h`, at every fixed
accuracy and down to accuracies `e^{-o(n)}`.**

**Status of this section.**  Paper proofs with explicit constants by workstream K, in full in
its report (§§2–4 there); read line by line by the coordinator; **refereed (R8,
`reviews/R8_referee_report.md`): "proved" — the referee re-derived the whole chain line by
line and found no critical and no major error; its ten minor points are corrected in the
text below** (see "What the referee checked" at the end of the section).  **Reviewed a second
time, from outside (Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0007; report
`docs/science/workstreams/R6_REPORT.md` on the branch `research/scientific-translation`):** an
accounting of Theorems 11.52 and 11.56 written before ours was read, with the same constant in
every term, and an own implementation (by its count `4075` literal runs without a violation); no
critical and no major finding.  Its minor points — four in the text of §11.18, one in the proof
of the lowered cap below, one on the two ways of counting evaluations, a sampler, a remark on
the harness — were each checked by us (`experiments/coordinator_checks/nested_review_R6/`) and are
applied where they belong, marked as the division's; so is its finite-`n` separation, remark
(1a) after Theorem 11.58.  The theorems rest
on Harper's vertex-isoperimetric theorem, the binomial median and Chernoff–Hoeffding
bounds, which are cited, and on Theorems 11.25(a) and 11.53, which are machine-checked.
Machine-checked here (`BoundedAccuracy.lean`): the algebra of the bracket and of the count
(four lemmas), the iteration of the final theorem, and the exact recursion of §11.18 —
defined in Lean, with every hypothesis of the convergence theorem proved for it.  Not
machine-checked: the algorithm, its events, the Harper term, the closing radius, sample
sizes, termination, the cost, the tail lemmas, Harper's theorem.

*Notation.*  On an outer cube `Q_m`: `E_r(m) = Σ_{j≤r} C(m,j)(e^{u(r+1−j)} − 1)` (the constant of the
upper tail lemma 11.43(b): if `{W > t}` has at most `|B(m,r)|` points, `r ≤ m−1`, then
`E(W − t)₊ ≤ t·2^{-m}E_r(m)`), `T_m(k) = Σ_j C(m,j)e^{-u(j−k)₊}` (the constant of the lower tail lemma
11.43(c): if `{W ≥ t}` has at least `|B(m,k)|` points, then `E min(W, t) ≥ t·2^{-m}T_m(k)`);
`c_η = (1−η)/(1+η)`; and the two ratios

    Γ̃(r) = E_r(m)/|B(m, r−1)|   (Γ̃(0) = e^u − 1),        Γ″(r) = E_r(m)/T_m(κ(r)),

`κ(r)` the largest `k ≥ 0` with `|B(m,k)| ≤ max{1, c_η|B(m, r−1)|}`.  `Γ̃` is the *one-sided* ratio of
Theorem 11.52 (tail against the mass of the level itself); `Γ″` is *two-sided* (tail against the
Harper lower bound for the whole mean).

**Lemma 11.55 (where a bounded ratio can be certified) [P; workstream K, Lemma K.4; checked on
exact tables for `m ≤ 12 800` by the workstream and for `m ≤ 400` in exact arithmetic by the
coordinator].**  Let `m ≥ 1`, `0 < η ≤ ½`, `m₀ = ⌈u^{-1} ln(1/c_η)⌉`.
(a) `Γ̃(r) ≤ 2e^u·m` for `0 ≤ r ≤ p_u(m+1)`.  It is never small for `r ≥ 1`:
`min_{r≥1} Γ̃(r) = 4e^u(e^u−1)(1−o(1))` (numerical; slightly below the limit at finite `m`, and
`Γ̃(0) = e^u − 1`), and `Γ̃(⌊p_u m⌋) ≍ √m` (numerical; `≈ 2.6√m` at `u = 1`).
(b) For `0 ≤ r ≤ p_u m`:  `Γ″(r) ≤ 2e^{u(m₀+2)}·P(Bin(m, p_u) ≤ r) ≤ 2e^{u(m₀+2)}·exp(−2(p_u m − r)²/m)`.
(c) Hence for every `0 < θ ≤ 2e^{u(m₀+2)}`: `Γ″(r) ≤ θ` for all `0 ≤ r ≤ p_u m − s`,
`s = √((m/2)·ℓ)`, `ℓ = ln(2e^{u(m₀+2)}/θ)` (for larger `θ` read `s = 0`); and if `s ≤ p_u m/2 − 1` — true
for `m ≥ ((√(ℓ/2) + √(ℓ/2 + 2p_u))/p_u)²` — the ball of radius `⌊p_u m − s⌋` has

    ln( 2^m/|B(m, ⌊p_u m − s⌋)| )   ≤   m·a + u·(1 + s) + (4/(3p_u))·(ℓ + 2/m) + ln(m+1).

(The first version of (c) had neither hypothesis and "`exp(−m·a − O(√m))`"; the explicit
form, with the leading constant `u` where Lemma K.4(d) has `u + ln 4`, is Lemma Q3 of
workstream Q: Taylor's formula for `KL(·‖½)` at `p_u`, whose slope there is `−u`.)  The `√m` is
really there: on exact tables the closing radius of Theorem 11.56 at a bounded threshold
lies between `0.5s` and `0.7s` below `p_u m` in five of the six cases of harness XVI.5.
(d) **At an extensive threshold the loss is a polynomial factor** (workstream Q, Lemma Q4;
re-derived by the coordinator; referee R12; harness XVI.5).  For `e ≥ 0` let `ρ_e ∈ [p_u, ½]` be
the solution of `KL(ρ‖p_u) = min(e, ε*)`, so that `θ_na(e) = KL(ρ_e‖½)`.  Then

    Γ̃(r)  ≤  (m+1)·e^{2u + e^u}·e^{m·e}          for 0 ≤ r ≤ min(m, ρ_e m + 1),

and therefore, for `θ ≥ c_η^{-1}·(m+1)·e^{2u + e^u + m·e}` and any `ν₁ ≥ 1`, the radius `r†` of Theorem
11.56 on `Q_m` and its ball satisfy

    r† ≥ min{m − 1, ⌊ρ_e m⌋ + 1},          ln(1/π†)  ≤  m·θ_na(e) + ln(m+1).

(*Proof.*  `E_r ≤ e^{u(r+1)}(1+e^{-u})^m` and `|B(m, r−1)| ≥ C(m, r−1) ≥ (m+1)^{-1}e^{mH((r−1)/m)}` give, by
(11.18.1), `Γ̃(r) ≤ (m+1)·e^{2u}·exp(m·KL((r−1)/m ‖ p_u))`.  For `(r−1)/m` between `p_u` and `ρ_e` the
divergence is at most `e`; just below `p_u`, within `(1−p_u)/m`, it is at most `e^u/m²` by the
`χ²` bound; and for `r ≤ p_u(m+1)`, (a) applies.  So `Γ̃(r′) ≤ c_ηθ` for every `r′` up to the stated
radius: [P] holds through its first entry and [N] because `(1−η)ν₀ ≥ ν₁ ≥ 1 ≥ c_η`.  The ball:
`C(m, r) ≥ (m+1)^{-1}e^{mH(ρ_e)}` for `ρ_e m < r ≤ m/2`.  ∎)  At `e = h`: `θ_na(h) = h`, because
`KL(ρ_h‖p_u) = KL(ρ_h‖½) = h` at `ρ_h = Λ₁/u`.  The lemma is sharp at `m = 1` and has a slack of
`5` to `18` nats at `m = 64 000` (the workstream's tables).  **This is the fact that separates
a level run at an extensive accuracy from a bounded level: `e^{O(ln m)}` against
`e^{O(√m)}`.**
*Proof idea.*  (a) Ratios of consecutive binomial coefficients are at most `e^{-u}` up to
`p_u(m+1)`, so `E_r ≤ (r+1)e^uC(m,r)`.  (b) `C(m,j)e^{-uj} = (1+e^{-u})^m P(Bin(m,p_u) = j)` turns `E_r` into a
lower binomial tail and `T_m(k)` into an upper one, which is at least `½` for `k ≤ p_u m` (median of
the binomial law); `κ(r) ≥ r − 1 − m₀`; Hoeffding.  ∎

So the one-sided test cannot certify a bounded ratio at radii near `p_u m` — which is where
the outer sample has the exponent `φa` — and the two-sided one can.  (The coordinator's
sketch of this step, a "window" of radii in which the one-sided test succeeds, was wrong as
a mechanism: `DEAD_ENDS.md`, D46.)

**Theorem 11.56 (one more level, at the price of an arbitrarily small constant) [P, refereed (R8);
workstream K, Theorem K1; the algebra of the width and of the count V].**  *Algorithm 2L⁺* is the two-level algorithm of Theorem
11.52 with four changes (complete text and all constants: `K_REPORT.md` §2.2):

1. the lower end is `max{ℓ, Σ}`, `Σ = Σ_{populated i}(1 − e^{-λ})e^{-b}s_i·p̲_i` — a lower Riemann sum of the
   layer cake over *all* populated levels (`certified_lower_sum_le_mean` **[V]**), not the
   largest single term;
2. at every populated level the running bound is also raised to the **Harper term**
   `ℓ ≥ s_je^{-b}·2^{-n_o}T_{n_o}(k)`, `k` the largest radius with `|B(n_o,k)| ≤ max{1, 2^{n_o}p̲}` (Lemma 11.43(c)
   on the outer cube: a certified *fraction* of fibres above a level forces mass around them);
3. the negligibility threshold is `M_j^neg = ν·s_j/(ℓe^b)` with `ν = K·ν₀`,
   `ν₀ = (1−η)^{-1}max{(J+1)(e^λ−1)/η′, ν₁}` and a free `ν₁ ≥ 1`;
4. Chernoff factors `1 ± η` instead of `2^{±1}`, levels `s_j = s₀e^{jλ}` instead of `s₀e^j`, and the
   initial bound `ℓ = e^{-ψ₀}((1+e^{-u})/2)^n` (so that `s₀ ≤ (2p_u)^n ℓ`).

Let `0 < λ ≤ 1`, `0 < η ≤ ½`, `0 < η′ ≤ 1`, `θ > 0`, `ν₁ ≥ 1`, tolerance `b`, inner bracket procedures of
accuracies `2un_i = x₀ > x₁ > … > x_L`, `x_L ≤ b`, with costs `C_l` and failure probability
`δ′ = δ/(4LM̄)`.  Then Algorithm 2L⁺ is a bracket procedure for dimension `n` with failure
probability `δ`,

    accuracy  ln[ (2p_u)^n + e^b·( e^λ(1+η)/(1−η) + η′ + θ ) ],
    cost      C_max = 1 + 2M̄ + Σ_{l=1}^{L} min{ 2M̄ , (J+1)·cnt(x_{l−1}) }·C_l,

where `J = ⌈(2un + b + n_o ln 2)/λ⌉`, `K = O(η^{-2} ln(nL/δ))`, `cnt(x) = max{K, 2(1+η)²(1−η)^{-1}e^λ·ν·e^x}`,
`M̄ = 2(1+η)e^λν₀·K/((1−η)π†)`, `π† = 2^{-n_o}|B(n_o, r†)|`, and `r†` is the largest radius `≤ n_o − 1` such that
`Γ̃(r′) ≤ θ(1−η)ν₀` and `min{Γ̃(r′)/c_η, Γ″(r′)} ≤ θ` for all `r′ ≤ r†`.  (The cost bound holds always:
before every query — the one query that gives a new outer point its trivial bracket, and
every inner call, counted with its cost bound `C_l` — the algorithm checks that it does
not take the number of queries beyond `C_max`, and aborts with the trivial bracket
otherwise; a pair with `L > U`, which can only arise off the good event, is replaced by
the trivial bracket as well — referee R8, m1.  The previous wording tested before inner
calls only, which proves `C_max + M̄`, not `C_max`: the point queries of a doubling after the
last admitted inner call were untested.  The rule for every query, which is the rule of
Theorem 11.52, is the Scientific Discovery Division's finding (SCI-REV-0016, m1).  On the
good event no test fails, so no number changes; it matters where a run is charged exactly
`C_max` as an inner procedure — remark (1b).)  On an event of probability
`≥ 1 − δ`: no abort; every certificate is true; and for every level reached and every `x > 0`
the count below holds.  *For every run, on or off that event* (the referee's observation):
every level that is left has closing radius above `r†`, every sample has at most `M̄` points,
and a bracket returned through the closure test has the stated width.  The count:

    M_j^neg · P(W > s_je^{-x})  ≤  (1+η)(1−η)^{-1}e^λ · ν · e^x        (the count; `close_points_bound'` [V]).

*What the statement says.*  The tolerance `b` is the accuracy of the finest inner bracket, and
it is the *only* quantity tied to it: one level adds `ln(e^λ(1+η)/(1−η) + η′ + θ) + o(1)` to the
accuracy, as small as one likes, at the price of factors `1/λ, 1/η², 1/η′, 1/θ` in the
polynomial part of the cost.  Everything exponential is in `1/π†` (the outer sample) and in
`e^{x_{l−1}}C_l` (the points within a factor `e^{x_{l−1}}` of a level, each of which needs an inner
bracket of accuracy `x_l`).
*Proof* (`K_REPORT.md` §2.4, nine steps; the architecture of Theorem 11.52).  Good event: every
potential inner call valid; Chernoff at the fixed thresholds `s_j`, `s_je^{-b}`, `s_je^{-x_l}` and the
sizes `K2^m`.  Validity: upper end by the layer cake and Lemma 11.43(b); lower end by the
Riemann sum, Markov and Lemma 11.43(c).  Width: four terms — `s₀ ≤ (2p_u)^nL`; populated levels
`≤ c_η^{-1}e^{λ+b}Σ` (`populated_part_le` **[V]**); negligible levels `≤ η′e^bℓ` by the threshold; tail
`≤ θe^bℓ` by the test (`width_le` **[V]**).  Closing radius: if a populated level fails the test,
then `min{Γ̃/c_η, Γ″} > θ` at its radius (the first through `ℓ ≥ s_je^{-b}p̲`, the second through the
Harper term); if a negligible one fails, `Γ̃ > θ(1−η)ν₀`.  Sample sizes: a level left as
negligible has `M < K/((1−η)π†)`, and the threshold of the next level is at most `e^λ` times
that, or — after a populated level — at most `ν e^λ/(c_ηπ†)`.  The count: the tolerance of "high"
and the tolerance of "negligible" are the same `b` and cancel, as in Theorem 11.52.
Termination at level `J` because nothing is high there and the threshold forces an empty
tail.  ∎

*Remark (the sample-size cap can be lowered to a constant multiple of `M†`)* **[P; coordinator,
in answer to the Computational Research Division, ENG-RES-0008; not refereed; harness
XVI.4].**  With `M† := K/((1−η)π†)`, the cap of the theorem is `M̄ = 2(1+η)e^λν₀M†`.  The division
found that in more than seven million runs, under a search over instances and inner
behaviours, no sample exceeded `1.8·M†`, while `M̄/M†` is of order `ν₀ ≈ J/η′` (`ln ν₀` between `8.9` and
`17.3` in its cells), and asked whether `M ≤ c·M†` can be proved.  It can.  Let `Δ := ⌈λ/u⌉`,
`π‡ := 2^{-n_o}|B(n_o, r† − Δ)|` and `M‡ := K/((1−η)π‡)` (`M‡ := K·2^{n_o}/(1−η)` if `r† < Δ`).  **In every run
every sample is `K` or has fewer than `2·max{e^λM†, M‡}` points**, and
`M‡/M† = |B(n_o, r†)|/|B(n_o, r†−Δ)| ≤ ((n_o+1)/(r†−Δ+1))^Δ`, which tends to `((1−ρ)/ρ)^Δ` when `r†/n_o → ρ`: at
a bounded accuracy, where `r† = p_un_o − O(√n_o)`, the cap is `2e^{uΔ}(1+o(1))·M†` (`2e·M†` for `u = 1`,
`λ ≤ 1`).  So `M̄` may be replaced by `2max{e^λM†, M‡}` in `C_max`, `m_max` and `δ′`: the first term of
`C_max` loses a factor of order `ν₀`; no exponent changes.
*Proof.*  `M` is doubled only after a pass that is unpopulated, fails the closure test and
has `M < M_j^neg`.  (1) *After a negligible level:* `M_j^neg ≤ e^λM_{j−1}^neg ≤ e^λM_{j−1} < e^λM†` (the
running bound does not decrease, and a negligible level that is left has `M < M†`), so
every sample of level `j` is below `2e^λM†`.  (2) *After a populated level `j − 1`* (level `0`
is populated at `M = K`): that level was left, so its closing radius exceeded `r†`; hence
`p̲_{j−1} > c_ηπ†`, the radius of its Harper term is at least `κ(r†+1)`, and
`ℓ ≥ s_{j−1}e^{-b}·max{c_ηπ†, 2^{-n_o}T_{n_o}(κ(r†+1))}`.  At an unpopulated pass of level `j` with `M ≥ M‡`,
`q = K/((1−η)M) ≤ π‡`, so the closing radius is `r ≤ r† − Δ`; and `E_{r−1} ≤ e^{-u}E_r` for every `r ≥ 1`
(compare the two sums term by term: `e^{u(r−i)} − 1 ≤ e^{-u}(e^{u(r+1−i)} − 1)`), so
`tail = s_j2^{-n_o}E_r ≤ s_{j−1}e^{λ−uΔ}·2^{-n_o}E_{r†} ≤ s_{j−1}·2^{-n_o}E_{r†}`.  By the definition of `r†`, either
`Γ″(r†) ≤ θ`, that is `E_{r†} ≤ θT_{n_o}(κ(r†)) ≤ θT_{n_o}(κ(r†+1))`, or `Γ̃(r†) ≤ c_ηθ`, that is
`E_{r†} ≤ c_ηθ|B(n_o, r†−1)| ≤ c_ηθ·2^{n_o}π†`; in both cases `tail ≤ θe^bℓ` and the algorithm stops.  All
of this supposes `r† ≥ Δ`, and none of the inequalities is strict, so the pass with `M = M‡`
exactly is covered: for `r† ≥ Δ` the size is doubled only below `M‡` at level `j`.  If `r† < Δ`,
then `M‡ = K·2^{n_o}/(1−η)`.  An unpopulated pass with `M > M‡` has `2^{n_o}q < 1`, an empty tail, and
stops.  The pass with `M = M‡` exactly — it belongs to the doubling sequence only for `η = ½` — has
`2^{n_o}q = 1`, closing radius `0` and `tail = s_j2^{-n_o}E_0 ≠ 0`.  For `1 ≤ r† < Δ` it stops as well:
`E_1 = (e^{2u}−1) + n_o(e^u−1) ≥ (n_o+2)E_0`, so with `λ ≤ 1` — here this hypothesis of Theorem 11.56 is
used, in the form `e^λ < n_o + 2` — `e^λE_0 < E_1 ≤ E_{r†}`, and `tail < s_{j−1}·2^{-n_o}E_{r†} ≤ θe^bℓ` as
before.  For `r† ∈ {0, −1}` it need not stop, and the size can be doubled once more, to `2M‡`
exactly; but then `π† ≤ 2^{-n_o}`, hence `M† ≥ M‡`, every sample of level `j` is at most
`2M‡ ≤ 2M† < 2e^λM†`, and the bound stated holds.  ∎
(The case `r† < Δ` was one sentence in the first version — "a pass with `2^{n_o}q < 1` has an empty
tail" —, which does not cover `M = M‡`.  Found and closed by the Scientific Discovery Division,
SCI-REV-0007 §2, which saw that pass fail to close in `1255` of `4500` targeted runs of its own
implementation.  Ours agrees (`experiments/coordinator_checks/nested_review_R6/t1_cap_corner.py`): for
`r† ∈ {0, −1}` the pass fails to close in `1283` of `2299` cases and the largest sample is `2M‡`
exactly in `1243` runs; for `1 ≤ r† < Δ` it closes in all `56` cases; no sample reaches the cap in
`4500` runs (the largest is `0.91` of it); and on exact tables the closing inequality of the main
case, `e^λE_r ≤ θ·max{c_η|B(n_o, r†)|, T_{n_o}(κ(r†+1))}` for `r ≤ r† − Δ`, holds in all `101 707` cases
tried, with the ratio `0.99` in the worst.)
In the constants of Theorem 11.52 the same argument gives **`M < 2e·M†` in place of `8Je²M†`**
(an unpopulated pass with `M ≥ max{M†, M_j^neg/(4Je)}` passes the closure test, and
`M_j^neg ≤ 4Je²M†`), so the first branch of the minimum in its cost bound loses the factor
`4Je`.  In the harness the cap is attained up to `9 %` (a sample of `3.7·M†` at `n_o = 24`, `u = ½`,
`λ = ½`, on a landscape "plateau, then cone", where the cap is `4.06·M†` and `M̄ = 627·M†`), so
the constant cannot be improved much by this argument; that the division's search stayed
below `1.8·M†` reflects its instances and its parameters, not a better bound.

*Remark (for the outer loop, radial landscapes are almost the whole class)* **[P; Computational
Research Division, ENG-RES-0008 §5; checked by us; the restriction to a common fibre offset
restored and the size of "almost" quantified after the Scientific Discovery Division's
review SCI-REV-0008, R7-THY-1].**  *For instances with a fibre offset common to all outer
points* — `ψ(a, 0) + ln W(a)` independent of `a`, e.g. product instances `ψ(a, b) = g(a) + F(b)` —
the outer loop sees an instance only
through the law of the fibre averages, i.e. through the tail function `m(t) = |{W > t}|` on
the outer cube.  (Step 1 of Algorithm 2L⁺ also reads `ψ(a, 0)` at every outer point, so in
general what the outer loop sees is the joint law of the pair `(W(a), ψ(a, 0))`; for fibres
that differ from point to point other than by their value at the reference the reduction
says nothing.  ENG-RES-0008 §5 states this limit; an earlier version of this remark
dropped it.)  For a `u`-Lipschitz landscape `m` is nonincreasing and right-continuous
with `m(te^{-u}) ≥ ∂(m(t))`, `∂(k)` the size of the closed neighbourhood of the initial segment
of size `k` of the simplicial order (the neighbourhood of `{W > t}` lies in `{W > te^{-u}}`, and
Harper's theorem); conversely every such function is the tail function of a `u`-Lipschitz
landscape whose level sets are initial segments.  So with a fixed inner behaviour and a common fibre offset the law of everything the outer
loop sees — hence of the bracket and of the cost, not only the mean run — is that of an
instance whose outer level sets are
initial segments, and monotone radial profiles — those with whole balls — differ from the
general case only by partial shells: every tail probability of a `u`-Lipschitz landscape
on the outer cube `Q_{n_o}` is within a factor `n_o + 1` of that of a monotone radial one
(`|B(r+1)| ≤ (n_o + 1)|B(r)|`; Proposition T(d) of that review) — negligible at the
exponential scale, and not small against the differences that the division's tables
resolve (`ln(n_o + 1)/(na) ≈ 0.06` at `n = 1000`, `u = 1`).  Our request THY-REQ-0001 had called radial
instances "a small subfamily of the class"; for the outer loop that was wrong.

With `λ = 1`, `η = ½`, `η′ = 1`, `ν₁ = 1` and `θ = e^{gn−b} − (3e+1) − (2p_u)^ne^{-b}` this is Theorem 11.52 again,
with accuracy *exactly* `gn` instead of `gn + O(log n)` (Corollary K1.b of the report), and the
levels of Theorem 11.54 can be assembled from it by asking each inner family only for an
accuracy rate slightly above its nominal one (Proposition E there) — an induction that
needs no left limits.

**Proposition 11.57 (exponents at a bounded accuracy) [P; workstream K, Propositions K0, K5 and
Theorem K2].**  Extend exponent functions to accuracy zero: `T(0)` is an exponent of a family of
bracket procedures *at bounded accuracy* if `limsup_d d^{-1} ln C(d, x, e^{-cd}) ≤ T(0)` for every fixed
`x > 0` and `c > 0`.
(a) *Base family.*  The two-sample bracket with the threshold at the `K`-th largest weight of
the first sample, closed by both tail lemmas, has ratio at most
`((1+η)/(1−η))·(1 + Γ″(r̂))`; with Lemma 11.55 its cost is `exp(d·a + O(√d))` at every fixed
accuracy: `T₁(0) = a`, and `T₁ = θ_na` on `(0, ∞)`.  (The reason given for this in the earlier text —
a bound `3 + 12Γ(r)` — does not work: that ratio is not bounded up to `p_u d`.)
(b) *One more level.*  If a family has the exponent function `T` on `[0, ∞)`, then for every
`0 < φ < 1` and rates `2u = ξ₀ > ξ₁ > … > ξ_{L−1} > 0` there is a family with the exponent function
`min(T(ξ), T′(0))` at `ξ > 0` (a procedure of bounded accuracy also serves every extensive one;
the workstream's "`T′ = T` on `(0, ∞)`" was not nonincreasing — referee R8, m2) and

    T′(0) ≤ max{ φa ,  max_{1≤l≤L−1} [ min(φa, (1−φ)ξ_{l−1}) + (1−φ)T(ξ_l) ] ,  min(φa, (1−φ)ξ_{L−1}) + (1−φ)T(0) }.

With a fine ladder the right-hand side is `sup_{γ≥0}[min(γ, φa) + (1−φ)T(γ/(1−φ))]` up to `ε′` — the
bracket of (11.18.2) at `g = β = 0` —, and with two rungs it is at most
`max{ φa + (1−φ)T(ξ) , (1−φ)(ξ + T(0)) }`.  (Theorem 11.56 with `b = x/2`,
`λ = η = η′ = θ = min(x/12, ⅓)`, `ν₁ = 2e^un_o/θ`, and Lemma 11.55(c): `r† ≥ p_un_o − O(√n_o)`, so
`M̄ = e^{φan + O(√n)}`.)  The same holds uniformly for accuracies `x_n → 0` with `ln(1/x_n) = o(n)`.
(c) *The necessary condition holds at accuracy zero:* if `T ≥ θ_hint` on `(0, ∞)`, then
`sup_{γ≥0}[min(γ, φa) + (1−φ)T(γ/(1−φ))] ≥ h` for every `φ` (take `γ = φa`: `φp_u + (1−φ)ρ_i = Λ₁/u` for the
inner radius `ρ_i = (Λ₁ + φa/(1−φ))/u`, and `KL(·‖½)` is convex).  No level undercuts the lower
bound.

**Theorem 11.58 (the adaptive exponent at every bounded accuracy) [P, refereed (R8): Theorems
11.25(a) and 11.53 (machine-checked), 11.56 and Proposition 11.57 (paper), Harper's theorem,
the binomial median and Chernoff–Hoeffding bounds (cited); workstream K, Theorem K3 and
Corollary K3′].**  For every `u > 0`,
every fixed `ε > 0` and `0 < δ < ½`, the least number of evaluations with which a randomised
adaptive algorithm without a hint is `(ε/2, δ)`-correct on all of `L_u(Q_n)` — in the worst case
over the class, and likewise in expectation — is

    exp( n·h + o(n) ),        h = KL(Λ₁/u ‖ ½).

The same holds for every sequence of accuracies `ε_n = o(n)` with `ln(1/ε_n) = o(n)` (no limit of
`ε_n` need exist).
*Proof.*  Lower bound: Theorem 11.25(a),(d), an algorithm without a hint being one with a
hint.  (The two bounds count differently, in the direction that is needed — Scientific
Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0007; the first version did not say it.  Theorem 11.25(a) bounds
from below the expected number of *distinct* points evaluated at one instance, the zero
function, for finite mixtures of deterministic algorithms; the upper bound counts evaluations
with multiplicity, in every run and at every instance, and an algorithm that makes at most
`C_max` draws from finite sets is such a mixture.  So the theorem holds for either way of
counting, in the worst case and in expectation.)
Upper bound: fix `0 < η < h`, put `φ = min(½, η/a)`, `ξ = min(ε*/2, φη)`.  There is a family whose
extensive exponent at the rate `ξ` is at most `h + η`: Theorem 11.53 for the exact recursion
(`exactRec_reaches_hint` **[V]**) gives a level `k` with `T_k(ξ/2) < θ_hint(ξ/2) + η/2 ≤ h + η/2`, and
the assembly gives a family with that exponent at the rate `ξ`.  Take the cheaper of it and
the base family (`t₀ ≤ a`) and apply Proposition 11.57(b) with two rungs `m` times:

    t_{m+1} ≤ max{ φa + (1−φ)(h + η) , (1−φ)(ξ + t_m) } ≤ max{ h + 2η , (1−φ)t_m + φη },

so `t_m ≤ η + max{h + η, (1−φ)^m a}` (`two_rung_bound` **[V]**), which is at most `h + 2η` for
`m ≥ ln(a/h)/φ`.  The midpoint of the logarithms of a bracket of ratio `e^ε` is `(ε/2, δ)`-correct.  ∎

**Theorem 11.58a (an explicit sub-exponential term: `n·h + O(√(n ln n))`) [P: workstream Q,
`docs/workstreams/Q_REPORT.md`, Theorems Q8 and Q9 — every step re-derived by the
coordinator; **refereed (R12, `docs/reviews/R12_referee_report.md`): "the main claim survives,
with the constants as stated", no major finding, every new statement re-derived; with
independent code about 220 million node checks of the nested design, 523 000 one-level
checks with worst-case inner families and 0.9 million checks in exact arithmetic,
without a violation; six minor points — applied here**; **reviewed with replication by the Scientific
Discovery Division (SCI-REV-0017, its workstream R17): "proved as stated, given its inputs", no
critical and no major finding, nine minor ones — applied here; the bound's numbers reproduced
from the text alone, the lower bound re-derived, and the outer loop of a slope step run against
a simulated inner oracle for the first time (530 runs, no violation of Theorem 11.56)**; rests on Theorem 11.56 with its abort test before every query (paper, refereed R8,
reviewed by the Scientific Discovery Division), Lemma 11.55, Proposition 11.57(a) and the
epoch arithmetic of the rate (**V**, `RateFull.lean`); harness XVI.5 for the two lemmas, the
arithmetic and the lower bound; not machine-checked].**
Fix `u > 0`.  Let `N(n; ε, δ)` be the least `C` such that some randomised adaptive algorithm
without a hint — a finite mixture of deterministic adaptive algorithms, the class of
Theorem 11.25(a); the algorithm of the upper bound is one (proof of Theorem 11.58) — makes
at most `C` evaluations in every run at every member of `L_u(Q_n)` and is `(ε/2, δ)`-correct on
the class.  Let `d_0 = h/(a−h)`, `J_m = ⌈d_m⌉`,
`d_{m+1} = d_m(J_m a + h)/(J_m a − h d_m)`, `k_0 = 1`, `k_{m+1} = k_m + J_m + 1` be the epoch sequences of the
rate, and `B_m = h(1 + 1/d_m)`, so that `B_0 = a`, `B_{m+1} = B_m·J_m a/(J_m a + h)` and
`B_m − h ≤ c₁/(k_m + c₂)`.
(a) *Explicit, for every `n`.*  For every `n ≥ 1`, `ε > 0`, `0 < δ < 1` and every number of
epochs `M ≥ 0` there is an explicit design — `k_M − 1` nested levels of Algorithm 2L⁺ over
the two-sample bracket (`k_M` counts the bracket), each built as in steps 3 and 4 of the
proof wherever it is defined (the accuracy is handed to the inner family otherwise); its
parameters are formulas in `(u, n, ε, δ, M)` and the closing radius of each level, which is
read from the tables of that level's outer cube — with

    ln N(n; ε, δ)  ≤  n·B_M + 𝓔_M(n, ε, δ),
    𝓔_M  ≤  C₁(u, ε)·√n  +  (k_M − 1 − M)·[ (a/h + 4)·ln n + O_{u,δ}(1) ]  +  M·O(ln n + ln(1/ε) + ln M)  +  O(ln n + ln(1/ε)),

the second line as long as `(k_M − 1)·O(ln n) ≤ n` (the explicit `𝓔_M`, a sum of one term per
level, and every `O`: the workstream's (5.2) and Proposition Q9a; the `O_{u,δ}(1)` of a slope
step is `31, 39, 60, 178` nats at `u = ½, 1, 2, 4` and `δ = 0.05`, uniform in the level and the
epoch, and in `δ` as long as `ln(1/δ) = O(n)` — the science division's computation).  Serving a
node by the admissible procedure with the smaller certified bound (remark (1b)) can only
lower the cost; the bound does not need it.  `C₁` is a convergent
series that does not depend on the number of levels — about `5.5` at `u = 1`, `ε = 1`.
(b) *The order.*  For every fixed `ε > 0` and `0 < δ < 1`,

    limsup_{n→∞} ( ln N(n; ε, δ) − n·h ) / √(n ln n)   ≤   C_*(u) = 2·√( (1 + r̄)·c₁·(a/h + 4) ),     r̄ = (2a−h)/(a−h)

(`C_* = 4.65, 8.64, 13.5` at `u = ½, 1, 2`), and there is `C(u, ε, δ)` with
`ln N(n; ε, δ) ≤ n·h + C·√(n ln n)` for all `n ≥ 2`; the same holds for accuracies `ε_n ≥ n^{−A}`, with
constants that depend on `A`.  `C` is not `C_*`: `C_*` bounds the limsup only (the referee:
over `2 ≤ n ≤ 10^{12}` the ratio `(bound − nh)/√(n ln n)` is at most `3.8` at `u = 1`, `ε = 1`,
`δ = 0.05`, but `32` at `u = 4`, where the error terms carry a factor of order `e^{2u}` and the
formula beats enumeration only from `n ≈ 5.6·10⁴`; and beyond `10^{12}` the ratio keeps falling
towards about `2√((a−h)(a/h + 4))`, a fifth of `C_*` — numerical).
(c) *Against the lower bound.*  For `0 < δ < ½`, `ε > 0` and every `n` with `k*(ε) ≤ n/2`,

    ln N(n; ε, δ)  ≥  n·h − max{1, (ε + ln 2)/u}·ln((1−ρ_h)/ρ_h) − ln(1/(1 − 2δ)),        ρ_h = Λ₁/u,

and with `(ε + ln 2)/u` in place of the maximum whenever `(ρ_h − p_u)·n ≥ 1 − (ε + ln 2)/u`; so
that for fixed `ε` and `δ < ½`

    n·h − O(1)   ≤   ln N(n; ε, δ)   ≤   n·h + O(√(n ln n)).

(The lower bound is Theorem 11.25(a) — machine-checked: `(1 − 2δ)·2ⁿ/|B(n, k*)|` distinct
evaluations in expectation at the zero function — and three lines on paper, the
referee's (its finding m1; re-derived): for `k ≥ p_u n` the binomial median gives
`2^{-n}E_k(n) > ½e^{u(k+1) − nΛ₁} − 1`, so the dip of radius `k` changes `ln Z` by more than `ε` as
soon as `k ≥ p_u n` and `k + 1 ≥ ρ_h n + (ε + ln 2)/u`; the least such `k` exceeds `ρ_h n` by less
than `max{1, (ε + ln 2)/u}` — by less than `(ε + ln 2)/u` if that radius is already at least
`p_u n` — and `k*` is at most that; then `|B(n, k)| ≤ e^{nH(k/n)}` and the convexity of `KL(·‖½)`,
whose slope at `ρ_h` is `−ln((1−ρ_h)/ρ_h)`.  Without the maximum the bound is confirmed
numerically wherever it was tested, the small sizes at which the proviso fails included
(the referee: 19 839 cases with `n ≤ 200`; harness XVI.5(f)).  The first version of this
theorem quoted "`n·h − O(ln n)`" for every `δ < 1` from Theorem 11.25(a),(d), which states
neither.  Numerically the hinted lower bound is `n·h + ½ ln n − O(1)`.  The upper bound
holds for every `0 < δ < 1`.)

*Why `√(n ln n)` and not `n^{3/4}`.*  The earlier heuristic (remark (2), first version)
counted `≈ 1/η` bounded levels, each losing `e^{O(√n)}`.  In the recursion whose rate is
proved there are two kinds of level, and only one of them is a bounded level.
A **slope step** (step (i) of the proof of the rate: outer fraction `g/h` at the accuracy
rate `g`) is built at accuracies `x̂ ≥ X₀(n) = 1 + ln(6(n+1)) + 2u + e^u + h` (a threshold: `13.7`
nats at `u = 1`, `n = 470`; below it the accuracy is passed to the inner family), on an outer
block of `n_o = ⌊(x̂ − X₀(n))/h⌋ + 1` sites — about `X₀(n)/h` fewer than `x̂/h` —, with the closure
threshold `θ = e^{x̂−1} − (3e+1) − (2p_u)^n/e ≥ e^{x̂−1}/2`; by Lemma 11.55(d) its closing radius is
at least `min{n_o − 1, ⌊ρ_h n_o⌋ + 1}` and its outer sample has at most `e^{P_M}·(n_o + 1)·e^{n_o h}`
points (bounds: the exact radius of the level as built is larger, `168` against `152` at
`u = 1`, `n = 2000`, `n_o = 400`), and the whole step loses a *polynomial* factor,
`(a/h + 4)·ln n + O_{u,δ}(1)` nats.  A **drop** (step (ii): a fixed outer fraction) works at a
bounded threshold and loses `e^{O(√n_o)}` by Lemma 11.55(c) — but there is one drop per
epoch, the number of epochs up to level `k` is `O(ln k)`, and the outer fractions of the
drops decrease geometrically, so all the `√`-losses together are `C₁√n`.  Hence `k` levels
lose `C₁√n + O(k·ln n)`, uniformly in `k`, and `n·c₁/k + k·ln n` is least at `k ≈ √(n/ln n)`.

*Proof* (the workstream's report has every constant; here the statements that carry it).
Call a family of bracket procedures with certified cost bounds `e^{b(d, x, δ)}` (dimension `d`,
accuracy `x`, failure probability `δ`) *of type* `(B, σ, R; E)` if for all `d`, all admissible
`x`, all `δ` and all `Λ ≥ ln(1/δ) + d·ln 2`

    b(d, x, δ)  ≤  d·B − σ·min(x, R·d) + E(d, x; Λ),

`E` nondecreasing in `d` and `Λ` and nonincreasing in `x`: a piecewise-linear majorant, as in
the proof of the rate, with an error term.  By Proposition 11.57(a) and Lemma 11.55(c) the
base family is of type `(a, 0, ∞; E_base)` with `E_base = u√((d/2)·ℓ⁰_x) + O(ln d + ln(1 + Λ))`,
`ℓ⁰_x ≤ ln(4/x) + 3u + ½` for `x ≤ 1`.
*1. One level, exactly* (Proposition Q1).  With `Λ_lev = ln 2M̄ = P_M + ln(1/π†)` and
`ln((J+1)·cnt(x)) = x + P_cnt`, where `P_M ≤ P_cnt` are the logarithms of the polynomial factors
`J`, `ν₀`, `K` of Theorem 11.56:  `ln C_max ≤ ln(L+2) + max{Λ_lev, max_l [min(Λ_lev, x_{l−1} + P_cnt) + ln C_l]}`.
*2. The failure probability handed down* (Lemma Q2):
`ln(1/δ′) + n_i·ln 2 ≤ [ln(1/δ) + n·ln 2] + ln(4L) + P_M`.  The `n_o·ln 2` that the outer sample adds
to `ln(1/δ′)` is taken out of the dimension, so the quantity `ln(1/δ) + (dimension)·ln 2` grows
by `O(ln n)` per level and by nothing else; every `K` in a nest of any depth is
`O(η^{−2}(n + k·ln n + ln(1/δ)))`, with `η = ½` in a slope step and `η = c_m` in the drop of epoch
`m` (only `ln K` enters the bound).
*3. The slope step* (Proposition Q6).  Let a family be of type `(B, σ, R; E)` with `B ≥ h`,
`0 ≤ σ ≤ 1`, and `R ≤ h` or `R = ∞`, `σ = 0`.  For the accuracy `x̂ = min(x, R′n)`, `R′ = Rh/(h + R)`
(`h` if `R = ∞`), take Algorithm 2L⁺ with `n_o = ⌊(x̂ − 1 − c_log(n))/h⌋`,
`c_log(n) = ln(6(n+1)) + 2u + e^u`, `λ = 1`, `η = ½`, `η′ = 1`, `ν₁ = 1`, `b = 1`,
`θ = e^{x̂−1} − (3e+1) − (2p_u)^n/e` and the ladder `2un_i > ⌈x̂⌉ > ⌈x̂⌉ − 1 > … > 1` (capped at
`⌈2un_i⌉ − 1`), served by the family; and pass the accuracy through if `x̂ < 1 + c_log(n) + h`.
Its certified accuracy is exactly `x̂`; `θ ≥ e^{x̂−1}/2` meets the threshold of Lemma 11.55(d)
at `e = h`, so `Λ_lev ≤ x̂ − 1 + P_M`; `R·n_i ≥ x̂`, so every rung is in the range of the
majorant; each rung costs its gap `1`; and the result is of type
`(B, σ + B/h − 1, R′; E′)` with `E′ = E + (1 + c_log(n) + h)·B/h + 1 + P_cnt + ln(n+3)`
`= E + (B/h + 4)·ln n + O(1)` for `Λ = O(n)`, where `E` is taken at the accuracy `min(x, 1)` and
with `Λ` raised by `ln(4L) + P_M = O(ln n)` (step 2): the outer block is short by
`(1 + c_log)/h` sites, which buys the polynomial slack of the lemma.
*4. The drop* (Proposition Q7).  Let a family be of type `(B, 1, R; E)` with `0 < R ≤ h ≤ B`.
With the outer fraction `φ = R/(a + R)` — at which the outer sample `e^{φna}` equals the
largest accuracy `R·n_i` of slope one — `λ = η = η′ = θ = c ≤ ⅓`, `ν₁ = 2e^un_o/c`, a ladder of step
one below `⌈R·n_i⌉` and the tolerance `β = α − w(c)`, `w(c) = ln(e^c(1+c)/(1−c) + 2c) + c ≤ 6.25c`,
every rung has the same exponent `n_i·B`, the accuracy is at most `α`, and the result is
of type `(B·a/(a + R), 0, ∞; E′)` with
`E′ = E + u√(φn·ℓ_c/2)·B′/a + O(ln n + ln(1/c))`, `ℓ_c = ln 2 + 3u + 2.25c + ln(1/c)` (`E` at the
accuracy `β`, `Λ` raised as in step 3): the
`√`-overhead of Lemma 11.55(c), moved from the cost into the dimension by a shift of the
outer block.
*5. The epochs* (Theorem Q8).  In epoch `m`, `J_m` slope steps raise the slope from `0` to
`J_m/d_m ≥ 1` on the range `h/J_m` (each adds `B_m/h − 1 = 1/d_m`), and one drop with `R = h/J_m`
turns `B_m` into `B_m·J_m a/(J_m a + h) = B_{m+1}`.  The accuracies: the drop of epoch `m` takes
`w(c_m)` with `c_m = ε̂/(13(m+1)(m+2))`, `ε̂ = min(ε, 1)`, so that the base family is called at an
accuracy above `0.519·ε̂` whatever `M` (the proof of Theorem 11.58 halves the accuracy at
every bounded level).  Unrolling the error terms gives (a): `k_M − 1 − M` slope steps, `M`
drops whose `√`-terms are `u√(φ_m n ℓ_{c_m}/2)·B_{m+1}/a` with `φ_m = h/(J_m a + h) ≤ r̄^{-1}(1+κ)^{-m}` — a
convergent series — and the base.
*6. The number of levels* (Theorem Q9).  `k_{m+1} < (1 + r̄)k_m`; with `ℓ_S = (a/h + 4) ln n + O_{u,δ}(1)`,
`k† = √((1 + r̄)c₁n/ℓ_S)` and `M` the last epoch with `k_M ≤ k†`:
`n(B_M − h) + k_M ℓ_S ≤ 2√((1 + r̄)c₁nℓ_S)`, and `M = O(ln n)`.  For `n` below the threshold of
the asymptotics, `N ≤ 2ⁿ`.  ∎

*Numbers.*  Evaluated from the formula of (a) at `u = 1`, `ε = 1`, `δ = 0.05` and the best `M`
(the workstream's table, formula evaluation only; `h = 0.2626a`): the bound is `0.71·na` at
`n = 6.4·10⁴` (13 levels, the bracket included), `0.37·na` at `10⁶` (43 levels), `0.273·na` at `10⁸` and `0.2637·na` at
`10^{10}`; it is below the non-adaptive exponent `n·a` from `n ≈ 2.1·10⁴` on (the referee's scan;
the workstream says `3·10⁴`);
`(bound − nh)/√(n ln n)` lies between `2.4` and `3.8` for `1.6·10⁴ ≤ n ≤ 10^{12}`, while
`(bound − nh)/n^{3/4}` falls from `1.0` to `0.013`.  The exact certified cost of the design was
evaluated by the workstream for three nested levels up to `n = 6.4·10⁴`, five up to
`1.6·10⁴` and seven up to `4·10³`: in the `3.8·10⁶` checks made in these nests — every slope and
drop node, and three accuracies (the two ends and the middle) of every ladder served by the
base bracket — every inequality of the induction holds (the science division's referee
checked every node of nests of the same design, the base brackets included: 2.8 million,
no violation).  The referee, with an implementation of its own: all twelve rows of
the formula table and every number of the nest tables reproduced; the two inductive
steps on `523 000` levels with worst-case inner families, far outside the epoch schedule
(least slack `2.2` nats for the slope step, against error terms of `48` to `8 096`: the step is
nearly sharp); nests of up to seven levels on `220` million nodes, awkward sizes
`n = 2 … 200` and extreme `ε`, `δ`, `u` included; the two lemmas of the closing radius in exact
arithmetic.
*What it is not.*  (i) **Not a competitive design at any size where it can be evaluated:**
three levels of this schedule are certified at `0.83·na` at `n = 6.4·10⁴` where the tuned
two-level design of remark (1b) has `0.54` and three tuned levels `0.43`; the schedule
copies the proof of the rate, which spends seven levels on what the exact recursion does
with two, and its slope steps treat the base family as if it cost `e^{da}` at every
accuracy.  Its purpose is the order of the error term.  (ii) **Not the true order:**
`√(n ln n)` is an upper bound for this method.  With a rate `C/k²` *for an explicit schedule
whose levels lose `O(ln n)`* the level term would drop to `O(n^{1/3}(ln n)^{2/3})` and the bound
would be `n·h + O(√n)` — a conjecture; the observed `0.65a/k²` concerns the exact recursion,
for which no such schedule is known (**since proved, with both terms gone: Theorem 11.58e
below has `n·h + O(n^{1/3}(ln n)^{2/3})`, by a schedule of convex families of lines**).  The `C₁√n` of *this schedule* comes from its drops,
which work at a bounded threshold on an outer block of positive fraction (Lemma
11.55(c)); the workstream's report takes a `√n` to be unavoidable for the family, because
the finest rung of the top level calls a bounded-accuracy procedure.  We do not think it
is (**since proved: Proposition 11.58c and Theorem 11.58d below — workstream Q2, refereed
internally; the sketch is kept as it was written**), and state the reason as a sketch only (**the coordinator's; not written out, not
refereed, nothing in the theorem depends on it**): a drop run at the accuracy `C·ln n`
with a polynomially large threshold closes above `p_u·n_o` and loses a polynomial factor
(Lemma 11.55(d) with `e·n_o = O(ln n)`); and from the accuracy `C·ln n` a bounded accuracy is
reached by levels whose outer block has only `Θ(ln n)` sites and is enumerated — every
such level multiplies the cost by `e^{O(ln n)}` at its fine rungs and removes `Θ(ln n)` sites
from the dimension, which pays for it once the block is long enough, so that a chain of
`n/ln n` of them adds `O(ln n)` in all.  What limits the order of this method is then the
rate alone.  (iii) **No lower bound**
beyond the hinted one of (c), `n·h − O(1)`.  (iv) **Extensive accuracies** — the `o(n)` of Theorem 11.54 — are not
treated: the step at an accuracy rate `g` has outer accuracy rate `g + θ_hint(g) ≥ h`, again
bounded away from zero, so `n·θ_hint(g) + O(√(n ln n))` is expected by the same method
(conjecture; not written — **since proved with a smaller term, `n·θ_hint(g) + O((ln n)²)`: Theorem
11.58e(g)**).  (v) **It rests on Theorem 11.56 far from the parameters at
which that theorem was simulated** — thresholds `e^{Θ(n)}` together with ladders of `Θ(n)`
rungs that end at `x_L = b` exactly, up to `√(n/ln n)` nested levels, inner failure
probabilities `e^{−Θ(n)}`, and the abort rule in the form "before every query, every inner
call counted with its certified bound" (with that rule a nested run costs exactly its
certified bound in every run and the test never fires on the good event; with the rule
as it was worded before this checkpoint the theorem would lose `ln(1 + k_M/2)` nats and
nothing else — the referee's argument).  The statement of Theorem 11.56 covers all this;
no run with real inner procedures does, and none can (the outer loop of a slope step has
been run against a simulated inner oracle by the science division — 27 designs, 530 runs,
thresholds `e^{12}` to `e^{79}`, valid and invalid inner answers — without a violation of any
claim of Theorem 11.56: SCI-REV-0017): the smallest slope step exists at `n = 187` (`u = 2.5`;
at `n = 202` for `u = 2`, `470` for `u = 1`), its certified bound there is `e^{142}` (`e^{125}`, `e^{101}`),
and a run of it that does not abort makes at least `e^{49}` (`e^{43}`, `e^{36}`) evaluations (the
referee's computation); the checks of this theorem evaluate bounds, not runs.  (vi) **The
composition at depth is not evaluated:** exact evaluation reaches seven levels and
`n ≤ 6.4·10⁴`, where the design is not yet better than the base family; where the theorem
says something new (`M = 5 … 32` epochs for `n = 6.4·10⁴ … 10^{12}`) it rests on the paper
induction and on one-level checks.

**Lemma 11.58b (one level over a family whose certified cost is a maximum of lines) [P: workstream
Q2, `docs/workstreams/Q2_REPORT.md`, Lemma U; refereed internally (`docs/workstreams/Q2_REVIEW.md`:
correct as stated; with an evaluator of the referee's own, 973 668 levels with inner families
that saturate their type, least slack `2.0` nats; part (ii) is the referee's answer to a question
of the coordinator, on 353 184 levels); rests on Theorem 11.56 and Lemma 11.55(d); harness XVI.9;
not machine-checked].**
Let a family of bracket procedures for the dimensions `d ≤ N` have certified costs

    b(d, x, δ)  ≤  max_i [ d·B_i − σ_i·min(x, R·d) ]  +  E(d, x; Λ)        (x ≥ x_min,  Λ ≥ ln(1/δ) + d·ln 2)

for finitely many lines `(B_i, σ_i)`, `B_i ≥ 0`, `0 ≤ σ_i ≤ 1`, a common range `R`, and an error function as in
the proof of Theorem 11.58a.  Let `n ≤ N`, a tolerance `b ≥ max(1, x_min)`, an outer block `1 ≤ n_o ≤ n − 1`
with `2u·n_i > b`, an outer accuracy rate `e ≥ 0`, a threshold `θ ≥ 3(n_o + 1)·e^{2u + e^u + n_o·e}`, and a cap `Ξ` with
`n_o·θ_na(e) ≤ Ξ ≤ min(n, R·n_i)`.  Algorithm 2L⁺ in dimension `n` with `λ = 1`, `η = ½`, `η′ = 1`, `ν₁ = 1`, this `n_o`, `θ`
and `b`, and the ladder of step one from `b + min{⌈Ξ − b⌉₊, ⌈2un_i − b⌉ − 1}` down to `b`, served by the family,
has accuracy `ln[(2p_u)^n + e^b(3·exp(1) + 1 + θ)]`, closes with `ln(1/π†) ≤ n_o·θ_na(e) + ln(n_o + 1)`, and

    ln C_max  ≤  max_i [ n_i·B_i + (1 − σ_i)·n_o·θ_na(e) ]  +  ℓ₀^b(n, Λ)  +  E(n, b; Λ + q^b(n, Λ)),

with `ℓ₀^b(n, Λ) = 3 ln n + ln(Λ + ln n) + O(1)` (`≈ 4 ln n` for `Λ = O(n)`) and `q^b = O(ln n + ln ln Λ)`, both explicit;
the failure probability handed to the family satisfies `ln(1/δ′) + n_i ln 2 ≤ Λ + q^b(n, Λ)`.
(ii) *Lines valid at all accuracies.*  The same holds with `R = ∞` and positive slopes, with the cap
`Ξ = n_o·θ_na(e)`, provided one of the lines is nonnegative at the accuracy `max(n_o·θ_na(e), b)` in the
dimension `n_i` — for instance the zero line `(0, 0)` is among them.  Without such a line the
inequality is false.  What the proof uses of the majorant of the family is only that it is
nonincreasing in the accuracy with slope at least `−1`.

*Reading.*  This is the finite-`n` form of the line `γ + (1 − φ)·T(γ/(1 − φ))` at `γ = φ·θ_na(e)` of the
exponent-level recursion (`StepLE.of_limit` **[V]**), with an explicit error of `≈ 4 ln n`: the outer
sample costs `e^{n_oθ_na(e)}`; rungs finer than `n_oθ_na(e)` are needed by `e^{x_l + O(ln n)}` points only and cost
`(1 − σ)x_l` more than `n_i·B`; coarser rungs are needed by all sampled points and their terms decrease
with slope `σ`; the maximum sits at the rung `≈ n_oθ_na(e)`.  The proof gives the sharper
`ln C_max ≤ ln(L + 2) + 1 + P_cnt + E + max_i[n_iB_i + (1 − σ_i)G]` with the level's own constants and
`G = (ln 2M̄ − 1 − P_cnt)₊ ≤ n_oθ_na(e)`, which is attained up to a fraction of a nat (harness XVI.9: least
slack `0.26`–`0.37`); at the sizes of exact tables `G` is far below `n_oθ_na(e)` — the closing radius is well
above its guaranteed value (`ln(1/π†) = 11` against `n_o·a = 33` at `n_o = 100`, `u = 2`) — so the displayed
form alone would not detect a wrong coefficient there.  *Two uses.*  At `e = h` it is the slope step
of Theorem 11.58a with the error `σ′·(1 + c_log(n) + h) + ℓ₀`, `σ′` the *new* slope, in place of
`(B/h)(1 + c_log(n) + h) + ℓ₀`: on average over an epoch `(9/2)·ln n` instead of `(a/h + 4)·ln n`.  At `e = 0` it is
part (a) of the next proposition.

**Proposition 11.58c (the drop without its `√`; a chain back to a bounded accuracy) [P: workstream Q2,
Propositions D′ and T; refereed internally as above (the chain by exact recursion: 3.5 million
levels of 10 962 chains away from the design, least slack `3.4` nats); harness XVI.9(d), (e)].**
(a) *The drop at a logarithmic accuracy.*  Let a family be as in Lemma 11.58b with a range `0 < R ≤ 1`,
let `0 < φ ≤ R/(a + R)` and `𝒳 ≥ b + ln(3·exp(1) + 2 + 3(φN + 1)·e^{2u + e^u})` (`= b + ln(φN + 1) + O(1)`).  The level of the
lemma with `n_o = ⌊φn⌋`, the rate `e = 0`, the cap `R·n_i` and `θ = e^{𝒳−b} − (3·exp(1) + 1) − (2p_u)^n e^{−b}` has accuracy
exactly `𝒳` and closes with `ln(1/π†) ≤ n_o·a + ln(n_o + 1)` — **no `√n_o`** —, and the family it defines (the
accuracy is passed through where the level is not defined) is of the flat type

    ( B′, 0, ∞;  E + B̃ + ℓ₀^b ),        B′ = max_i [ (1 − φ)·B_i + (1 − σ_i)·φ·a ],     B̃ = max{1, bφ/(2u(1 − φ))}·max_i (B_i − (1 − σ_i)a)₊ .

For one line of slope one and `φ = R/(a + R)`: `B′ = B·a/(a + R)` — the drop of Theorem 11.58a without its
`u√(φnℓ_c/2)`.  The price is the accuracy: the family delivers `𝒳 ≈ ln n`, not a bounded accuracy.
(A drop at a bounded threshold stops closing at `p_un_o − Θ(√n_o)` and pays `e^{n_oa + Θ(√n_o)}` for its
block — more than `n_o·a + 1.4·u√n_o` on the exact tables of the harness; a polynomial threshold
closes above `p_un_o`.)
(b) *The chain.*  Let a family be of the flat type `(B′, 0, ∞; E)` with `0 < B′ ≤ ln 2` and least accuracy
`𝒳 > 1`, and let `0 < α ≤ 1`.  In dimension `d` take Algorithm 2L⁺ with a **short** outer block of `m` sites,
`λ = η = η′ = θ = c = α/(13⌈N/m⌉)`, `ν₁ = 2e^um/c`, and a ladder of two rungs `2u(d − m) > 𝒳 > b_d`: the coarse rung
is served by the family in dimension `d − m`, the fine rung by *the same construction* in dimension
`d − m` (and below a dimension `d₀ = O(m + 𝒳 + ln(N/α))` by the base bracket).  The procedure has
accuracy at most `α` in every dimension `d ≤ N`, and its certified cost satisfies

    b(d, ·, δ)  ≤  d·B′  +  E(d, 𝒳; Λ*)  +  A_T(d, Λ*)  +  j(d)·[ 𝒳 + P̄_cnt + ln 4 − m·B′ ]₊ ,

`j(d) ≈ d/m` the number of levels of the chain, `Λ*` the value of `Λ` at its bottom.  If the block is long
enough, `m·B′ ≥ 𝒳 + P̄_cnt + ln 4` — that is `m = Θ((ln N + ln(1/α))/B′)` — the last term vanishes and
`Λ* < Λ + d·B′`: **a chain of any length costs its additive term once**,

    A_T  ≤  (ln 2/B′ − 1)·(𝒳 + P̄_cnt) + O(ln N)  =  O(ln N + ln(1/α))

(`(a/B′ − 1)` in place of `(ln 2/B′ − 1)`, up to `O(√(m ln(1/c)))`, when Lemma 11.55(c) applies to the block).
*Why once.*  At every level the coarse rung is needed by all `≈ e^{ϖ + P_M}` outer points
(`ϖ ≥ ln(1/π†)` of the block) at `e^{(d−m)B′}` each: `ϖ − mB′ + P_M` nats more than `e^{dB′}`.  The fine rung is needed
by `e^{𝒳 + P_cnt}` points only, and the procedure that serves it lives in dimension `d − m`: its cost
`e^{(d−m)B′ + A}` is `e^{dB′ + A}·e^{−mB′}`, which pays for the `e^{𝒳 + P_cnt + ln 4}` as soon as the block is long enough.
So the maximum over the chain is the first term of its *first* level; with a shorter block every
level adds the deficit (harness XVI.9(e): with half the block the excess grows by `57`–`73` nats
over four to six levels).

**Theorem 11.58d (the bounded levels need no `√n`) [P: workstream Q2, Theorems A and B, Proposition
A′; refereed internally: correct as stated given Theorem 11.56 with the abort rule before every
query, Lemma 11.55(c), (d), Proposition 11.57(a) and the epoch arithmetic; the nested design
evaluated exactly by the workstream and reproduced to the last digit by the referee for one to
three epochs up to `n = 8·10³` (`729 000` nodes of the induction, no violation); not
machine-checked].**
In the schedule of Theorem 11.58a replace every drop by the drop of Proposition 11.58c(a) followed
by a chain (b), and the base bracket at a bounded accuracy by the base bracket at the accuracy
`ln 12 + 2 ln(n+1) + 2u + e^u` followed by a chain.  Then for all `n ≥ 1`, `ε > 0`, `0 < δ < 1` and every number of
epochs `M ≥ 0`

    ln N(n; ε, δ)  ≤  n·B_M + 𝓔′_M(n, ε, δ),

where `𝓔′_M` is an explicit sum of `k_M − 1 − M` slope-step terms, `M` drop terms, `M + 1` chain terms and the
base term, each `O(ln n + ln ln(1/δ))` — the top chain `O(ln n + ln ln(1/δ) + ln(1/min(ε, 1)))` — as long as
`(k_M − 1)·O(ln n) ≤ n`: **no term of the order `√n`.**  Consequently, for fixed `u` and `δ`, there are `n₀` and `C′`
with

    ln N(n; ε, δ)  ≤  n·h + 2·√( (1 + r̄)·c₁·n·ℓ̄_S ) + C′·( (ln n)² + ln(1/ε) )        (n ≥ n₀,  0 < ε ≤ 1),      ℓ̄_S = (9/2)·ln n + O(ln ln n),

    limsup_{n→∞} ( ln N(n; ε_n, δ) − n·h ) / √(n ln n)   ≤   C_*′(u) = 3·√( 2(1 + r̄)·c₁ )

for every sequence `ε_n ∈ (0, 1]` with `ln(1/ε_n) = o(√(n ln n))`; `C_*′ = 3.50, 6.56, 10.57` at `u = ½, 1, 2`
(`C_* = 4.65, 8.64, 13.5`).  Against Theorem 11.58a: (i) the `C₁(u, ε)·√n` is gone — behind the level term
stands `O((ln n)²)` (`M + 1` chains and `M` drops at `O(ln n)` each, `M = O(ln n)`); (ii) the accuracy enters
