hint, Theorem 11.110(e) gives at most the order `(e^{Δ} − 1)/ε`; **worst case against worst
case the hint is worth the factor `(1 − e^{−Δ})/ε` — at most `1/ε`, and `Δ/ε` for a narrow
sandwich.**  (Harness XXIV.11: `N_KL` is within 4 per cent of `2 ln(2/δ) sinh²(Δ/2)/ε²` at five
pairs `(Δ, ε)`; on two-level members the exact failure probability of the plug-in estimate
is at most `0.0072` at `δ = 0.05` with `N_KL` evaluations and at least `0.16` with a quarter of
them; and the exact number of bits at which the two binomial laws of the lower bound are
at total variation `1 − 2δ` lies between the Pinsker bound and `N_KL`, within a factor `3.5`
of each.)
*Illustration (arithmetic only, on numbers reported by the science division for its
twenty-residue instance, SCI-MSG-0020: deterministic bracket of width `0.0605` nats, its
sampled brackets of width `5.0·10⁻³` from 50 000 samples):* (c) gives a width of at most
`7.6·10⁻⁴` nats from 50 000 samples at `δ = 0.05`, and `5·10⁻³` from 1 200.  **The division has
since run it** (SCI-MSG-0025 §4; its numbers, not re-run by us): `[518.26204, 518.26279]`, a
width of `7.4·10⁻⁴`, from 50 000 accepted of 851 939 proposals on its own sandwich — its
earlier bracket from the same number of evaluations was seven times wider — and
`[518.26231, 518.26252]` on the pair-form sandwich of Theorem 11.18d(c′); on enumerated
instances the truth was inside the bracket in 1 460 of 1 460 repetitions.

**Proposition 11.113a (nested sandwiches: the inner bracket at the price of free
rejections) [P; harness XXIV.12] (an answer to the division's question P6-T3,
SCI-MSG-0025 — "is there a statement of this kind for the envelope itself, of which every
share allocation is an upper bound?"; elementary, nothing claimed new).**  Let
`m₋ ≤ e₋ ≤ E ≤ e₊ ≤ m₊` pointwise, where `Z(m₋)`, `Z(m₊)` are known and the Gibbs measure of `m₋`
can be sampled (the *outer* sandwich), while `e₋`, `e₊` can be computed at any given state
without an evaluation of `E` but have no computable partition functions (the *inner*
sandwich).  With `q` and `W` as in Proposition 11.113 for the outer sandwich and
`A = Z(m₋) − Z(m₊)`, put

    β = (e^{−e₊} − e^{−m₊})/(e^{−m₋} − e^{−m₊}),     ρ = (e^{−e₋} − e^{−e₊})/(e^{−m₋} − e^{−m₊}),     W_in = (e^{−E} − e^{−e₊})/(e^{−e₋} − e^{−e₊}).

(a) `β`, `ρ`, `β + ρ` and `W_in` lie in `[0, 1]`, and `W = β + ρ·W_in`: of the variable of the outer
sampler only the part `ρ·W_in` needs an evaluation.  (Where `e₋ = e₊` the energy is known,
`ρ = 0`, and `W_in` is not needed.)
(b) `Z(e₊) = Z(m₊) + A·E_q β` and `Z(e₋) − Z(e₊) = A·E_q ρ`, and a draw of `q` accepted with
probability `ρ(x)` has the law of the inner sandwich's own sampler.  So the inner sampler
runs by **free rejection**: propose from the outer sampler, compute `ρ`, evaluate `E` only
if accepted — at the fraction `E_q ρ = (Z(e₋) − Z(e₊))/(Z(m₋) − Z(m₊))` of the proposals — and
the two partition functions of the inner sandwich are estimated from the proposals alone.
(c) (**Sharpened and made precise by the division's review SCI-REV-0015, m7 and m8:
the first version had `2t_f` and did not state the sampling scheme.**)  Let `N_f` be fixed
in advance, the proposals independent draws of `q` (no evaluation; sample means `β̄`, `ρ̄`),
and let the proposals that are evaluated be chosen among the accepted ones by a rule
that looks at the acceptance indicators only — all of them, the first `N`, or an
independent stream of `N` accepted draws; `N` is the number evaluated and `W̄_in` their mean.
Then, with probability at least `1 − δ`,

    | Z(E) − Z(m₊) − A·(β̄ + ρ̄·W̄_in) |   ≤   A·( t_f + ρ̄·t ),       t_f = √(ln(6/δ)/(2N_f)),   t = √(ln(6/δ)/(2N))

(Hoeffding's inequality for `β`, for `β + ρ` — the two ends `Z(e₊)`, `Z(e₋)` of the inner
bracket, both variables in `[0, 1]` — and for `W_in`, the last conditionally on the
acceptance pattern: the error is `(E_qβ − β̄) + (E_qρ − ρ̄)·μ + ρ̄·(μ − W̄_in)` with
`μ = E W_in ∈ [0, 1]`, and its first two terms are affine in `μ`, hence at most the larger of
their values at `μ = 0` and `μ = 1`).  With any three two-sided confidence half-widths the
bound is `max(h_β, h_{β+ρ}) + ρ̄·h_W`.  A free term cannot be dropped altogether (the
division's simulation: 20 112 misses in 28 000 runs without it; in 168 000 runs at
`δ = 0.05` and `0.3`, 12 misses of this bound and none of the first version's, both far
inside the allowance; harness XXIV.12); it costs proposals only.  The bound is not proved if proposals are
drawn *until* `N` have been accepted (`N_f` is then a stopping time and `ρ̄` is biased, of
relative order `1/N`), nor for a stopping rule that looks at the running bracket.
*A variant for variance-sensitive half-widths* (the division's, SCI-RES-0017 §2 (iii);
its review found the proof right; re-derived).  `c = β + ρ/2` needs no evaluation and
`E_q W = E_q c + E_q ρ·(μ − ½)`, so
`|E_q W − (c̄ + ρ̄(W̄_in − ½))| ≤ h_c + h_ρ·(|W̄_in − ½| + h_W) + ρ̄·h_W`.  With Hoeffding half-widths
the two-end form is never wider; with the empirical Bernstein bound of Proposition
11.113(c′) this one is narrower wherever `c` varies less than either end — on the
division's instances in every row (standard deviations under `q` on one of them: `β` 0.18,
`β + ρ` 0.19, `ρ` 0.37, `c` 0.012).
(d) **In evaluations the price is that of the inner sandwich.**  As `N_f → ∞` the half-width
is `(Z(e₋) − Z(e₊))·t`, that of Proposition 11.113(c) for the inner sandwich up to the factor
`√(ln(6/δ)/ln(2/δ))` (`1.14` at `δ = 0.05`), which disappears if a vanishing share of `δ` is
given to the two free events; and, where the inner sampler is fine-grained and the inner
bracket of bounded width, no algorithm does better in order over the box `{e₋ ≤ E ≤ e₊}`
(Proposition 11.113(d)).  The outer sandwich determines the free computation — about
`1/(E_q ρ)²` proposals per evaluation for the two errors to balance, which needs the second
or third sampling scheme of (c): if every accepted proposal is evaluated there are
`1/E_q ρ` proposals per evaluation — and nothing else.
*Against the plain sampler* (the division's review, m9 and m10; the arithmetic
re-derived for the bound of (c)).  At equal numbers of evaluations the bound of (c) is
narrower than that of Proposition 11.113(c) on the outer sandwich iff
`√(N/N_f) + ρ̄ < κ(δ) := √(ln(2/δ)/ln(6/δ))` (`0.855`, `0.878`, `0.910` at `δ = 0.1, 0.05, 0.01`): never
for `ρ̄ ≥ κ`; otherwise for `N_f > N/(κ − ρ̄)²`; and if every accepted proposal is evaluated
(`N = ρ̄N_f`), only for `ρ̄ < ((√(1 + 4κ) − 1)/2)²`, which is `0.316` at `δ = 0.05`.  So with
Hoeffding half-widths the gain over the plain sampler is at most `κ/E_q ρ`, and **whether
the nested sampler is worth its proposals is decided by `E_q ρ`** — about `p^{m−k}` for an
outer form of level `k` at order `m` in a nearly frozen ensemble (the ratio of the two laws
`2p^kΓ` of Proposition 11.18f(a); the division measured `0.55, 0.57, 0.20, 0.14` on four
instances where this rule gives `0.54, 0.54, 0.28, 0.18`).
*For the anchored expansion* (Theorem 11.18d): `e_∓ = I_{m−1}E ∓ Σ_{T ⊆ S(x)} c_T`, the envelope —
computable at a state from the evaluated ball and the constants of the subsets of its
changed sites — and `m_∓` any share model of Theorem 11.18d(c′) with exact partition
functions.  **Every share form — sites, pairs, triples, any allocation of Proposition
11.18f — then costs the same evaluations, those of the envelope**, which vanishes on
every state with fewer than `m` changed sites (there `ρ = 0`: the energy is known and never
evaluated again).  What a share form buys is exact solvability: the bracket without
sampling, and the acceptance rate.  The interpolant computed exactly at the proposed
state also removes the slack of replacing the evaluated terms of orders `3, …, m − 1` by
banded minorants and majorants.  On the numbers the division gives for one instance
(valine, eight residues, order 4: envelope `0.0016` nats where triples give `0.011`) the
half-width at a fixed number of evaluations would fall about seven times; for serine on
a helix at order 4, where the division finds that no allocation certifies beyond
enumeration (its addendum A17 (15): at six residues sites, pairs, triples give `1.54`,
`0.85`, `0.48` nats and the envelope `0.27`), the envelope is what a sampled bracket would
pay for.  **The division has since run it** (SCI-RES-0017, SCI-MSG-0027 §4; its
numbers on its own instances, not re-run by us).  Validated by enumeration on two
instances: the identities of (b) to `3·10⁻¹⁴`, and the truth inside the bracket in 100 of
100 repetitions at each of three budgets.  At twenty residues and order 4, from the same
1 200 evaluations: a bracket of `1.2·10⁻³` nats with the first version of (c), `9.4·10⁻⁴`
with the two-end form, against `4.3·10⁻³` for the plain sampler of Proposition 11.113 —
and `2.7·10⁻⁴` with one known mean and empirical Bernstein half-widths, which on its
instances is worth more than the nesting (the energy sits in the middle of the
envelope: the true remainder is `0.0003` to `0.0024` of it at the evaluated states).  On a
charged twelve-residue sequence whose certified bracket is `0.057` nats the sampler
brackets `ln Z` within `3·10⁻⁵` nats, with probability `0.95` given the sandwich, from 60
evaluations beyond the ball; on a mixed-charge sequence whose certified bracket is `4.3`
nats, within `0.041` from 12 000 — a sandwich several nats wide is usable when proposals
are cheap.  Since then (SCI-RES-0019 §4): the charged sequence again from the ball of one
order lower — 96 366 evaluations instead of 1.6 million, a certified bracket of `1.41`
nats, the sampled bracket `0.0060` nats with 12 000 evaluations, containing both earlier
intervals — and a twenty-residue serine sequence (`8.2·10¹⁵` states) within `1.0·10⁻³` nats,
with the envelope bracket, the width of the bound of (c) and the width of the
variance-sensitive variant all predicted in its log before the ball existed, to a few
per cent.  A practical point of the division's for mobile ensembles: nearly every
proposal has its own changed set (296 795 distinct sets among 400 000 proposals), so
the envelope has to come from a table of all constants rather than from one closed-form
sum per set.  What is given up: with free sampling the bracket is probabilistic before
the first evaluation.

**Proposition 11.113b (one side at a time: what a floor alone and a ceiling alone
certify) [(a) V — the Scientific Discovery Division's Lemma A17.16, `ScienceA17.sandwich_cost`,
written and machine-checked by it and adopted unchanged as `SandwichCost.lean`; (b), (c) P,
elementary — the coordinator's answer to the division's question A16-T2 (SCI-MSG-0026); not
refereed; harness XXIV.13].**
Let `E` be an energy on a finite set (`β = 1`), `m₋ ≤ E ≤ m₊` two models with known partition
sums whose Gibbs measures `q₋`, `q₊` can be sampled, and `⟨·⟩` the mean under the true ensemble
`∝ e^{−E}`.  Write `a = E − m₋ ≤ A` and `b = m₊ − E` for the two bands.
(a) *The two free bounds, and what each loses.*  Without any evaluation
`ln Z(m₊) ≤ ln Z(E) ≤ ln Z(m₋)`, and

    ⟨b⟩ − ⟨b²⟩/2  ≤  ln Z(E) − ln Z(m₊)  ≤  ⟨b⟩ ,        ⟨a⟩  ≤  ln Z(m₋) − ln Z(E) = ln⟨e^{a}⟩  ≤  ⟨a⟩ + (e^{A}/2)·⟨a²⟩ .

The ceiling loses at most its mean band under the true ensemble.  The floor loses at
least its mean band and, beyond it, an amount that no moment of the band controls: a
state of true probability `1/D` whose band is `D` gives the mean band `1` and costs the floor
`D − ln D`, while the same band above costs the ceiling less than `2/D`.  (In the division's
words: a ceiling never delocalises, a floor can.)
(b) *A floor and its sampler certify both sides, at the price of the floor's own
excess.*  Under `q₋` the weight `W = e^{−a}` lies in `(0, 1]` and has mean `Z(E)/Z(m₋) = e^{−x}`, `x`
the excess of the floor.  With `N` evaluations at samples of `q₋`, with probability `1 − δ`,

    ln Z(m₋) + ln(W̄ − t)  ≤  ln Z(E)  ≤  ln Z(m₋) + ln(W̄ + t) ,        t = √( ln(2/δ) / (2N) ) ,

for every `E ≥ m₋`, with no ceiling.  The half-width is about `t·e^{x}`: an accuracy `ε` costs
`N ≈ ln(2/δ)·e^{2x}/(2ε²)` evaluations (of the order `e^{x}/ε²` with a variance-sensitive bound,
since `Var W ≤ E W`; Proposition 11.113(c′)).  The exponential cannot be avoided: on the
class `{E′ ≥ m₋}` every `(ε/2, δ)`-correct algorithm makes at least
`(1 − 2δ)·⌊(e^{x} − 1)/(2(e^ε − 1))⌋` evaluations at an instance of excess `x` at which no single
state carries that dip weight (Theorem 11.110(d) on the box `[m₋, E]`, a subclass).
(c) *A ceiling and its sampler certify the lower side only.*  Under `q₊` the weight
`W = e^{b} ≥ 1` has mean `Z(E)/Z(m₊)`, and so has every truncation at most:
`1 ≤ E_{q₊} min(W, c) ≤ Z(E)/Z(m₊)` with `min(W, c) ∈ [1, c]`.  Hence, with probability `1 − δ`,

    ln Z(E)  ≥  ln Z(m₊) + ln( mean of min(W, c) − (c − 1)·√( ln(1/δ) / (2N) ) )

— any number of evaluations improves the free bound, validly, for every `E ≤ m₊`.  But **no
algorithm certifies a finite upper bound of `ln Z` on the class `{E′ ≤ m₊}` with fewer than
`(1 − δ)·|X|` evaluations in expectation**: lowering the energy at one state that has not
been evaluated by `D` stays below the ceiling, changes no evaluated value and raises `ln Z`
by at least `D + ln π_E(a)` — the needle of Proposition 11.18e(b′)(i).  An estimate of
`E_{q₊}W` with its standard error is therefore not an upper bound (`DEAD.28`).
*Reading.*  The two sides answer two questions in opposite ways.  As a bound without
evaluations the ceiling is the safe side — its loss is a mean under the true ensemble —
and the floor the dangerous one.  As a place to sample from it is the other way round:
from the floor both sides can be certified, and the price is exactly the loss that made
the floor dangerous, paid exponentially in samples; from the ceiling the upper side
cannot be bought at any price short of evaluating every state.  What a ceiling adds to
the floor's sampler is a factor: with both, the sandwich sampler of Proposition 11.113
has the half-width `(e^{x} − e^{−y})·t` in place of `e^{x}·t` (`y` the defect of the ceiling), so
its cost is the floor's times `(1 − e^{−(x+y)})²` — nothing when the floor is far, everything
when the sandwich is narrow, where the cost falls from `1/ε²` to `(x + y)²/ε²`.  In the
vocabulary of Theorem 11.110 the floor's excess is the dip weight `Z(lo)/Z(r) − 1` and (b) is
its term `(Z(lo)/Z(r) − 1)/ε`; the ceiling's term is at most `1/ε` because a bump can only
remove mass that the sampler of the instance sees.
*Which sampler, in the Scientific Discovery Division's data* (SCI-RES-0019 §3; arithmetic
with the formula of (b) on its logged brackets, the floor-only sampler not run).  On four
of its sandwiches — floor's excess `3.67, 1.21, 0.131, 0.030` nats — the floor-only sampler
of (b) would need `6.9·10⁶, 2.3·10⁶, 9·10⁶, 7·10⁹` evaluations for the widths
`0.041, 0.0060, 0.0010, 3.3·10⁻⁵` that the nested sampler of Proposition 11.113a reached
with `12 000, 12 000, 1 200, 60`.  An outer ceiling is worth little where the floor is far
(the first two rows, as the factor `(1 − e^{−(x+y)})²` says); what makes the difference is
the *inner* sandwich — evaluations are spent only where the envelope leaves room.  Its
criterion: the ratio of the envelope's own bracket to the floor's excess.

**Corollary 11.114 (a ratio of two macrostate weights in a box class) [(a)–(c) V; (d) P]
(`BoxRatio.lean`, `BoxAdditions.lean`; harness XXIV.8).**  Let `A`, `B` be disjoint sets of
states, each of positive weight, `W_M(r) = Σ_{x∈M} π(x)e^{−r(x)}`, and `U_M`, `V_M`, `p_M(η)` the total
dip weight, the total bump weight and the detection bound of Theorem 11.110(c) for the
weights restricted to `M`; `U_M, V_M > 0` in (a) and (b), as there.  (The Lean statements of
(a) and (b) do not use disjointness; (c) asks that the perturbed set avoid the other
macrostate.  Both remarks: the division's review SCI-REV-0013, m6.)
(a) (`ratio_core`, `ratio_detect_ge`)  A member of the box whose `ln(W_A/W_B)` differs from
that of `r` by more than `η > 0` differs from `r` on a set of probability at least
`½·min(p_A(η), p_B(η))` under the mixture of the two macrostates' samplers — at the *same*
level `η` as for one partition sum: the worst case is a change of one macrostate alone, and
the price of a ratio is one factor two.
(b) (`ratio_spotCheck_correct`)  So the spot check with that mixture and
`N = ⌈ln(1/δ)/min(1, ½ min(p_A(ε/2), p_B(ε/2)))⌉` samples certifies the log-ratio within `ε/2`
on every class inside the box.
(c) (`logRatio_dipAlt_gt`, `logRatio_dipAlt_lt`, `logRatio_bumpAlt_lt`, `logRatio_bumpAlt_gt`,
`ratio_expected_queries_ge`, `ratio_expected_queries_ge_mixed`)  A set inside one
macrostate, disjoint from the other, whose dip weight exceeds `(e^ε − 1)W_M` changes the
log-ratio by more than `ε` when lowered to the floor, and so does one whose bump weight
exceeds `(1 − e^{−ε})W_M` when raised to the ceiling (the two bump lemmas are the division's,
machine-checked in its review and adopted — m5); pairwise disjoint such sets, of either
kind and in either macrostate, force of every randomised algorithm that is
`(ε/2, δ)`-correct for the log-ratio on the box, **at the instance `r` at which they are
heavy, `(1 − 2δ)` evaluations each in expectation** (the division's review SCI-REV-0015
read the Lean statement and its proof term and found the sentence faithful once "at
`r`, in expectation" is said).
(d) Hence, for `ε ≲ 1`, where no single state has that much dip or bump weight and
`U_M, V_M > 0` in both macrostates, **the cost of certifying a free-energy difference
between two macrostates in a box class is, up to a factor depending on `δ` only and an
additive constant,

    max_{M∈{A,B}} [ (W_M(lo)/W_M(r) − 1)/ε  +  (1 − W_M(hi)/W_M(r))/ε ]

— the larger of the two macrostates' own costs**, each computed inside its macrostate;
the second term, at most `1/ε`, is the whole cost near the floor of a macrostate.  (With
`a_M = W_M(lo)/W_M − 1` and `b_M = 1 − W_M(hi)/W_M`, for `ε ≤ 1` the division's review gives
`(1 − 2δ)·(max_M (a_M + b_M)/(6.9ε) − 1) ≤ cost ≤ ln(1/δ)·(10.7·max_M (a_M + b_M)/ε + 1) + 1` — its
constants, not re-derived by us.  The machine-checked lower bound of (c) is the sum over
the two macrostates of the larger of the dip and the bump packing, within a factor 2 of
the display on either side; the sampler of (b) is governed by the worse macrostate.)  (The
first version of this display had the dip term alone and the bumps in a parenthesis —
the defect that had just been removed from Theorem 11.110(e): at the floor of both
macrostates it was zero, while bumps force `(1 − 2δ)·10, 40, 200` evaluations at
`ε = 0.2, 0.05, 0.01` in the division's example.  Its review, m5.)
Three consequences.  (1) The cost does not depend on the weights of the macrostates: a
rare macrostate is not expensive as such — provided `π` can be sampled *conditionally* on
it, which is the tractability assumption here.  (2) Nothing cancels: in a class without
geometry the remainder on `A` says nothing about the remainder on `B`, and each macrostate
pays its own distance.  (3) If `A` and `B` partition the domain, the ratio costs at least
as much as `ln Z` (`Z(lo)/Z` is a weighted mean of the two ratios `W_M(lo)/W_M`) and can cost
arbitrarily more: a macrostate of weight `10⁻⁶` with a floor `8 k_BT` deep in a box that is
`0.1 k_BT` deep elsewhere has cost number `e^{8} − 1 ≈ 2980` for the ratio and `0.11` for
`ln Z`.  This settles the first instance of §12 item 11(a) — the class without geometry;
with geometry the question is open.  Part (f) of Theorem 11.110 applies to each
macrostate with the conditional measure: with floors `b_M` and variances `σ_M²` of the
remainder under `π(·|M)`, the difference of the two first-order estimates errs by at most
`W(b_A, σ_A²)` on one side and `W(b_B, σ_B²)` on the other.
*The range before any evaluation* (the Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-MSG-0025 §7, its
addendum A17(13); elementary).  In a box class the ratio itself lies between
`W_A(hi)/W_B(lo)` and `W_A(lo)/W_B(hi)`, and a population between
`Z_hi(A)/(Z_hi(A) + Z_lo(Aᶜ))` and `Z_lo(A)/(Z_lo(A) + Z_hi(Aᶜ))` — sharply, by the member that is
at the floor on one set and at the ceiling on the other; this is the box counterpart of
the transport range of §11.28, and what the cost of this corollary is the cost of
narrowing.  Where floor and ceiling are solvable models both ends are computed without
an evaluation: on the division's twenty-residue sandwich every single-site rotamer
population is certified within a relative 1.2 per cent from the triple form of Theorem
11.18d(c′) at order 5, and not at all from the site form at order 4 (its numbers).

*The floor as a function: lower models.*  Nothing in Theorem 11.110 needs `lo` constant.
With `m = f̂ + lo` — a *lower model*, `m ≤ E` pointwise — the cost number of (e) is

    Z(m)/Z(E) − 1  =  e^{F(E) − F(m)} − 1,          F = −ln Z,

the free-energy distance between the truth and its lower model, and both halves of the
sampler of (c) are rejection samplers from the Gibbs measure `π_m ∝ e^{−m}` of the lower
model: accept `x ∼ π_m` with probability `1 − e^{−(r(x) − lo(x))}` for the dip half and with
probability `e^{−(r(x) − lo(x))} − e^{−(hi(x) − lo(x))}` for the bump half (**[P]**, two lines from
the definitions of the dip and bump weights).  So what the theorem needs is a lower model
with a known partition function whose Gibbs measure can be sampled.  The pairwise lower
model of third order (Theorem 11.18a, `thirdOrderLowerModel`) is one, on interaction graphs
of small treewidth: stated this way, this section and the third-order certificates of
§11.4 are one result — the science division's observation (SCI-RES-0007 §3(2)).  The two
caveats are the two hypotheses: third-order constants obtained by enumeration or by
fitting are not certified, and a pairwise model on a general graph cannot be sampled
exactly.

**Proposition 11.112 (the floor is the end `p = ∞` of a family) [P — brought to this
programme by the Scientific Discovery Division: addendum A17 of
`docs/science/INFERENCE_LIMITS_ADDENDA.md` on its branch, summarised in SCI-RES-0007 §3;
parts (a)–(e) re-derived by the coordinator on paper and tested in harness XXIV.7; not
machine-checked; not refereed.  **In print**, as that division found afterwards
(SCI-RES-0009 §3, its reading): the cost table without a hint, in the sampling model and
with matching lower bounds, is the main result of Block and Shetty, *Partition function
estimation under bounded f-divergence* (arXiv:2602.23535, February 2026; in the
proceedings of the Conference on Learning Theory 2026 according to the record we found
ourselves, at the level of a search summary), and the rows for
Rényi orders are earlier in Kunsch, Novak and Rudolf (2019) and in the literature on
mean estimation with heavy tails.  What is not in what it read: the reading of the table
as a *verification* cost with a hint, the finite deterministic form, and part (f)].**  Write `Y = e^{−r}`, `μ = E_π Y = Z/Z₀`, `π_r = πY/μ` for the
true ensemble, and `D_p(π_r‖π) = (p/(p−1))·ln(‖Y‖_{L^p(π)}/μ)` for its Rényi divergence of
order `p` from the model (`D_∞ = ln max(Y/μ)`; `D_1` is the Kullback–Leibler divergence).  A
floor `r ≥ −ρ₋` is the bound `‖Y‖_∞ ≤ e^{ρ₋}`.  For `1 < p ≤ ∞` let `𝓑_p(B) = {r : ‖Y‖_{L^p(π)} ≤ B}`.
(a) *Detection.*  Two members of `𝓑_p(B)` that differ exactly on `D` satisfy
`π(D) ≥ (|μ − μ′|/B)^{p/(p−1)}` (Hölder's inequality; `Y` and `Y′` are non-negative, so no factor
two), with equality in the limit of a flat alternative on an empty background.
(b) *With a hint.*  The spot check of a hint `r̃ ∈ 𝓑_p(B)` with
`N = ⌈ln(1/δ)·(B/((1 − e^{−ε})μ̃))^{p/(p−1)}⌉` samples of `π` itself refutes every member with
`|ln μ − ln μ̃| > ε` with probability at least `1 − δ`.  If `B₀ = ‖Ỹ‖_p < B` and no state has
more mass than `q_low = ((e^ε − 1)μ̃/(B − B₀))^{p/(p−1)}`, every randomised algorithm that is
`(ε/2, δ)`-correct on the class makes at least `(1 − 2δ)⌊1/(2q_low)⌋` evaluations at `r̃` in
expectation (the alternative `Ỹ + (B − B₀)π(D)^{−1/p}·1_D` stays in the class by Minkowski's
inequality and raises `μ` by `(B − B₀)π(D)^{1−1/p}`; packing as in Theorem 11.110(d)).  In
terms of the bound `κ = (p/(p−1))·ln(B/μ̃)` that the class puts on `D_p` at the hint, for
`B − B₀ ≥ B/2` and `ε ≤ 1`:

    cost with a hint   =   Θ( e^{κ} / ε^{p/(p−1)} ),

with constants depending on `δ` and on `p` (bounded for `p` away from 1).  The case `p = ∞` is
Theorem 11.110 at a constant floor — there with the sharper instance-wise constant
`Z(lo)/Z − 1` in place of `e^{κ}` and the dip-weighted sampler in place of `π`; the case
`p = 2` is `(1 + χ²)/ε²`, `χ²` the bound on the chi-square divergence of the true ensemble
from the model.  The same sample size serves the class `{r : D_p(π_r‖π) ≤ κ}` itself — a
cone, not a ball: there `‖Y′‖_p ≤ e^{((p−1)/p)κ}μ′`, and the Hölder step in each of the two
directions gives `π(D)^{1−1/p} > (1 − e^{−ε})e^{−((p−1)/p)κ}` (our remark; **[P]**, three lines,
not in the harness).
(c) *Without a hint, `p ≥ 2`.*  `‖Y‖₂² ≤ μ^{(p−2)/(p−1)}B^{p/(p−1)} ≤ B²` (equality at two-level
members), so `[μ̂ − B/√(Nδ), μ̂ + B/√(Nδ)]` with the plain sample mean `μ̂` of `Y` under `π` is a
certificate valid for every member and every `N` (Chebyshev), and relative accuracy `ε`
needs at most about `e^{κ}/(δ(1 − e^{−ε})²)` evaluations.
(d) *A Kullback–Leibler bound.*  For the class `{r : D_1(π_r‖π) ≤ κ}` at its centre `r̃ = 0`:
every alternative with `|ln μ′| > ε` differs from the centre on a set of mass at least
`exp(−(κ + ln 2)/(1 − e^{−ε}))` (data processing; attained up to a per cent at `ε = ln 2`),
and two-level alternatives with `ln μ′ = ε` exist on every set of mass above `q_κ`, where
`(1 − e^{−ε})·ln((e^ε − 1)/q_κ) = κ + ε − O(q_κ ln(1/q_κ))`.  So the cost at the centre is
`e^{κ/(1 − e^{−ε})}` up to factors that depend on `ε` and `δ` only (the division first stated
`e^{Θ(κ/ε)}` and, after its literature search, `exp(Θ(κ/ε))/ε` with or without a hint and
beyond the centre — Block and Shetty; the two-sided form at the centre is our reading of
its two bounds): finite, and exponential in `κ/ε`.
(e) *Where such a bound comes from.*  For a product measure `π` and a remainder with
one-site oscillations `c_i`:

    D_p(π_r‖π)  ≤  Σ_i [ (p − 1)c_i²/8 + L(c_i) ]  ≤  (p/8)·Σ_i c_i²  ≤  p²Σ_i c_i²/(8(p − 1)),

in particular `D_2 ≤ Σ_i c_i²/4`.  (The last, weakest form is the bounded-differences bound
on the moment generating function with `μ ≥ e^{−E_π r}`, and is what the first version of
this part stated; the sharp first form is the division's, SCI-RES-0009 §3: the conditional
law of a site in the true ensemble, given the earlier sites, is a tilt of the model's
marginal with a log-ratio of range at most `c_i`; for such a pair the Rényi divergence of
order `p` is at most `(p − 1)c_i²/8 + L(c_i)` — a variance bound for the tilted law plus the
largest Kullback–Leibler divergence, the `L` of Theorem 11.110(a) — and Rényi divergences
add along the sites.  Re-derived here; it cites Cesar–Rogers and Bun–Steinke for the two
steps.)  At the additive instance on the uniform cube
`D_p = n[ln cosh(pu/2) − p ln cosh(u/2)]/(p − 1)`, which the sharp form attains as `u → 0`
(to within `0.3 %` at `u = 0.05` for the orders `1.5`, `2`, `4`).  At a fixed slope per site this is `e^{nu²/4}/ε²` — exponential, and
weaker than the samplers of §11.9; what it adds is the regime that the fixed-slope
asymptotics do not see: **square-summable first-order constants make certification by
plain reweighting polynomial, `e^{Σc_i²/4}/(δε²)` evaluations, with no hint and no
adaptivity.**
(f) *What does not suffice.*  A bound on a polynomial moment of the remainder energy under
the model *alone* — its mean, its root mean square, `E_π|r|^k` — does not bound the cost by
anything below the number of states: a dip of depth `d` on a state of mass `q` uses `q d^k`
of the budget and changes `μ` by `q(e^d − 1)` (a root mean square of `0.1 k_BT` allows a dip of
`100 k_BT` on a state of mass `10⁻⁶`, a change of `ln μ` by `86`).  Together with a floor it
does: Theorem 11.110(f).

*What the family says* (the division's reading, which we share).  A "typical norm" that
certifies a free energy must be an exponential moment of the remainder under the model —
a divergence of the **true ensemble from the model** — or a variance next to a floor; the
root-mean-square remainder that a fit reports is neither.  The direction matters: the
Gibbs–Bogoliubov principle minimises the opposite divergence `D_1(π‖π_r) = ln μ + E_π r`,
the gap of the cheap side, and a model chosen variationally can ignore a basin of the
true ensemble altogether.  And the rows compete: which a-priori bound is cheapest to pay
for depends on the instance.  *Not checked by us:* the division's statements for orders
`1 < p < 2` without a hint and its worst-case lower bound without a hint (its A17.3(ii),
(iii), the latter a sketch by its own account); its planted control on fits; that the
lower bound of (d) holds away from the centre.  *Open:* an instance-optimal sampler for
`p < ∞` (the analogue of the dip-weighted sampler; the division's request A17-T2).

*Without a hint.*  The spot check verifies a proposed remainder.  Without one, the sample
mean of `e^{−r(x_i)}`, `x_i` independent draws from `π`, with
`m = ⌈3 e^{w} ln(2/δ)/(1 − e^{−ε/2})²⌉` samples is `(ε/2, δ)`-correct on the whole box
(multiplicative Chernoff bound for a variable in `[0, e^{ρ₋}]` with mean at least `e^{−ρ₊}`
**[K]**): worst case `e^{w}/ε²`, which is the right order at members whose weight is dominated
by rare deep dips.  Instance-wise, an empirical Bernstein inequality (Maurer–Pontil 2009,
Theorem 4 — **[K]**, the form confirmed from a search summary of the paper, the paper not
opened: `docs/prior_art/L10_box_classes.md`; its coverage is tested by simulation in harness
XXIV.5) turns the same samples into a bracket for `E_π e^{−r}` of half-width

    √(2 V̂ ln(4/δ)/m)  +  7 (e^{ρ₋} − e^{−ρ₊}) ln(4/δ) / (3(m − 1)),

`V̂` the sample variance of `e^{−r}`: **the typical norm of the remainder sets the width of the
bracket, the floor of the class sets the number of samples below which nothing is
certified.**  The naive interval "mean ± two standard errors" is not a certificate: at a
member with a rare deep dip the sample variance is zero with probability close to
`e^{−mp}` (harness DEAD.28; `DEAD_ENDS.md` D56).

*What this does and does not say about measured remainders.*  An earlier version of this
paragraph illustrated the theorem with two sup-norm widths from the science division's
torsion-space pilot (`3.7` and `15.6 k_BT`) and the words "whatever the chain length".  Both
were badly chosen, as the division pointed out (SCI-RES-0007 §3(1), SCI-MSG-0017).  The
largest remainder of that solvent term against an explicitly pair-additive function
grows with the chain — `0.8, 1.7, 3.9, 8.1 k_BT` at two to five residues and `15.6` at eight
(its pilot, **[M]**) — so the floor that would have to be certified grows with it, and
the cost with its Boltzmann factor.  And a two-sided width is the wrong number to quote
in any case: the theorem charges the *one-sided* free-energy distance `ln(Z(lo)/Z)`.  The
division has since measured that distance, by exact enumeration, on 74 rotamer instances
of its own (homopeptides of five side-chain types — valine, leucine, serine, lysine,
phenylalanine — and one mixed sequence on fixed backbones; a force-field vacuum energy as known part, a generalised-Born solvent term as
remainder; SCI-MSG-0017, SCI-MSG-0018; **[M]** — its numbers under its labels, not
replicated here; with the *perfect* floor `lo = min r` of each instance, so these are the
prices that a certificate would have to pay, not certificates).  With the vacuum part
alone as known part, `ln(Z(lo)/Z)` is `0.07–1.7` for valine although the remainder is
`7–11 k_BT` wide at twelve residues, `10–56` for serine and `30–243` for two to four lysines;
it grows linearly with the chain, by `0.005` to `9 k_BT` per residue, in the three neutral
families that were measured at four to six lengths (valine, leucine, serine) — for lysine
there are three lengths and the values just quoted, steeper than `9` per residue and not a
fitted rate, and for phenylalanine and the mixed sequence values only.  Once
the pair part of the solvent term is moved into the known part it is at most `3.7` in all
74 instances (at most `0.22` for the neutral side chains); on the 53 instances for which
they were computed, the centred cumulant `K` of (a) is below `10⁻³` and the bracket (f),
evaluated with each instance's exact floor and variance, is within a factor five of it
(median ratio `1.04`).  (Three details of this paragraph were corrected by the division, which
we had asked to check it against its own text — SCI-RES-0010 §2: "six" side-chain types, linear
growth "in every family", and `K` "in all 74 instances".)  **The split matters more than
anything else in this paragraph** (the division's benchmark B10, SCI-MSG-0022; its numbers,
exact sums, not replicated): with the vacuum force field as the model the chi-square
divergence `D_2` of the solvated ensemble from the model is `4.0–45` for serine with three to
six residues; with a one-body fit of the solvent term added, `0.20–1.3`; **for independent
residues fitted to the solvated energy itself, `0.0015–0.096`** — a model with no pair terms at
all is ten to a hundred times closer than the complete vacuum pair terms with a one-body
correction, because the solvent term cancels 97 % of the vacuum pair variance on strand and
PPII backbones (screening; 75 % on the helix; nothing for valine).  So "the known part alone
as the model" is the worst of the natural splits for polar side chains, and in the model of
ignorance of this report — a known part plus a residual in a class — **the choice of the
known part is itself a modelling decision with an effect of orders of magnitude on the
certified cost**; the physically given split is not the one with the small residual.  The
division's conclusions, which we adopt as the reading of this section: the sup-norm width
is the wrong coordinate even for a floor; the quality of a fit does not predict the price
of a model that is far from the truth (for serine on a helix, with the vacuum force field as
the model, the root-mean-square error under the surrogate falls with the chain length while
the price rises by thirteen orders of magnitude) — for tractable families *fitted to the
solvated energy* it does predict the chi-square price, within a factor `2.5`, and it does not
predict the floor (`D_∞` over the root-mean-square remainder ranges from `0.7` to `386`), which
is what a certificate needs (the division's own qualification of its sentence, SCI-MSG-0022,
where a prediction of its benchmark is reported as refuted for `D_2` and confirmed for the
floor); and the rows of Proposition 11.112 compete (in one of its instances the chi-square
row is cheaper than the floor row by two orders of magnitude).

*A first certificate beyond enumeration* (the science division's workstream P3,
SCI-MSG-0020 — its result, summarised here because it is what this section and §11.7 were
asked for; model-relative: a force-field energy on a rotamer grid with a rigid backbone;
its paper proofs, its code, **not machine-checked and not reviewed by us** except for the
two combinatorial statements that are now Theorem 11.18d).  Bounding the third-order
constants of the solvent term by analysis alone is rigorous and useless: the certified
constants are 33 to 1 400 times the measured ones, because a bound that treats atom pairs
one at a time cannot see the cancellation between self and cross terms of a neutral
molecule.  What works is to evaluate the remainder on the Hamming ball of radius `m − 1`
around an anchor and to bound only what lies beyond, by site penalties from certified
constants of order `m` (Theorem 11.18d): the energy is then sandwiched between two banded
pairwise models, `m₋ ≤ E ≤ m₊`, with exact partition functions and exact samplers.  For a
twenty-residue homopeptide (`3.5·10⁹` states) and `m = 5` it reports, from 87 441
evaluations, `ln Z ∈ [518.2332, 518.2937]` with no random number, a bracket of width
`5·10⁻³` with 50 000 samples, and an independent uncertified estimate inside all its
brackets.  Its cost numbers `Z(m₋)/Z(E) − 1` show what a floor that is a *function* buys
over a constant one: `6.3` against `0.022` in one of its instances.  It fails on helices and
for charged side chains at affordable orders.  The floor of this section is its `m₋`;
Proposition 11.113 is the sampler that its sandwich calls for.

Three things are missing between this and a statement about a
molecule, and the theorem says which: (i) a certified floor — and for (f) a certified
variance — by analysis of the functional form of the remainder, not by fitting and not by
enumeration; (ii) exact sampling from the known function, which
needs a known part that is tractable *in the chosen variables* — an atom-pair-additive
function is not nearest-neighbour in backbone torsions, so either the tractable part is
smaller and the box wider, or the variables are different.  (The division has since made
the measurement it ranked first, SCI-MSG-0015: in rotamer variables on a fixed backbone
the vacuum force field is *exactly* residue-pairwise and the solvent term is pairwise to
`10⁻²`–`10⁻¹` kcal/mol for neutral side chains.  A pairwise function can be sampled exactly
when its interaction graph has small treewidth, not in general; and the width of the box
depends on how the energy is split between known part and remainder — moving a pairwise
term from one to the other changes it — which is the division's observation for the
second-order interface, and holds here for the same reason.  On its homopeptide
instances with strand or polyproline backbones the division finds that a chain model
with couplings up to next-nearest neighbours already leaves a remainder with a floor of
`0.1 k_BT`, and that a helix needs a window of four — addendum A17(9), **[M]**, obtained
from full enumerations and therefore an extrapolation at any size beyond them.)
(iii) The result concerns free energies at positive temperature — `ln Z` of the whole
domain and, in a box class, differences between macrostates (Corollary 11.114; in a class
with geometry §11.28 gives the range and the cost is open) — not minima.

*Prior art* (`docs/prior_art/L10_box_classes.md`).  Our own search was three queries at
the level of search summaries.  The science division then read the literature in full
text where it could (its workstream A3, 47 sources; SCI-RES-0009, whose reading levels we
quote and have not repeated), with this result: **every ingredient of this section is in
print, and the statement of Theorem 11.110(c)–(e) as a theorem was not found.**
Part (a) is Hoeffding (1963) maximised over the mean, with Specht's ratio as its constant;
the same quantity is the "maxkl" of bounded-range mechanisms in differential privacy.
Part (b) is the stopping criterion of the provable partition-function algorithms of
computational protein design (it cites Georgiev, Lilien and Donald 2008, Proposition 3: a
function floor from pairwise lower bounds, no ceiling) — that literature concerns sequence
design, which is outside the scope of this programme, and is cited for the certificate
scheme on one fixed state only.  The cost quantity `Z(lo)/Z` is the sample-size parameter
of importance sampling with weights bounded by an upper-bounding model (Liu, Fisher and
Ihler 2015: "the expected number of samples will depend on `Z_trw/Z`") and the `1/(εμ)` term
of the optimal stopping-rule theorem (Dagum, Karp, Luby and Ross 2000, read through
restatements; a later note reports that its proof has a gap that the author's own
sharper threshold repairs: cite the theorem, not the proof).  "With a hint" is Aaronson's
randomised certificate complexity.  The unhinted bracket of "without a hint" is, as
stated, a corollary printed in Liu–Fisher–Ihler (their Corollary 3.2, attributed to Maurer
and Pontil).  Part (f) is Hoeffding's Theorem 3; its use as a certified second-order bound
for free-energy perturbation was not found, with one relevant paper inaccessible.
Proposition 11.112 is Block and Shetty (2026) and Kunsch, Novak and Rudolf (2019) without
a hint.  In the free-energy-perturbation literature itself the sample size
`exp(KL(target‖sampled))` is a heuristic in its authors' words (Jarzynski 2006; Wu and Kofke
2005), a theorem at one pair of ensembles in Chatterjee and Diaconis (2018), and a minimax
theorem over divergence balls only in the two preprints of Block and co-authors; a theorem
to cite next to the documented refutation DEAD.28 is Chatterjee–Diaconis, Theorem 2.1 (the
sample variance cannot test the convergence of importance sampling).  **What was not
found in print**, and is therefore all that may be called ours — elementary as it is: the
instance-wise two-sided statement with a hint in the query model, with its dip- and
bump-weighted sampler (Theorem 11.110(c)–(e)), and its version for ratios (Corollary
11.114); what is the science division's: the reading of the divergence table as a
verification cost, the negative statement on polynomial moments, and the measurements.
"Not found" in two extended searches is all that is claimed, by either division.

*Harness.*  Block XXIV: XXIV.1 (the Jensen bracket and its two-point extremum; the exact
range after evaluations; the mass a deterministic certificate needs), XXIV.2 (dip and bump
weights bound the change of `Z`, with equality at the ends of the box; the detection
probability — in the linear relaxation between `p` and `2p`, both ends attained; the spot
check), XXIV.3 (the lower bound and the size-free bracket at four sizes from `4·10³` to
`4·10⁵` states), XXIV.4 (Corollary 11.111 on the cube), XXIV.5 (coverage of the empirical
Bernstein bracket; a simulation), XXIV.6 (parts (a) and (f): Hoeffding's bound with the
mean known, the bracket `0 ≤ K ≤ W`, its two-point extremum, monotonicity, the second-order
bounds on both sides, the comparison with `L(w)`), XXIV.7 (Proposition 11.112(a)–(f), with
cases in which each bound is attained to within a per cent), XXIV.8 (Corollary 11.114),
XXIV.9 (parts (d), (e) with floor and ceiling; the proportional case; the rule without a
hint, with its exact failure probability), XXIV.10 (Proposition 11.113), DEAD.28 (the
naive interval), with 41 mutations.


### 11.31 Barriers and traps: cut certificates checked by the existing kernels

*Origin and status.*  The Scientific Discovery Division's workstream K (its message
SCI-MSG-0005 and its report `docs/science/workstreams/SK_REPORT.md` on its branch) observed
that a lower bound on a minimax barrier is a *cut*, and that a cut is checked by the
kernels that exist already: the `(min, max)` algebra enters only through the definition
of the barrier.  The statements and the first Lean file are that division's.  We have
adopted its file with the declarations unchanged (`proofs/Frontiers/KineticsCertificates.lean`) and, at its
request K-T1, written and machine-checked the checker for the tree format it specified
(`proofs/Frontiers/BarrierCertificate.lean`, our workstream BK; the statements were read
by the coordinator, the proofs are checked by Lean).  **Not refereed.**  There is no
harness test: the checkers are tested inside Lean, by certificates that the kernel
evaluates — accepted ones and, for each of the three checks, a rejected one.

*Setting.*  A finite configuration space with a move graph.  The barrier `B_E(a, b)` is the
least, over walks from `a` to `b`, of the largest energy on the walk; its height above `a` is
`B_E(a, b) − E(a)`.

**Theorem 11.115 (barrier and trap certificates) [V] (`KineticsCertificates.lean` — the
division's; `BarrierCertificate.lean` — ours).**
(a) *Cuts* (the division's `cut_sound`).  If every move that leaves a set `S ∋ a`, `S ∌ b`
lands on energy at least `L`, every walk from `a` to `b` visits energy at least `L`.  (That
the best cut attains the barrier, `B(a, b) = max(E(a), max_S min_{∂⁺S} E)`, is classical — the
division cites Edmonds and Fulkerson, 1970 — and is not formal.)
(b) *Box cuts* (the division's `box_cut_barrier`, `box_cut_barrier_residual`,
`certified_trap_height`).  Under single-site moves the wall of a box is the union of `n`
boxes; `n` accepted certificates of the min kernel on them certify the barrier out of the
box, and with the residual kernel they certify it for every residual of the class,
together with the height above an evaluated anchor.
(c) *Tree cuts* (`bverify_sound`, `bcheck_sound`, `bverify_sound_real`, `bverifyR_sound`,
`bverifyR_trap_height`, `bverifyRTop_sound`).  A certificate is a decision tree whose leaves
carry a box and one of three labels: *inside*, *wall* with a certificate of the min kernel
(or of the residual kernel), *outside*.  The checker accepts iff every wall certificate is
accepted on its box for the bound `L`, no inside box is adjacent to an outside box, and `a`
lies in an inside box and `b` in none.  If it accepts, every walk of single-site moves from
`a` to `b` visits a configuration of energy at least `L`; with residual leaves, of true
energy at least `L` for every residual of the class, and the barrier is at least
`L − (E₀(a) + v_a)` above an anchor `a` with evaluated value `v_a`.  A tree can describe
regions that no box can: on a four-site instance (`maze_barrier_exact`) a tree cut
certifies the exact barrier while every box cut around either end point certifies only
the trivial bound (`maze_boxCut_start_le`, `maze_boxCut_target_le`).
(d) *Adjacency is exact* (`Dom.adjacent_iff`, `cutCheck_boxAdjacent_iff`; both for at least
one site, and with "single-site move" including the null move — the division's review
SCI-REV-0013, m10).  Two boxes contain
the two ends of a single-site move iff both are non-empty and at most one site has
disjoint domains; so the second check rejects exactly the trees with a move from an
inside box to an outside box.  The non-emptiness clause is needed
(`sep_card_le_one_not_sufficient`): the criterion as the division specified it, "at most
one coordinate has disjoint domains", fails for empty boxes; soundness never depended on
it.
(e) *Site-graph products* (`bverifyOn_sound`, `Dom.adjacentOn_iff`).  The same for move
graphs in which every site moves along its own relation — a torsion to a neighbouring
arc — where, unlike on the Hamming graph, cuts along one coordinate are not vacuous
(`scan_barrier_exact`, with the same certificate rejected on the Hamming graph).
(f) *Traps* (the division's `trap_survival`, `trap_certificate`, `box_trap_certificate`).
For every stochastic kernel that is stationary for weights `w` — no reversibility — the
probability of not having left a basin `A` after `T` steps, started from `w` restricted to
`A`, is at least `1 − T·U/Lo` whenever `U` bounds the weight of the wall from above and `Lo` the
weight of the basin from below; the two bounds are outputs of the partition kernel on
the wall boxes and on the box.

*The weight domain of the partition kernel* (the division's question K-T2; workstream BK,
**[N]** in the sense that the evidence is a compiled file that is not part of the
library).  The soundness of the partition kernel with its elimination rules
(`zverify2_sound`) uses nothing of the rationals beyond a commutative semiring with a
compatible partial order, and decidable `≤` and `=` for the checker: a copy of the 1 363
lines of its proof with `ℚ` replaced by such a semiring `R`, and four tactic calls replaced
by the monotonicity lemmas they stand for, compiled without further change.  Over
polynomials with the coefficientwise order one certificate then brackets every level
partition function of a site-additive statistic, exactly for chains — what the division
asked for.  Not done: the refactoring of the library itself (mechanical: about a hundred
signatures), and a truncated-polynomial semiring that Lean's kernel can evaluate.  In a
partial order the thermal prune rule applies less often; soundness is not affected.

*What is not here.*  Exactness of the robust interval of barrier heights beyond the two
admissibility lemmas, the query-model statements and the passage to continuous surfaces
(the division's K5–K8: its paper proofs, not checked by us); completeness of the tree
format; any statement on the size of a certificate.  The division's negative results
stand as its own and should be read with the positive ones: a multiplier on a counting
constraint certifies nothing beyond the trivial bound; coordinate cuts certify nothing
under unrestricted single-site moves; deciding whether the barrier between two
zero-energy configurations of a translation-invariant chain is zero is PSPACE-complete
(it cites Wrochna), so there is no transfer matrix for barriers; and a discrete rate is
relative to the move set — the trap bound is first of all a certified diagnosis that a
sampler has not equilibrated.  Its requests K-T3 and K-T4 are not started.

### 11.32 Known parts with interactions along the chain: a nearest-neighbour coupling changes the exponents, and in which direction depends on the envelope

*Origin and status.*  Every exponent of §§11.9–11.26 is for a known part that is a product
measure, or a function of the type.  A known part with interactions *along* the chain — a
nearest-neighbour Gibbs measure, i.e. a Markov chain — was the question of our workstream Y
(`docs/workstreams/Y_REPORT.md`, with its scripts in `experiments/workstreams/Y/`; delivered
at the fourteenth checkpoint and held back, unverified, until now).  It has since been
examined twice, independently: by our referee R11 (`docs/reviews/R11_referee_report.md`,
`experiments/reviews/R11/`: every statement labelled as proved re-derived, every number
recomputed with code written from the statements, **no critical finding, two major findings
on what the brackets are brackets of**), and by the Scientific Discovery Division (its
workstream R10, review SCI-REV-0010: the same verdict on proofs and numbers from a third
code, **and one finding that changes the headline: the direction of the effect depends on
the slope**, with a small-slope law that replaces a numerical observation by a theorem).
What follows is the workstream's result with both reviews applied; who found what is said
at each place.  The coordinator re-ran the decisive cells with the workstream's functions
and wrote independent code for the harness (block XXV, three tests, fifteen mutations).
**Machine-checked: the lower bound for every algorithm, Theorem 11.116(c)**
(`SoftMinLowerBound.lean`, on top of Theorem 11.27) — the one statement of the section that
is about algorithms without any condition.  Everything else is on paper: the bounds on game
functions are paper proofs by one author re-derived by two reviewers, and their
evaluations are floating-point computations with duality brackets (no interval
arithmetic).  One model — a two-state chain with one coupling and one slope, no field;
nothing is fitted to a molecule.

*Setting.*  Sites `1, …, n` with finite alphabets and site envelopes `d_i` (zero diagonal,
triangle inequality, not necessarily symmetric), `d(x, y) = Σ_id_i(x_i, y_i)`, the class
`𝒞_d = {ψ : ψ(x) − ψ(y) ≤ d(x, y)}` and `A_π(ψ) = E_πe^{−ψ}` as in §11.26, and the reference
measure `π(x) ∝ exp(−Σ_if_i(x_i) − Σ_{i<n}J_i(x_i, x_{i+1}))` with known `f_i`, `J_i`.  For a finite
space `(X, π, d)` and `0 < t < 1` the *site function* is

    F*_X(t)  =  max_M  −t·ln Σ_x ( Σ_φ M(φ)·π_φ(x)^t )^{1/t}  =  min_Q max_{φ∈𝒞_d} (1−t)·D_t(π_φ ‖ Q) ,

`π_φ ∝ πe^{−φ}`, `M` a law on the vertices of the class; `E_X = lim_{t↓0}F*_X(t)/t`,
`a_X = lim_{t↑1}F*_X(t)/(1−t)`, `h_X = max_tF*_X(t)` (Theorem 11.99 for a site with any alphabet
and law, hence for any finite space).  *Running example:* binary sites, the symmetric chain
with flip probability `p` (`e^K = (1−p)/p`, `λ₂ = 1 − 2p`), Hamming envelope of slope `u`.

**Theorem 11.116 (a chain as known part: two exact reductions to products of blocks, a lower
bound for every algorithm, a recursion, the limit) [(c) V: `softMin_expected_queries_ge`,
`softMinLabel_admissible`, `renyiG_eq` (`SoftMinLowerBound.lean`; on top of Theorem 11.27(b),
`genDip_expected_queries_ge_exp_weights`); (a), (b) V in their two-block form:
`cut_coupling_admissible`, `cut_coupling_partition`, `gap_embedding_admissible`,
`gap_embedding_partition` (`BlockReductions.lean`; the iteration over the cuts is on
paper); the rest P — workstream Y, Theorems Y1, Y3,
Lemmas A–C, Propositions D, F, Theorem E; every part re-derived by referee R11 and by the
reviewer of SCI-REV-0010; harness XXV.1, XXV.2(a)].**
(a) *Cut interactions move into the residual (upper reduction).*  Cut the chain between
sites `c` and `c + 1`, `c ∈ 𝒦`; let `ρ` be the product over the blocks of their free-boundary
Gibbs laws and `g(x) = Σ_{c∈𝒦}J_c(x_c, x_{c+1})`.  Then `π = ρe^{−g}/E_ρe^{−g}`,
`ln A_π(ψ) = ln A_ρ(ψ + g) − ln A_ρ(g)` with a known last term, and

    ψ ∈ 𝒞_d   ⟹   ψ + g ∈ 𝒞_{d⁺},     d⁺_c = d_c + δ⁻_c,    d⁺_{c+1} = d_{c+1} + δ⁺_c,
    δ⁻_c(a, a′) = max_b[J_c(a, b) − J_c(a′, b)],       δ⁺_c(b, b′) = max_a[J_c(a, b) − J_c(a, b′)]

(a gauge `J_c = r_c + s_c + J°_c` may be split off first).  So every correct algorithm for the
block-product landscape `(ρ, d⁺)` is one for the chain, with the same evaluation points and
of the same kind — non-adaptive, hinted, adaptive.  The slacks are attained (cones leave
none) and neither can be dropped.  Symmetric chain: slopes `(u + K, u, …, u, u + K)` on a block.
(b) *Blocks with gaps embed exactly (lower reduction).*  For blocks `B₁ < B₂ < …` separated by
gaps of `m_j ≥ 0` sites the marginal of `π` on the blocks is `⊗_jπ_{B_j}·Π_jρ_j(x_{e_j}, x_{s_{j+1}})`, `ρ_j` the
ratio of the joint law of the last letter of one block and the first of the next to the
product of its marginals.  With `ε⁻_j(a, a′) = max_b[ln ρ_j(a, b) − ln ρ_j(a′, b)]`,
`ε⁺_j(b, b′) = max_a[ln ρ_j(a, b) − ln ρ_j(a, b′)]` and `d⁻` the envelope on the block sites reduced by
`ε⁻_j` at the end of block `j` and by `ε⁺_j` at the start of block `j + 1`: for every `ψ′ ∈ 𝒞_{d⁻}`,

    ψ := ψ′∘proj + Σ_j ln ρ_j(x_{e_j}, x_{s_{j+1}})  ∈ 𝒞_d ,            A_π(ψ) = A_{⊗π_{B_j}}(ψ′)   exactly.

The block-product landscape `(⊗π_{B_j}, d⁻)` sits inside the chain's problem at the same
accuracy.  (It needs a non-empty class; for the symmetric chain `ε^± = κ_m` on unequal letters,
`κ_m = ln[(1 + λ₂^{m+1})/(1 − λ₂^{m+1})]`, `κ₀ = K`, so the gap must be long enough that `u > κ_m`.)
(c) *A lower bound for every algorithm, every `n`, any reference measure.*  For any finite
`(X, π, d)`, any law `M` on members of the class and `0 < t < 1` let
`γ* := −t⁻¹ln Σ_φM(φ)e^{−tφ̃}`, `φ̃ = φ + ln E_πe^{−φ}`.  Then `γ* ∈ 𝒞_d` and **every randomised
`(ε/2, δ)`-correct algorithm — adaptive or not, with any hint — makes at least
`(1 − 2δ)·exp(G_t(M) − tε)` evaluations at `γ*`**, `G_t(M) = −t ln Σ_x(Σ_φMπ_φ^t)^{1/t}`.  No product
structure is used: the whole chain is one super-site.  (The class is closed under soft
minima; `Φ_φ := φ̃ − γ̃*` has `E_{π_{γ*}}e^{−Φ_φ} = 1`, the alternatives `γ* − (r − Φ_φ)₊` are members
that raise `ln A` by at least `r`, and `Σ_φM(φ)(π_φ/π_{γ*})^t` is the constant `e^{−G_t(M)}`;
Theorem 11.27(a), (b).  In Lean: for every `r > ε` at least `(1 − 2δ)·exp(G_t(M) − tr)`
evaluations at `γ*`, for any finite set, any known part and any envelope function; with
exhaustive evaluation as the algorithm the same theorem gives `G_t(M) ≤ ln|X|`,
`renyiG_le_log_card`, which shows that its hypotheses can be met.  What is not in Lean is the
identification of `sup_MG_t(M)` with the site function and every evaluation of it.)
(d) *The Markov recursion: slack at one end.*  For every member `φ`, every Markov chain `Q`
with kernels `q_i` and `0 < t < 1`,

    Σ_x π_φ(x)^t·Q(x)^{1−t}  ≥  Π_i c_i ,     c_i = min_b min_{γ∈Lip(d*_i)} Σ_a q_i(b, a)^{1−t}·( P_i(b, a)e^{−γ(a)}/Z )^t ,

with the envelopes `d*_n = d_n`, `d*_i = d_i + G_i`,
`G_i(a, a′) = max{ln[Σ_bP_{i+1}(a′, b)w(b)/Σ_bP_{i+1}(a, b)w(b)] : w > 0, w(b′) ≤ w(b)e^{d*_{i+1}(b, b′)}}`; hence
`F*_n(t) ≤ Σ_i max_bF*[P_i(b, ·); d*_i](t)`, and the same for the chain of `L`-blocks: for the
symmetric chain, `F_∞(t) ≤ L⁻¹·max_bF*[P^{(L)}(· | b); (u, …, u, u*)](t)` with the **one-sided**
slack `u* = u + ln[((1−p)e^{u*} + p)/(pe^{u*} + 1 − p)] < u + K` (`u* = 1.218, 1.526, 1.981, 2.750` at
`u = 1` for `p = 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1`).  It is a bound on the game function, not a reduction of
algorithms.  (The conditional expectations `V_i = E_π[e^{−φ} | x_{≤i}]` are Lipschitz in `x_i` with
`d*_i`; the conditional law of `x_i` under `π_φ` is a Gibbs law of a member of `Lip(d*_i)`.)
Without the slack the product bound is false — for the uniform field on eight sites at
`p = 0.1`, `u = 1`, `t = ½`, with the chain itself as `Q`, the left side is `0.667` and the product
without slack `0.866` (with it: `0.267`; harness XXV.2).
(e) *The limit.*  For a stationary homogeneous chain let `F⁺_L` be the site function of a
segment of `L` sites with its free-boundary law and the slack of (a) at both ends, `F⁻_L` that
of its marginal law with the reduced envelope of (b).  Then `F⁺_L` is **exactly
sub-additive**, `F⁻_L` **exactly super-additive**, and

    F⁻_L(t)/L  ≤  F_∞(t) := lim_L F⁺_L(t)/L  ≤  F⁺_L(t)/L      for every L,          F*_n(t)  ≥  n·F_∞(t) − 2t(u + K)

(the constant for the symmetric chain, for every `p` — referee R11, m5; in the other
direction `F*_n ≤ nF_∞ + tC` with `C = 2(u + K)` where the reduced envelope of (b) needs no gap,
and with a larger constant otherwise; where `u < 2κ₀` the lower bracket starts at `L = 2` or
uses a gap).  `F_∞(t)/t` is nonincreasing, `F_∞(t)/(1−t)` nondecreasing;
`E_∞ = lim E_n/n`, `h_∞ := max_tF_∞(t)`, `a_∞ := sup_tF_∞(t)/(1−t)`.  The plain `F*_L/L` is neither
monotone nor a bound.
*Without homogeneity the limit need not exist* (Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0022,
finding F2 — our audit had classified stationarity and homogeneity as needed by the proof
only; the argument was read and checked here given (a), (b), Theorems 11.98–11.99 and one
number of our audit script AA2 S3, and not recomputed).  What holds for arbitrary couplings
is the bracket block by block: for every partition of the chain into blocks (with the gaps
of (b) where the reduced envelope needs them), `Σ_jF⁻(B_j)(t) ≤ F*_n(t) ≤ Σ_jF⁺(B_j)(t)`, by (a), (b)
and the additivity of the site function over independent blocks at a common `t`.  But with
the coupling of `p = 0.3` inside the blocks of lengths `2^{j²}` with `j` odd and no coupling
elsewhere (`u = 1`), `F*_n(0.45)/n` has limit points at least `0.0346` (at the ends of the odd
blocks: twelve coupled sites and a gap of one embed exactly, Proposition 11.117) and at
most `0.0291` (at the ends of the even blocks: the cube).  For stationary ergodic sequences
of couplings a limit would follow from the sub-additive ergodic theorem; that is not
proved here, and no bound on the width of the bracket of one block is claimed in general.
(f) *What is a statement about algorithms* (referee R11, finding M1; the workstream's table
named no regime).  **Lower bounds are unconditional and hold at every accuracy:** by (c)
and (e), for every `n` and every `ε ≥ 0` every correct algorithm makes at least
`(1 − 2δ)·exp(n·F_∞(t) − tε − 2t(u + K))` evaluations at an explicit member of the class; so
the hinted exponent at the hardest instance is at least `h_∞`, at bounded accuracy and at
vanishing extensive accuracy, and a bounded number of evaluations cannot suffice below
the threshold `E_∞`.  **Upper bounds on costs are conditional and for extensive accuracies
only:** by (a) and Theorem 11.101(b) applied to the landscape of `L`-blocks, adaptive
algorithms without a hint cost at most `exp(n·max_t[F⁺_L(t)/L − tε₁] + o(n))` for
`0 < ε₁ < E⁺_L/L`, and the limits are iterated — `n → ∞` at fixed `L`, then `L → ∞`; the `o(n)` grows
with the alphabet `q^L`, nothing is uniform in `L`, and **at bounded accuracy no upper bound
on the cost of any algorithm for the chain is proved** (for the cube that is Theorems
11.25(c), (d) and 11.58).  For non-adaptive algorithms both sides are conditional:
`θ_∞(ε₁) = max_τ(F_∞(τ) − τε₁)/(1−τ)` is the exponent given (b), the every-`n` bound of Theorem
11.98(d) for block landscapes, (a) and Theorem 11.95.  So `h_∞`, `a_∞`, `E_∞` below are numbers
of the game function; as statements about algorithms, read "at least" for `h_∞` and `E_∞`
without condition and everything else with these conditions.

**Proposition 11.117 (the symmetric binary chain: what a nearest-neighbour coupling does)
[P for the bounds, N for their evaluation; (a), (c) workstream Y, replicated by R11 and by
SCI-REV-0010; (b), (d) the Scientific Discovery Division's — its Propositions R10.1, R10.2
and finding M1 —, re-derived by us for (b) and re-computed for (d); harness XXV.2, XXV.3].**
(a) *At slope `u = 1` all three numbers are above the uniform cube's.*  Per site:

| `p` | `h_∞` | `a_∞` | `E_∞` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0.5` (cube) | `0.029139` | `0.110944` | `0.120115` |
| `0.4` | `[0.0340, 0.0362]` | `[0.1168, 0.1215]` | `0.1691` |
| `0.3` | `[0.0401, 0.0450]` | `[0.1264, 0.1409]` | `0.2324` |
| `0.2` | `[0.0445, 0.0544]` | `[0.1297, 0.1608]` | `0.3108` |
| `0.1` | `[0.0443, 0.0628]` | `[0.1166, 0.1730]` | `[0.4017, 0.4037]` |

At `p = 0.3`: `h_∞` is larger by 38 % to 54 %, `a_∞` by 14 % to 27 %, and the threshold is
`1.935` times the cube's.  *Lower ends of `h_∞`:* label laws that are i.i.d. over blocks of 12 to
16 sites with the exact boundary term (a moment Lyapunov exponent of products of `2×2`
matrices; workstream Y, Proposition I) — any block law gives a valid bound, and the fifth
decimal of the workstream's values depended on an unstated stopping rule (R11, m1), hence
four digits here.  *The direction does not depend on that computation:* with block labels
whose end slopes are reduced as in (b) of the theorem the product of block Gibbs laws is the
Gibbs law of a member, so `G_t` of **one** block of `L` sites, divided by `L + m`, is a lower
bound for every algorithm at every `n = k(L + m) − m` — `0.0317, 0.0358, 0.0386, 0.0347` for
`p = 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1` with `L ≤ 16` (referee R11, §4.4: no Lyapunov exponent, no unrefereed
input, an enumeration of `2^L` configurations; reproduced in the harness at `p = 0.3`, `L = 10`:
`0.0328`).  *Upper ends:* the tilt-state recursion of the workstream (a relaxation that
keeps one-step consistency of the conditional tilts, with a discretisation that errs on
the safe side), evaluated independently by both reviewers; at `p = 0.1` the workstream's scan
of the reference chain had stopped at its edge and both reviewers improved it (`0.0668` to
`0.0628` for `h_∞`; `0.1928` to `0.1730` for `a_∞` by R11 and to `0.1721` by the division — two
valid bounds, the table has the first; R11, m2; SCI-REV-0010, m6; SCI-REV-0014, m11).  *Mechanism:* the hard
perturbations are local fields that are constant over domains of 3 to 5 sites and exploit
the cooperative response of the chain; with labels that are independent from site to site
the bound is *below* the cube (`0.0282` at `p = 0.3`, by Jensen's inequality).  The hardest
instance is their soft minimum — a function of the bond pattern, with multi-body terms,
neither additive nor constant over domains — and the Rényi centre is not a Markov chain.
(b) *Small slopes: the factor is a variance* (the division's Propositions R10.1, R10.2).
For every finite `(X, π)` and **symmetric** envelope `u·d₀` (`d₀(x, y) = d₀(y, x)`),

    F*_X(t)  =  ( t(1−t)/2 )·u²·V + O(u³) ,       V := max{ Var_π f : f is 1-Lipschitz for d₀ } ,

attained at a vertex; so `E = a = u²V/2` and `h = u²V/8` to second order (centre `Q = π` from
above; the two labels `±uf*` from below — `−f*` is a member because `d₀` is symmetric).  **Without
symmetry the statement is false:** on two points with `d₀(0,1) = 1`, `d₀(1,0) = 0` the labels form
a segment, whose radius is half its length, and `F* = (t(1−t)/2)·u²V/4 + O(u³)` (the division's
counter-example, SCI-REV-0014, M1 — the proposition is its R10.1, which has the hypothesis;
our first version of this part dropped the word, although the Setting of this section
allows envelopes that are not symmetric; ratios `0.2470 … 0.2500` and `0.2286 … 0.2487` of `F*` to
the displayed term for `u = 0.4 … 0.025`, reproduced by us).  The `O(u³)` depends on the diameter
of `(X, d₀)`: nothing is uniform in `n`.  For binary sites with the Hamming envelope and an
**associated** law — a ferromagnetic chain with any fields — `V = ¼·Var_π(Σ_is_i)`, attained by
the uniform field: for a 1-Lipschitz `f` both `½Σs_i ± f` are nondecreasing, so their covariance
is nonnegative, and it equals `¼Var(Σs_i) − Var f`.  Hence, at fixed `n` and to second order in
`u`, the three numbers of the symmetric chain are those of independent sites times
`Var(Σs_i)/n` (`1.792` at `n = 4`, `p = 0.3`), which tends to the structure factor at zero wave
vector, `(1 + λ₂)/(1 − λ₂) = (1−p)/p` — `2.33` at `p = 0.3`; the workstream had the limit as a
numerical observation (`[2.27, 2.33]` at `u = 0.05`).  For the limit `F_∞` (first `n → ∞`, then
`u → 0`) the upper side is proved (the recursion (d) with `L = 1` at second order); the lower
side is exact for `E` and a sketch for `h` and `a` (the distinction between a fixed length
and the limit was blurred in the first version of this sentence and in two summary rows:
SCI-REV-0014, m2).  **"The
susceptibility" is right for this chain and false in general:** for an antiferromagnetic
chain the maximiser is the staggered field and `¼Var(Σs_i)` is strictly smaller (`0.43`
against `1.23` on three sites at `p = 0.7`); the general quantity is the largest variance
per site of a Lipschitz function — the dominant collective mode.
*A cross-reference* (**[K]** for the names, from memory of the sources of §3.2 and
`docs/prior_art/L6_transport_entropy_and_information_limits.md`, not re-read).  `V` is what
the literature on concentration calls the *spread constant* of the metric probability
space `(X, d₀, π)` (Alon, Boppana and Spencer 1998; Bobkov, Houdré and Tetali 2006), and
with the reference itself as centre the numbers of the game function are bounded by
functionals of the cumulant generating functions `Λ_f(λ) = ln E_π e^{λ(f − E_π f)}` of the
1-Lipschitz functions: the threshold by `max_f Λ_f(u)` — the Laplace functional of §3.2,
the zero-evaluation gap of Theorem 11.14 — and `F*(t)` by `max_f [tΛ_f(u) − Λ_f(tu)]` (this is
the upper bound used above and in harness XXV.3).  So at weak envelopes the certification
exponents of a reference measure are its spread constant; and a transport inequality
`T₁(σ²)` for `π` in the envelope metric, which by Bobkov and Götze is `Λ_f(λ) ≤ σ²λ²/2` for
all 1-Lipschitz `f`, bounds the threshold with centre `π` by `u²σ²/2` at every slope.  For the
chain the centre `π` is not optimal, so these are upper bounds only, and the reversal at
large slopes of part (d) is invisible in them.
(c) *The threshold rises at every slope.*  `E_n ≥ ln[Z_n(u/2)/Z_n(0)]` for every `n` (`Z_n(h)` the
partition function in a uniform field; the two uniform-field labels), hence

    E_∞  ≥  E_F := ln[ (1−p)cosh(u/2) + √( (1−p)²sinh²(u/2) + p² ) ]  >  ln cosh(u/2)      (p < ½)

(for `p > ½` the second inequality fails — `E_F(0.7, 1) = 0.0540 < 0.1201` — and the same holds
with `1 − p` in place of `p` and the staggered field in place of the uniform one, by the gauge
`s_i → (−1)^i s_i`, which leaves the Hamming class invariant; so `E_∞ > ln cosh(u/2)` for every
`p ≠ ½`: SCI-REV-0014, m1), with equality `E_n = ln[Z_n(u/2)/Z_n(0)]` exactly when the uniform field maximises `KL(π‖π_φ)`
over the class — true over all vertices for `n ≤ 4` (harness) and `n = 5` (the workstream, a
dual certificate over 395 094 vertices).  Numerically `E_∞ = E_F` for `p ≥ 0.14` at `u = 1` (the
safe recursion returns `E_F + 7·10⁻¹¹`; R11, m4, and SCI-REV-0010, m8 — the workstream's margins
of `10⁻⁴` were an artefact of its end cells); at `p = 0.1` the relaxation with the chain itself
as reference is not tight, and `E_∞ ∈ [0.4017, 0.4037]` with a better reference (the division).
*Conjecture (the workstream's; the division asks whether it fails at strong coupling,
R10-T5):* `E_n = ln[Z_n(u/2)/Z_n(0)]` for every `n` and `p`.
(d) *Large slopes: two of the three numbers fall below the cube's* (the division's finding
M1 — **the first line of the workstream's summary, "Yes — upwards", is not the answer to its
question**).  By (d) of the theorem with blocks of three sites — all 96 vertices of the cube
with slopes `(u, u, u*)`, duality brackets below `10⁻⁹`:

| `(p, u)` | chain: proved upper bound | cube | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a_∞`: `(0.3, 3)` | `0.4958` | `0.5023` | `0.987` |
| `a_∞`: `(0.2, 3)` | `0.4675` | `0.5023` | `0.931` |
| `a_∞`: `(0.1, 4)` | `0.5097` | `0.6031` | `0.845` |
| `h_∞`: `(0.1, 4)` | `0.2331` | `0.2393` | `0.974` |

and likewise `a_∞` at `u = 3, 4, 6` for each of `p = 0.3, 0.2, 0.1`, at `u = 2.5` for `p = 0.2, 0.1`, at
`u = 2` for `p = 0.1`, and `h_∞` at `u = 4, 6` for `p = 0.2, 0.1` (the division's table; the four rows
above re-computed by us with the workstream's own functions, and the second with
independent code in the harness; for `h_∞` at `(0.1, 4)` the division's own bound is `0.2293`,
ratio `0.959` — two valid bounds for the same cell).  Between about `u = 1.5` and these slopes
the direction of `a_∞` is open, with every lower bound below the cube.  With blocks of one
site the recursion does not show it (the bound stays above the cube at every slope
computed; confirmed by the division on 24 cells); with blocks of two sites it already
shows at `(p, u) = (0.2, 3), (0.1, 4), (0.1, 6)` for `a` and at `(0.1, 4), (0.1, 6)` for `h` (the
division's computation, SCI-REV-0014 §4; not re-computed by us); and, by a heuristic
argument of the division's, no symmetric Markov reference can prove it by the tilt-state
route (the period-four label leaks exactly like the cube; its safe tilt-state bound for
`a` stays above the cube for `u = 1 … 3` at `p = 0.3`).  *Reading* (the division's, heuristic): an envelope below about one
`k_BT` per site is answered cooperatively, and the product-measure exponents are optimistic
by the structure factor; an envelope of several `k_BT` per site can pin single
configurations, and there the coupling removes hiding places — a label leaks to a single
flip with a weight that the coupling multiplies for an isolated spin and divides inside a
domain — so the product-measure values of `a` and `h` are pessimistic.  The threshold does
not reverse because it is governed by the cooperative perturbation at every slope.
*Where the direction turns — what blocks can and cannot decide, and a weak-coupling
coefficient* (the Computational Research Division's enumeration X-013 at its commit `c81166b`
and the Scientific Discovery Division's SCI-RES-0033; neither is a result of ours).  Certified
bounds from blocks of four sites add seven cells below the cube (`a_∞` at `(0.4, 4)`, `(0.4, 6)`,
`(0.3, 2.5)`, `(0.2, 2)`; `h_∞` at `(0.3, 4)`, `(0.3, 6)`, `(0.1, 3)`); fourteen cells stay undecided
for each exponent, and for thirteen of them a certified lower bound of the five-site block
quantity lies above the cube: **no enumeration of blocks of five can decide them** — the map
of the crossover is not a matter of longer blocks.  For weak coupling the Scientific
Discovery Division derives, at a fixed block length and for site-wise labels (one sign
per site), the increment of the block quantity per added site,

    a_cube(u) + (K²/4)·F*(u) + O(K⁴),      K = ln((1−p)/p),   t = tanh(u/2),
    F*(u) = t⁴(1 − t⁴)/2 − u·t³(1 − t²) + (1 − t²)²(u − t(1 + t²))²/(2t²),

with one sign change, at **`u₀ = 1.505534`** (positive below: the coupling raises the exponent;
negative above); the optimal input is an Ising chain.  [Its derivation, "not written as a
proof"; the coefficient was confirmed here by brute force — a capacity computation of our
own over the `2^L` site-wise labels, `L = 4, 5`, agreeing with `F*` to `3·10⁻⁵` at five slopes —
and the single sign change with a stable evaluation at large slopes:
`experiments/coordinator_checks/sci_res_0033/`.]  At `(p, u) = (0.4, 1)` the second-order value
`0.1201` lies inside the bracket `[0.1168, 0.1215]` of (a); at `p = 0.3` (`K = 0.85`) it does not,
which is where the expansion ends.  **Open** (the division's question to us): whether
`a_∞(p, u) = a_cube(u) + (K²/4)F*(u) + O(K⁴)` at fixed `u` — it needs that site-wise labels stay
optimal for long blocks and that the increment converges to `a_∞`; the expansion is not
uniform as `u → 0`, where (b) applies instead.
(e) *Against §11.25, and the fixed sample.*  There is no contradiction with "no known part
that is a function of the type is harder than the cube" (referee R11, finding M2 and §5).
Corollary 11.91 covers the hinted exponent of symmetric instances and the exponent of
fixed samples, for exchangeable reference measures; for those the problem is
`S_n`-invariant, the optimal centre is exchangeable, and the bound (c) of the theorem is one
that symmetric instances give — in a mean-field model the enhanced variance sits in one
collective mode, which contributes `O(1)` and not `O(n)` (with the same code: the excess over
the cube decays like `1/n` per site for Curie–Weiss known parts and is constant per site for
the chain).  A nearest-neighbour energy is not a function of the type, and every block
longer than a correlation length carries an enhanced mode of its own.  For the fixed
sample the stratified construction of Theorems 11.76 and 11.95 does **not** transfer: the
class-wise quantile truncation of an admissible residual is not admissible for
Markov-type classes — `n = 4`, `u = 1`, `q = ½`, `ψ = d_H(·, 0100)`: `1101` lies in the class
`{1101, 1011}` with values `2, 4`, level `4`, while `0101` is a class of its own with value `1`, at
distance one; `4 − 1 > 1` (the division's example for the truncated residual, its m2 — the
workstream's own example showed only that the quantile *levels* are not Lipschitz across
classes, R11, m13; in the two reviewers' brute force the truncation leaves the class in 188
of 300 and in 464 of 600 cases, and in none for type classes of the cube).  Optimality of a fixed sample
with polynomial losses is open for chains.

*What the result is, and is not.*  It is the first known part in this report for which the
exponents are provably not those of independent sites in either direction: a
nearest-neighbour coupling without a field **raises** the cost of certification where the
envelope is weak (below about one `k_BT` per site, by up to the structure factor) and
**lowers** two of the three where it is strong and the coupling is not weak (in the cells
computed: `a_∞` for `p ≤ 0.3` from `u = 3`, `h_∞` for `p ≤ 0.2` from `u = 4`; at `p = 0.4, 0.45` neither
is proved lowered at any computed slope; "raises" is a lower bound for every algorithm,
"lowers" a statement about numbers of the game function, which as a statement about costs is
conditional — Theorem 11.116(f)), while the threshold rises throughout.  It is not a formula: `F_∞` is a regularised, multi-letter quantity — the Rényi
capacity per site of the vertex channel of long blocks — known only in brackets; the
crossover slope is not located (the recursion with blocks of four and five sites would
decide it: the division's request R10-T2, with a computation asked of the engineering
division, R10-E1); the limit of the small-slope factor is proved on one side; upper bounds
on costs are conditional and not at bounded accuracy; and everything is for one synthetic
two-state chain.  For a helix–coil chain the division computes a small-slope factor of
`σ^{−1/2}` at the midpoint, limited by the length for a peptide (`11.5` at twenty residues for
`σ = 10⁻³`, with the second-order regime ending near `0.14 k_BT` per residue; its numbers,
exact transfer matrices, not re-computed by us).  Beyond chains (strips; `ℤ^d` along boxes,
where both reductions lose a surface term; trees, where the sandwich does not close) the
workstream has sketches only.

*Prior art.*  Not searched by us for this section; the division searched at snippet level
only and claims no novelty for its additions.  The ingredients are classical — transfer
matrices, association (the Harris/FKG inequality; Newman's inequalities for associated
variables, recalled from memory by the workstream), Rényi capacities and their
regularisation for channels with memory, moment Lyapunov exponents of random matrix
products.  That the query complexity of certified free energies around a Markov reference
has these exponents, and that the direction of the effect of the coupling turns with the
envelope, we have not found; it has not been looked for systematically.

*Harness.*  Block XXV: XXV.1 (the two reductions and the lower bound on random
inhomogeneous chains with asymmetric envelopes), XXV.2 (the Markov recursion; the
threshold; the block certificate at `u = 1`; the reversal at `(p, u) = (0.2, 3)`), XXV.3 (the
small-slope law, association, the antiferromagnetic counter-example, the structure
factor); fifteen mutations.  The workstream's own numbers are reproduced by
`experiments/reviews/R11/` (22 scripts) and by the division's `experiments/science/ws_R10/` on
its branch.

### 11.33 The nested algorithm on an arbitrary probability space: what the level theorem needs, where it works, where it cannot

*Origin and status.*  The level theorems of §§11.18–11.19 (Theorems 11.52, 11.56) are stated
for the cube.  Under the research owner's directive on generality a workstream was asked
which properties of the cube their proofs use, and for the theorem in the structure it
uses (`docs/workstreams/N_REPORT.md`, workstream N: paper proofs; the outer loop simulated on
2 624 runs in valid settings without a violation; no Lean).  **Refereed internally**
(`docs/workstreams/N_REVIEW.md`; the referee's own code throughout): the abstract level
theorem and its variants "correct as stated"; the false-certificate example below
reproduced from its description alone; one proposition found to be a plan and not a
proof (the assembly of the levels — stated here as a plan); one claim about a non-sharp
tail function wrong (corrected here); one proof incomplete for randomised procedures
(repaired by the referee).  The audit of the cube's proof finds 31 uses of the cube, 15 of
them in validity or in the probability of the good event; every one of those is an
instance of four facts about an *outer integrand* on a probability space.  **Reviewed with
replication by the Scientific Discovery Division** (SCI-REV-0027, its workstream R26, a
referee that had seen neither this section nor our review; own implementation of the
algorithm, 990 + 81 runs on Theorem 11.118 without a violated claim): Theorems 11.118,
11.119(b), 11.120(a), (b) and Proposition 11.121(a)–(c) **proved as stated**; three
sentences wrong or misleading and replaced below (the description of the false
certificate; "a hub is not a counterexample"; the sentence on chains), seven minor points
applied; its eight differences on the assumption table are listed at the head of
`docs/workstreams/N_REPORT.md`.

**Tail functions.**  Let `V > 0` be measurable on a probability space `(X, μ)`.  An *upper tail
function* `Ξ` and a nondecreasing *lower tail function* `Θ` of `V` satisfy, for all `s > 0`, `0 < q ≤ 1`:

    (TU)   μ(V > s) ≤ q   ⟹   E(V − s)₊ ≤ s·Ξ(q),            (TL)   μ(V ≥ s) ≥ q   ⟹   E min(V, s) ≥ s·Θ(q)

(`Θ(q) = q` is always admissible).  For an envelope `ρ` on `X` (`V(x) ≤ V(z)e^{ρ(x,z)}`: the class of a
Lipschitz condition) the functions `Ξ_ρ(q) = sup{∫_D (e^{ρ(x→Dᶜ)} − 1)dμ : μ(D) ≤ q}` and
`Θ_ρ(p) = inf{∫ e^{−ρ(S→x)}dμ : μ(S) ≥ p}` are tail functions of the class, the best ones when `ρ`
