satisfies the triangle inequality: tail functions are isoperimetric profiles.  (Convention:
`Ξ_ρ(1) = +∞` — for `D` the whole space the exit cost is the infimum over the empty set; a
literal implementation with "`D` a proper subset" at `q = 1` returns false brackets, and `q = 1`
occurs at every level below the minimum: SCI-REV-0027, F4.)  On the cube
they are Lemma 11.43 (Harper) and the lower tail lemma of Theorem 11.56.

**Theorem 11.118 (one more level, on any probability space) [P: workstream N, Theorem N1 —
the proof of Theorem 11.56 with its uses of the cube replaced; refereed: correct as
stated].**  Let `V > 0` on `(X_o, μ_o)` with `A = ∫V dμ_o < ∞` have tail functions `Ξ`, `Θ`; let numbers
`0 < ℓ₀ ≤ A` and a cap `V ≤ V_max` be known; let independent points of the law of `(X_o, μ_o)` be available;
and let `V(a)` have refinable brackets — a trivial one of ratio `e^{x₀}`, and for accuracies
`x₁ > … > x_L ≤ b` randomised procedures with failure probability `δ′` and costs `C_l` in every
run.  Then Algorithm 2L⁺ — with the tail term `s_j·Ξ(q)`, the lower-tail update
`s_je^{−b}·max(p̲, Θ(p̲))`, and a stop when the ladder passes the cap — returns `L ≤ A ≤ U ≤ e^{x_out}L`,
`x_out = ln[κ₀ + e^b(e^λ(1+η)/(1−η) + η′ + θ)]`, except with probability `δ`, at the cost formula of
Theorem 11.56 with `M̄ ∝ 1/π_*`, where the **closing level**

    π_*  =  sup{ π : Ξ(q) ≤ θ(1−η)ν₀·q   and   Ξ(q) ≤ θ·max(c_ηq, Θ(c_ηq))   for all q < π }

takes the place of the closing radius.  *Validity uses (TU), (TL), `ℓ₀ ≤ A`, the cap, valid
inner brackets and independent outer points — nothing else; the cost uses the two
ratios `Ξ(q)/q` and `Ξ(q)/Θ(c_ηq)` on all `q` below the closing level — nothing else.*  A tail
function that is too large costs evaluations; one that is too small costs validity.
Atoms, integrality of radii and the convention `s₀ ≤ min W` of the cube are not used.  With
the cube's conventions every constant of Theorem 11.56 is reproduced (ten parameter
sets, against the evaluator of workstream Q).  *Without a cap* (an unbounded integrand)
the theorem holds with an upper bound `u₀ ≥ A` and termination through the closing level
(Theorem N1′ of the workstream) — a positive closing level is then a hypothesis of its
own: it can be zero for the *exact* tail function of a class with a finite exponential
moment, and then there is no cost bound (SCI-REV-0027, F7).  (TU) and (TL) are used at the
levels of the ladder only (its F8).
*What `π_*` is and is not* (the referee's correction): it is a design constant, a supremum
over **all** smaller `q`, and bounds the sample in every run; a run may close far earlier.
With the transport bound as tail function on the cubes of dimension `m = 30` and `60` (`u = 1`), `π_* = 2^{−m}` and the cap on
the sample is `10^{14}`–`10^{24}`, yet runs close validly with about `10³` points at threshold
rates above `u²/8`; below that rate they do not close before the atom.  The workstream's
sentence "at every accuracy rate below `0.589u` the algorithm does not close before the
atom" confused the two and is withdrawn.

**Theorem 11.119 (two blocks; dependence under bounded influence) [P: workstream N,
Theorems N3, N4; refereed: correct as stated].**
(a) *Product measures.*  For a class of functions on `X_o × X_i` with `μ_o ⊗ μ_i`, the level
theorem applies to `V_ψ(a) = ∫e^{−ψ(a,b)}μ_i(db)` as soon as the fibres `ψ(a, ·)` lie in a class with
inner bracket procedures and the fibre averages have known tail functions under the outer measure.
For a Lipschitz class of a quasi-metric `d` on the product the envelope of the fibre average is
`ρ_o(a, a′) = sup_b d((a′, b), (a, b))`.  *Nothing here asks the metric to be a sum over the
blocks* — that is needed for the cost (Theorem 11.120).
(b) *A known part that is not a product.*  Let `μ` on `X_o × X_i` have the outer marginal `μ_o(da)` and
conditional laws `μ(·|a)`, let the inner procedures be valid under every conditional
law, let `ψ` be Lipschitz in the outer variable for a quasi-metric `d_o(a′, a)`, and let `ι ≥ 0` satisfy

    ∫ w dμ(·|a)  ≤  e^{ι(a,a′)}·∫ w dμ(·|a′)        for all a, a′ and all fibre weights w = e^{−ψ(a″,·)} of the class

(the **class-relative influence**).  Then `V_ψ(a) = ∫e^{−ψ(a,b)}μ(db|a)` has the envelope
`d_o(a′, a) + ι(a, a′)`, and the level theorem applies with tail functions of that envelope:
**dependence costs slope** — on the cube, `u ↦ u + ι` per outer flip.  The class-relative
form is sharp where the pointwise bound `dμ(·|a)/dμ(·|a′) ≤ e^{ι}` is not: for conditional
laws `Bernoulli(p(a))^{⊗k}` and `u`-Lipschitz fibres,
`ι(a, a′) = k·max_± ln[(1 + p(a)(e^{±u} − 1))/(1 + p(a′)(e^{±u} − 1))]`, attained by a uniform field (the
largest slope of `−ln V` in a simulation: `1.3120`, where the pointwise bound gives `1.754`).
The theorem supposes inner procedures that are valid under every conditional law; for
conditional laws that are not products this section has none with a cost bound below
enumeration.  *Band models* (replacing our sentence "for a nearest-neighbour chain the
nesting is valid without cutting the chain, with a one-sided slack at the boundary site";
Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0027 §3, its statements R26.1–R26.4, paper proofs of
its referee replicated on random models, not re-derived here): for a band model of
bandwidth `r` the conditional law of the inner block depends on the last `r` outer sites
only.  **Conditioning on them** — `q^r` sub-problems with weights from the transfer matrix —
reduces the problem to product known parts with no hypothesis on any influence (part
(a)).  Without conditioning the envelope is `u·d_H + ι` with `ι` charged at the boundary
sites only and at most the smaller of the oscillation of the change of the energy across
the cut and `u·k`; its exact tail function does not contain `ι` below the least probability
of a boundary state, and a bound that charges `ι` to every set is valid but has no usable
closing level at a bounded accuracy.  So for band models "dependence costs slope" is true
and the wrong tool: **condition on the boundary layer, or do not nest**; validity is
decided by which tail function is used, not by the size of `ι`.

**Theorem 11.120 (Gauss space: where nesting gains nothing) [P, given the Gaussian
isoperimetric inequality (Sudakov–Tsirel'son, Borell; quoted from memory) and, for (c), a
spherical cap bound; workstream N, Theorem N9, Propositions N10, N11; refereed: correct
as stated, with the precisions given].**  Let `−ln V` be `L`-Lipschitz for the Euclidean norm
on `(ℝⁿ, γ_n)`.
(a) *Exact, dimension-free tail functions.*  With `t = Φ^{−1}(1 − q)`, `c = Φ^{−1}(p)`:

    Ξ_L(q) = e^{L²/2 − Lt}·Φ(L − t) − Φ(−t),        Θ_L(p) = p + e^{Lc + L²/2}·Φ(−c − L),

attained by `e^{L(x₁ − t)₊}` and `e^{−L(x₁ − c)₊}`: the same in every dimension.  At the scale `L²/2` the
exponent functions are those of the Gaussian pair: `Θ_hint(e) = (L/2 − e/L)²/2`,
`Θ_na(X) = (L − √(2X))₊²/2`.
(b) **Obstruction.**  Split the coordinates into two fixed blocks and consider the linear
instance `ψ(a, b) = −L⟨a, ω⟩`, `ω` a unit vector of the outer block.  For every dimension of
the blocks, any valid tail functions, any inner procedures and any parameters with
`x_out < L²/2`, every run of the algorithm on its good event draws at least

    (2K/(1+η))·exp( (L − √(2x_out))²/2 )

outer points: the outer problem is a full copy of the original one, at any dimension.
(The bound counts outer points; it counts evaluations when each outer point costs at
least one — the referee's precision.)  In the analysis of the levels the operator
satisfies `R_G[T] ≥ max(T, Θ_na)` for every `T`: the recursion is the identity.  **Nesting over a
fixed split of the coordinates gains nothing** when the envelope is not additive over
the blocks.  Not excluded: blocks that are random subspaces.
(c) *The hinted lower bound does hold in high dimension.*  For `0 < t ≤ L` and
`n ≥ max{4t², L(L + 1.2816)²t}`, every randomised algorithm that is `(ε/2, δ)`-correct for
`ε < ln(1 + 0.112·e^{L²/2 − Lt} − ½Φ(−t))` — adaptive, with any hint — makes at least `(1 − 2δ)·e^{t²/2}`
evaluations in expectation at `ψ ≡ 0`: the alternatives are dips on balls of radius about
`n/t` centred at distance `n/t`, which a query hits with probability at most `e^{−t²/2}`
(half-space dips would be detected from far away).
(d) *With the sum metric* (`ψ` Lipschitz for `Σ_i |x_i − z_i|`) Gauss space is an exact instance
of Theorem 11.118 at every `n` — exact tail functions, extensive, and the pair of exponent
functions is the Gaussian pair of Theorem 11.53b exactly; a lower bound is open there.
So on Euclidean Gauss space the adaptive exponent without a hint lies between
`Θ_hint(ε + O(1))` and `Θ_na(ε)` — the situation of the cube before Theorem 11.54 — and the
tool that closed the gap on the cube provably does not close it here.  **The dividing
line is whether the envelope is additive over independent parts, not whether the space
is discrete or continuous.**

**Proposition 11.121 (unbounded influence: a false certificate) [(a)–(c) P, (d) N:
workstream N, Proposition N12; reproduced by the referee with independent code; reviewed
with replication by the Scientific Discovery Division (SCI-REV-0027): (a)–(c) proved as
stated, the description of the runs in (c) and the remark (d) corrected — both as below].**
Let the outer block be the cube of dimension `m` with the uniform marginal and the inner block the cube of dimension `k` with the
conditional law `Bernoulli(p(a))^{⊗k}`, `p(a) = σ(J(τ − |a|))` — a complete bipartite coupling of
strength `J` per pair — and let the residual be `ψ(a, b) = u|b|`, a member of the cube class.
(a) `V(a) = (1 − p(a) + p(a)e^{−u})^k`, and across the threshold `|a| = τ` its logarithm jumps by
`k·c(J, u)`, `c ↑ u` as `J → ∞`: `−ln V` has no Lipschitz constant below `k·c`, and the hypothesis on
fibre averages fails by the factor `e^{kc − u}`, exponential in the size of the inner block.
(b) The tail inequality (TU) for the slope `u` is violated as soon as `kc > u(m − τ + ½)`.
(c) *What the algorithm then does* (`m = 12`, `k = 16`, `u = 1`, `J = 4`, `τ = 10.5`: `A = 1.0747·10⁻³`, of
which the 13 points with `|a| ≥ 11` carry `99.99` per cent; largest edge ratio `e^{11.77}`; (TU)
violated by the factor `1.7·10⁵`).  Run with the tail function of the assumed class it
**returns an invalid bracket in every run** — 80 of 80 (workstream), 120 of 120 (referee) —
with the certified upper end below `A` by factors of about `300` (threshold `θ = 20`) and
`2 800`–`4 600` (`θ = 1`).  Every certificate obtained by sampling is true and the Chernoff
events hold in every run.  **Two steps are false, and which one decides depends on the
threshold and on the ladder** (Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0027 §2.1, 592 runs
with its own implementation — our first version said "the false step is the tail bound,
and the run closes below the spike", which is what happens at `θ = 20` and, at `θ = 1`, for
some ladders only): when the run closes before the spike is populated, the *upper* tail
bound is false and the upper end is below `A` by factors of `10²` to `10^{3.6}`; when the spike
is populated first (six of that division's seven parameter sets at `θ = 1`), the *lower*
tail function — the Harper term of Theorem 11.56 — is false and the lower end is above `A`,
by `2.4` to `3.9`; for still smaller thresholds the two false bounds cross and the abort rule
returns the trivial bracket.  Run with the tail functions of the true class it is valid,
at a large multiple of the cost of enumerating the outer cube (the multiple depends on
constants that the texts do not fix: `25` to `225` in the workstream, up to more than `1 000`
for our referee, `872` for that division's).
(d) *Influence confined to boundedly many outer sites (a hub; for a band model: the last
`r` sites of the outer block) is repaired by conditioning on them* — as many product
sub-problems as the hub has states, with exactly known weights — *and is **not** harmless
without it.*  Our first version read "Not a counterexample: an unbounded influence of
boundedly many outer sites (condition on them)"; read literally that exempts every band
model, and it is false at finite size (SCI-REV-0027 §2.2): without the conditioning the
failure is the one of (c) whenever `e^ι` exceeds what the product-class tail function allows
to a set of the measure of a hub state.  On a nearest-neighbour chain of four outer and
sixteen inner binary sites with a coupling of `14` across the cut — one hub site — that
division's runs return false brackets in 260 of 300 cases; on the uniform cube of
dimension `12` with Harper's functions, from two hub sites on.  Checked here without the
algorithm and with our own code (`experiments/coordinator_checks/sci_rev_0027/hub_chain_check.py`):
on that chain `ln(V₁/V₀) = 11.4486`, and (TU) for the exact tail function of the product-class
envelope fails by the factors `1.75·10⁴` to `2.58·10⁴` over the levels, while with the
influence added at the boundary site, and without the coupling, the worst ratio is exactly
one.  Only for a fixed hub and outer blocks growing without bound does the failure need
the influence to be spread.
*This is the hypothesis whose failure a dependent known part produces, and it yields a
false certificate, not a higher cost.*  (It is not the only validity hypothesis — the
lower tail function, the bound `ℓ₀`, the cap, the inner brackets and the sampling law are
validity hypotheses as well; the referee's correction to the workstream's "the only".)
A certificate format built on the level theorem must carry the bound on the influence
**for both tail functions**.

**Proposition 11.122 (unbounded oscillation) [P: workstream N, Proposition N13, with the
referee's repair for procedures that may fail with probability `δ`].**  For the class
`{ψ : ψ(z) − ψ(x) ≤ d(z, x)}` on `(X, μ)`: `sup{A(ψ) : ψ(x₀) = ψ₀} = e^{−ψ₀}∫e^{d(x₀,x)}μ(dx)`.  If this exponential
moment is infinite, no procedure can return a finite upper bound after finitely many
evaluations; if it is finite, one evaluation gives a two-sided bracket.  The level
theorem then needs no cap on the integrand: an upper bound of `A` and a positive closing
level suffice.

**Proposition 11.123 (from a tail profile to a pair of exponent functions; which sites
the outer block takes) [P: workstream N, Propositions N7, N8; refereed: correct as
stated].**
(a) Let `w` be a continuous profile (the exponent of `Ξ_m(e^{−mθ})` per site) with `w(0) > 0` and
`w(θ) + θ` nonnegative, nonincreasing, strictly decreasing down to its zero `a`.  Then
`θ_hint := w^{−1}` and `θ_na(x) := min{θ : w(θ) + θ ≤ x}` satisfy (11.18.1) and every field of the
structure `HintPair`, so the level recursion built on `θ_na` converges to `θ_hint` (Theorem
11.53).  If `w` is convex, `J(t) = min_θ[θ + t·w(θ)]` is a game function (Theorem 11.66) and is
the dual function of Theorem 11.53a.  The condition `w′ ≤ −1` is a hypothesis, not a
tautology: the relative tail exponent must not increase as the set gets smaller, and
for a transport-type profile it does.
(b) For families whose game functions are additive over blocks of sites of several
kinds (§11.26): no split of the sites between the blocks undercuts the hinted exponent,
and the proportional split has it as a fixed point — in the limit of many levels it
does not matter which sites the outer block takes.  At two levels it does: the best
outer block is not proportional, it prefers the steep sites (numerical: `0.5051·a` against
`0.5129·a` in one example).
**Not proved — a plan.**  That the levels assemble, for a family with a uniform tail
profile, into an adaptive algorithm of cost `exp(n·θ_hint(ξ) + o(n))` at the accuracy `ξn`
(Proposition N6 of the workstream) is the induction of Theorem 11.54 with substitutions
that the workstream checked step by step and did not rewrite; the referee names two
items that even the plan lacks (the tail function must be one of the class itself for
the base family; the last step needs the Lipschitz continuity of `θ_hint`).  The adaptive
theorems of this report beyond the uniform cube remain those of §§11.20 and 11.26.

**Instances** (the workstream's §4, with the referee's corrections).

| instance | tail functions | what follows |
|---|---|---|
| uniform cube | exact (Harper), every `n` | Theorems 11.52–11.58a, with identical constants |
| Gauss space, sum metric | exact, every `n`; atomless, unbounded | the level theorem without a cap; the Gaussian pair; lower bound open |
| Gauss space, Euclidean metric | exact, dimension-free | Theorem 11.120: nesting over a fixed split gains nothing |
| biased cubes; finite alphabets and site types | sharp at the exponential scale (Theorems 11.63, 11.97(c)), relative to the flat-histogram reference | the level theorem at extensive accuracy as a corollary; **bounded accuracy open** — it needs a two-sided tail estimate with polynomial precision |
| site-dependent slopes | a sorted-slope Harper bound: valid for every `n`, not sharp (`0.0974` against `0.0525` in the example) | exponents through site types (§11.26); nothing sharp at finite `n` |
| continuous sites | ball-volume and transport bounds: valid, not sharp (`0.197` for `0.029` at `u = 1` on the cube) | valid brackets at a higher cost; concentration alone gives no useful closing level |
| nearest-neighbour chain | none for Markov measures | validity of the nesting (Theorem 11.119(b)); no cost statement beyond §11.32 |

**The assumptions of the level theorems, classified** (25 rows in the workstream's §6; the
referee reclassified six; counts after that: essential 4, proof technique only 5,
convenience 6, replaceable by a weaker quantitative condition 7, removal changes the
complexity 9, removal makes the result false 3; `docs/ASSUMPTION_AUDIT.md`).  The three
that matter most: **the sum metric** — cost-only in the proof and yet the whole gain
(changes the complexity of the algorithm; whether it changes the complexity of the
problem is not known); **the tail function of the true class of fibre averages** — what
a dependent known part breaks, at the price of validity; **the isoperimetric input** —
exact isoperimetry is not needed, concentration is not enough (the method needs the
tail of *small* sets relative to their measure, uniformly), and a bounded accuracy
needs a two-sided estimate that exists for the uniform cube and Gauss space only
(since the twenty-fourth checkpoint also for products of sites with different slopes or
biases, as a computation and — up to polynomial factors, for a fixed number of slopes —
in closed form: Proposition 11.124).

**Proposition 11.124 (tail functions on a product of sites, by induction over the sites)
[(a)–(d) P: the coordinator's `docs/workstreams/I_REPORT.md`, unrefereed, nothing
machine-checked; sharpness N; (e) negative results and a conjecture].**  Let the sites be
finite sets with laws of full support and costs `ρ_i ≥ 0` vanishing on the diagonal, `μ` the
product measure, `ρ` the sum of the costs, and for a set `E` and a budget `t` let `E(t)` be the
set of points within cost `t` of `E`.  A *growth bound* is a function `g(m, t)`, nondecreasing
in both arguments, with `μ(E(t)) ≥ g(μ(E), t)` for every nonempty `E`.
(a) *Induction over the sites.*  If `g′` is a growth bound for a product, then for one more
site with law `π` and cost `c`

    g(m, t) := inf{ Σ_y π(y)·max_x g′(m(x), t − c(x, y)) : Σ_x π(x)·m(x) ≥ m }        (g′ := 0 at negative budgets)

is a growth bound for the larger product: the fibre of `E(t)` over a letter `y` is the union
over the letters `x` of the neighbourhoods of the fibres of `E`, and a union is at least its
largest member.  Starting from a point (`g = 1`), this is a computation that returns a valid
bound for any product; on a grid of `−ln m` the rounding can be arranged so that the grid
costs sharpness only.
(b) *Both tail functions from a growth bound.*  With `M(q, t) := sup{m : g(m, t) ≤ q}`,
`Ξ(q) := ∫₀^∞ e^t M(q, t) dt` and `Θ(q) := ∫₀^∞ e^{−t} g(q, t) dt` satisfy (TU) and (TL) for the class of
`ρ` (the points of a set `D` at exit cost above `t` have their `t`-neighbourhood inside `D`).
(c) *The lower tail in closed form.*  For every set `E` and every `λ ≥ 0`,
`∫ e^{−λρ(E → y)} dμ(y) ≥ exp(−Φ^λ(ln 1/μ(E)))`, where `Φ^λ` is the max-plus convolution over the
sites of the least concave majorants of `d ↦ sup{ min_Q [D(Q‖μ_i) + λ·T(P, Q)] : D(P‖μ_i) ≤ d }`
(`T` the optimal transport cost of the site) — a tensorisation by the chain rule with no
error term.  So `Θ(q) = exp(−Φ¹(ln 1/q))` is a lower tail function at every size.  For uniform
bits with several slopes (so many sites of each) the maximiser has one slope common to all types — the
structure of the exponents of §11.26, as an inequality at every `n`.
(d) *Blocks.*  Growth bounds `g₁`, `g₂` of two factors give
`μ(E(t)) ≥ min{ max over splits of the budget of g₁(a, t₁)·g₂(s, t₂) : a·s ≥ μ(E)/(2K) }`,
`K = ⌈log₂(2/μ(E))⌉` (layer cake over the fibre measures and a pigeonhole).  With Harper's
theorem in each block, a uniform cube with a fixed number of slopes has growth bounds and
tail functions in closed form that are sharp up to polynomial factors: products of balls are
extremal up to such factors.
*Numbers.*  The recursion (a) reproduces Harper's theorem at ball sizes within the slack of
the grid (`n = 12`: `0.04` nats); on a biased cube (`n = 14`, `p = 0.2`) it gives the values of the
balls around the **rare** vertex within `0.11` nats; on three products of four sites
(uniform; two costs; biased with asymmetric costs) all 65 534 sets satisfy the growth
bound, which is attained, and the tail functions of (b) (within `2.2` per cent above, attained
below) and of (c) (within `0.15` per cent).  On the uniform cube the closed form of (c) is
`≈ 2/√n` times the exact lower tail function for `n = 32 … 2048`.  Harness XXVII.1 (products of
three sites, exhaustive, without a grid; nine mutations, all caught).
(e) *What is not true, and what is conjectured.*  A Harper theorem for the biased cube is
false in the concentration regime: exhaustively for `n ≤ 4` and five biases, the ball around
the rare vertex is an exact minimiser in all 78 cases in which its neighbourhood is not the
whole cube, and is not in the 17 cases in which it is (harness DEAD.29; D69).  The
piecewise-linear interpolation of ball values is not preserved by the induction on a biased
cube.  The one-variable recursion for `Ξ` (a minimum of integrals for an integral of minima)
is valid, exact in dimension one and two, and exponentially lossy — it credits a set
confined to a subcube with its depth inside the subcube.  *Conjecture:* the single-letter
(Chernoff) potential fails the induction step of (a) by at most a constant over `n` —
numerically `n·defect ≤ 0.632 = 1 − 1/e` on the uniform cube for `n ≤ 1000`, the mean of a Bregman
gap of size half the variance of one site over the total variance — which would give a
closed-form growth bound on every finite product, sharp up to a polynomial factor.
*What it changes.*  Theorem 11.118 can be run on an outer block that mixes slopes (the case
the Computational Research Division's type-aligned design avoids) or biases, with tail
functions that are valid at the block's size.  *What it does not:* for a field the reference
of the algorithm is the flat-histogram instance, whose budget depends on the type of the
exit point and is not an additive cost (Theorem 11.63); no closed form with polynomial
precision beyond a fixed number of slopes on the uniform cube; no run of the algorithm
with these functions; no referee.  *Prior art:* the induction is classical (the fractional
form of Harper's theorem of Bollobás and Leader, 1991, which treats the weighted cube for
down-sets; Talagrand's inductions); the exponents of isoperimetry in product spaces are
known asymptotically (Ahlswede–Zhang; L. Yu, arXiv 2205.07596, with a dimension-free bound
in the concentration regime); (c) is Marton's coupling with the exact single-letter
trade-off, and no novelty is claimed for it beyond its use as a tail function.

### 11.34 Phase II: what observational information is worth (pointer)

*Added in Phase II (branch `research/phase2-foundations`, 2026-11-28).  Statements, proofs, status and the
comparison with the science division's `INFERENCE_LIMITS.md` are in `docs/phase2/PHASE2_REPORT.md`; this section
only records what was established, in the numbering of that report.  Not refereed by a human; internal review:
`docs/phase2/PHASE2_REVIEW.md`.*

Besides evaluations the algorithm receives information about the normalised ensemble `wπ/A(w)`.

* **Theorem A [P; cores V] (`tolerant_oracle_packing`, `tolerant_oracle_packing_nonadaptive`, `LogLip.convex_comb`,
  `massOf_convex_comb_eq`, `ensOf_convex_comb`, `sum_translates_eq`, `hoeffding_iid_mean`).**  Means of `M` arbitrary
  observables with values in `[−1, 1]`, each to an absolute tolerance `τ` (any answer inside the tolerance may be
  returned): both lower bounds of §§11.10, 11.16 lose at most the factor `L = ⌈2τ^{−2} ln(4M/η)⌉`,
  `E|Q| ≥ (1 − η)(1 − 2δ)·2ⁿ/(L·|B|)`.  Hence **both exponents (`a`, `h`) are unchanged whenever `ln(1/τ) = o(n)` and
  `ln ln M = o(n)`**; the same for `q` adaptive statistical queries.  Mechanism: the average of `L` independent
  uniform translates of a dip is admissible, has the same partition function, and its ensemble means are within
  `τ` of the uniform ones with probability `1 − η` (Hoeffding).
* **Theorem A′ [P; uses the bounded-differences inequality (K); the mean-zero identity V] (`sum_tuples_sup'_bias_eq_zero`, `abs_sup'_sub_sup'_le`).**  With `L` narrow dips (a maximum,
  each carrying the `L`-th part of the excess) the adaptive exponent at tolerance `e^{−γn}` with `ln ln M ≈ βn` is at least
  `h̄(2γ + β)`, `h̄(λ) = KL(ρ₀ − λ/u‖½) − λ = h − (1 − ℓ)λ + O(λ²)` (`ℓ` the Chernoff parameter, `L` of §11.18), for every
  `2γ + β < a` — positive on that whole range, with a double zero at `a`.  Mechanism: the bias of a maximum of random
  dips against a centred observable has mean exactly zero over the centres, overlaps included, and one centre
  moves it by at most twice the mass of a dip, so the bounded-differences inequality applies.  (The first version,
  by Hoeffding for the main term and Markov for the overlaps, needed `h̄(λ) > γ`; the present form was written after
  the first internal review of Phase II and reviewed separately by a second AI referee, who found it correct for
  `δ ≤ ½` and sharpened a constant — `docs/phase2/PHASE2_REPORT.md` §2.3, §10; `docs/phase2/PHASE2_REVIEW_A1.md`.)
* **Theorem A″ [P; identity V] (`hiding_law_sum`, `flat_mixture`, `flat_mixture_truncated`).**  For any reference
  measure and any kernel with constant row sums, cones scaled to equal mass and mixed with the law
  `q(c) ∝ E_π e^{−u d(·,c)}` add up to a constant; this gives the analogue of Theorem A on every vertex-transitive
  space and, with a non-uniform reference, a positive but smaller exponent: for a field `KL(κ*‖θ)` at the constant
  weight (`0.0109` at `p = 0.3`, `u = 1`), 49 % and 22 % of the class exponent of Theorem 11.59 at the best tilt in the two
  cases computed (two earlier statements of ours about this were wrong: D71).
* **Proposition 2.7 [P] (absorption).**  For a reference `e^{−f}π₀/Z_f` with a known `κ`-Lipschitz energy `f`, `κ < u`:
  every lower bound for the reference `π₀` at the slope `u − κ` holds (with or without observations), and every
  algorithm for `π₀` at the slope `u + κ` applies; so for a uniform `π₀` the adaptive exponent lies in
  `[h(u − κ), h(u + κ)]` — the only statement of the programme that covers interacting known parts together with
  arbitrary observables; not sharp (compare Theorem 11.59 for a field).
* **Theorem B [P; cores V] (`sum_mul_char_eq_zero`, `ensemble_mean_eq_of_spectrum`, `exists_separating_tuple`,
  `parity_balanced`, `exists_generators_cube`, `exists_generators_kill`).**  *Exact* means of observables whose joint
  Walsh spectrum has `M` non-zero frequencies cost at most the factor `|C| < 2(M + 1)` (a subgroup whose annihilator
  avoids the spectrum; for this method the bound on `|C|` is tight up to the factor 2); refined exponent `h̄(ln M/n)`; for all marginals of order
  `αn`: `h̄(h₂(α)) ≤ θ(α) ≤ (1 − α)h`.  The statement for marginals of order `o(n)` is the science division's
  (Theorem 4, addenda A1, A8); Proposition 11.104 is its non-adaptive half.
* **Theorem C [P].**  With the exact joint law of `θn` coordinates (or that law to total variation `τ ≤ c·εδ`) the
  exponents are **exactly `(1 − θ)h` and `(1 − θ)a`**; hence neither hypothesis of Theorem A can be dropped.  With
  every bounded observable to tolerance `τ ≤ c·εδ` a bounded number of evaluations suffices for randomised
  algorithms (`random_cell_failure_le`, `abs_log_le_of_abs_sub_one_le`), while deterministic ones need `τ·2ⁿ` up
  to polynomial factors.
* **Theorem E [P].**  With `m = e^{νn}` independent samples of the ensemble, `E|Q| ≥ exp(n[h̄(ν) − ν] − o(n))` for
  `ν < ν*`, `h̄(ν*) = 2ν*` (`ν* = 0.4024·h` at `u = 1`): a birthday bound for the number of basins and hiding for
  the basins not sampled.  No algorithm with samples below `e^{nh}` is known.
* Also machine-checked there: Chebyshev's inequality for the mean of independent draws (`chebyshev_iid_mean`),
  the probabilistic core of Theorem 11.44 (plain Monte Carlo); the bound on the relative variance over the class
  remains a paper proof.
* **Added after the owner's collaboration update of 2026-11-28 (a division on certified MBAR): the bridge note,
  `docs/phase2/BRIDGE_NOTE.md` — [P], unrefereed; exact steps V (`proofs/Frontiers/BridgeOverlap.lean`:
  `bridge_identity`, `overlap_ge_of_tail_bound`, `tv_ge_of_agree_off`, `one_two_dips_gap`, `mixture_mean_diff_le`,
  `ratio_within`, `harmonic_between_min`, `sq_sum_sqrt_mul_le`); harness XXVIII.5.**  *Theorem F:* by Lemma 11.43(b),
  every member of the cube class has `E_π min(w/A, s) ≥ min(½, s(V(n, r_s)+1)/2ⁿ)`, `r_s` the largest radius with
  `s·m_{r+1} ≤ ½`; in particular `1 − TV(π, μ_w) ≥ e^{−nh−O(log n)}`, attained by the cone — so the largest two-state
  effective resistance of bridge sampling over the class has the exponent `h` of adaptive evaluation.
  *Corollary F1:* with `e^{ν₁n}` samples of the ensemble, `e^{(θ_na(ν₁)+o(1))n}` non-adaptive evaluations suffice on the
  whole class (the bridge identity `A = E_π[min(w,θ)]/E_μ[min(1,θ/w)]` on a grid of thresholds): `a` without
  samples, `h` with `e^{nh}` of them, `0` with `e^{n ln cosh(u/2)}` — the curve `θ_na` of Theorem 11.44, with the number of
  samples in the place of the accuracy.  *Proposition F2:* one approximate sample of the ensemble costs at least
  `e^{n(h−o(1))}` evaluations.  *Proposition F3:* weights that agree off `D` have ensembles at total variation at
  least `μ₀(Dᶜ)(1 − A₀/A₁)` — no hiding pair of this report is hard for samples.  *Theorem J:* with means of functions
  of the *energy* at tolerance `e^{−γn}` the exponent lies in `[θ_hint(γ), min(h, θ_na(γ))]`, and the cost is bounded
  beyond `γ* = ln cosh(u/2)`: an exact threshold, where for observables of the position (Theorem A′) the two bounds
  are far apart.  The note also relates these to the statements of the MBAR division (a counterexample to
  the convexity of its allocation problem for correlated samples; a second derivation of the dual form of its
  allocation theorem, which that division had found first).

## 12. Strongest unresolved questions, and what a publication would need

1. **The exponent theorems (11.9, 11.15).**  The lower bounds are machine-checked for every `n`;
   the upper bounds are paper proofs resting on the type covering lemma.  A publication needs
   (a) a careful write-up of the credit-distortion reduction and of the heterogeneous case
   (sites of unequal type; only finitely many types are covered here); (b) the second-order
   term (the polynomial prefactor visible in the layer counts); (c) interacting known parts.
   For a chain with pairwise `E₀`, Hamming envelope `c` and zero residual the partition-function
   bound gives, by the Gibbs variational principle,
   `n⁻¹ ln N ≥ max_t [p_E(t) − ln(1+(k−1)e^{−tc})] = sup_ν [h(ν) − h_b(δ_ν) − δ_ν ln(k−1)]`,
   `δ_ν = e_ν/c`, the supremum over stationary measures `ν` with `δ_ν ≤ (k−1)/k` (the constraint
   `t ≥ 0`; without it the right-hand side can exceed the left), entropy rate `h(ν)` and mean
   excitation energy `e_ν` per site, `p_E` the pressure (computable from the transfer matrix).
   This is the *Shannon lower bound* of the rate–distortion function of the process `ν` at
   distortion `δ_ν`, and we expect the true exponent to be `sup_ν R_ν(δ_ν)` — equal to the bound
   when the optimal `ν` is below its critical distortion, as for binary symmetric Markov sources
   (Gray 1970), and strictly larger otherwise.  None of this is proved here, and it is further
   from proof than it sounds: type covering for Markov types with a distortion budget fixed by
   the pair marginal is not an off-the-shelf lemma (second referee).  For independent sites the
   same remark explains when the Boltzmann choice of weights in Theorem 11.8 is optimal
   (two-state sites with zero residual: always) and when general weights are needed.
   *Added in cycle 9:* for homogeneous chains the exponent is `sup_ν R_ν(e(ν))` (Theorem 11.40),
   by a proof that avoids Markov-type covering; the Shannon lower bound above vanishes on a
   window (Proposition 11.41).  Open: a computable form of the exponent below the critical
   distortion; inhomogeneous chains; the finite-temperature exponents of a chain.
   (c') the exponent of Theorem 11.15 for exponentially small accuracies `ε_n = e^{−λn}`: between
   `max(R_β, max{H(Q) : KL(Q‖π) < λ})` and `max_Q R(Q; s, (KL(Q‖π) − λ)₊/β)`.
   (d) a careful comparison with the source-coding literature on exponential moments
   of distortion and on guessing (Merhav 2011; Arikan–Merhav 1998): Theorem 11.15 is a
   corollary of the former, read here only in part; whether the zero-temperature statement with
   its credit distortion and the dichotomy also appear there in some form is not settled.
2. **Algorithms.**  On additive instances the exponent `R*` is reached without knowing the
   residual (learn-then-cover), and no algorithm, randomised or not, does better
   (Theorem 11.23).  Open:
   (a) instances that are only approximately additive — the cover computed from the
   interpolant must be robust to the pair remainder;
   (b) **the randomised exponent at finite temperature.**  On the cube at the zero residual
   it is known in every accuracy regime (Theorem 11.25).  At additive instances of identical
   sites it is `R^gen_β(ε₁)` (Theorem 11.27: lower bound for every `n`; upper bound by a paper
   proof that an independent referee checked).  For a publication the proof needs a careful
   write-up and a machine check of at least its single-letter part; the relation to the
   fixed-measure isoperimetric theorem (is the black-box bound always equal to the game
   value?) is open, as are sites of several types, exponentially small accuracies beyond the
   cube, non-additive instances and interacting known parts;
   (c) **thresholds.**  Settled for identical independent sites: at additive instances
   (Theorem 11.28(c)) and, without a hint, for the whole class and every alphabet (Theorem
   11.28(d): the smallest oscillation of the tilted site pressure; closed form for two-state
   sites in (e); finitely many site types by averaging).  Open: the cost of non-additive
   instances below the class threshold; chains as known parts — the one-reference sandwich
   and the minimax identity hold there too, but the width is no longer a single-site
   quantity (workstream B gives a lower threshold by a transfer-matrix formula and a
   conjecture for the upper half);
   (d) **algorithms without a hint** on the cube class.  *Settled at the level of exponents
   in cycle 10* (§§11.16, 11.18, 11.19): non-adaptive algorithms have the exponent
   `θ_na(ε₁) = min{KL(ρ‖½) : KL(ρ‖p_u) ≤ ε₁}` (and `a = KL(p_u‖½)` at every fixed accuracy), adaptive
   ones the hinted exponent `θ_hint(ε₁) = KL((Λ₁+ε₁)/u ‖ ½)` — at extensive accuracies (Theorem
   11.54, refereed) and at every bounded accuracy down to `e^{-o(n)}` (`h = θ_hint(0)`, Theorem
   11.58, refereed: R8).  Open: (i) **below the exponential scale** — with a hint the cost
   at the zero function is `2ⁿ/|B(n,k*)|` up to a polynomial factor; without one the upper
   bound is `e^{nh + O(√(n ln n))}` (Theorem 11.58a, twenty-second checkpoint: an explicit
   schedule of `≈ √(n/ln n)` levels; the earlier versions of this item had an unquantified
   `o(n)` and the heuristic `n^{3/4}`).  Between the hinted lower bound — `n·h − O(1)` proved,
   `n·h + ½ ln n − O(1)` numerically — and `n·h + O(√(n ln n))` nothing is known: can
   `e^{nh + O(√n)}`, or `poly(n)·2ⁿ/|B(n,k*)|`, be reached without a hint — the
   first would follow from a rate `C/k²` for an explicit schedule whose levels lose
   `O(ln n)` — or is there a lower bound `e^{nh + ω(log n)}`?  And the same term at extensive
   accuracies (Theorem 11.54), where the method should give `O(√(n ln n))` as well.  Any such bound must come from non-flat instances (on the
   flat one the doubling two-sample bracket stops at the hinted cost up to a polynomial
   factor).  (ii) **Depth** — `k` nested levels have the exponent `τ_k > h` at bounded accuracy,
   `τ_k − h = (2π²h²θ_hint″(0) + o(1))/k²` (Theorem 11.53b; a paper proof, `0.641·a/k²` at `u = 1`); is there a lower bound for a restricted class (a bounded
   number of levels, or of rounds of adaptivity) that matches `τ_k`?  **Rounds** (§11.24;
   refereed, SCI-REV-0003): every nested algorithm with fixed levels needs a number of
   rounds independent of `n`; the two-round exponent is at least `0.359a` (`liminf`) and at
   most `0.624a` (`limsup`) at `u = 1` — strictly between the fixed-sample and the adaptive
   exponent, asymptotically: no separation at a finite size is shown — and **whether
   three rounds, or any fixed number, reach `h` is open**; so are the existence and the
   value of the two-round exponent, what two rounds cost *at* the flat-histogram instance
   (where the lower bound holds for the expected cost), strict monotonicity in the number
   of rounds, and the rate of convergence.
   And **finite sizes** — two
   levels beat the plain bracket only from `n ≈ 500` on at bounded accuracy and `u = 1`
   (beyond `e^{45}` evaluations; `n ≈ 250` at the flat instance only — the worst instance at
   finite `n` is not the flat one, ENG-RES-0008, and which instance maximises the cost of
   Algorithm 2L⁺ at a given `n` is not known beyond that division's search) and from
   `n ≈ 2000` at extensive ones; is there an adaptive algorithm that
   wins at sizes that can be simulated, or a lower bound showing that the gain needs
   `n ≫ 1/θ_hint`?  (iii) **instance by instance** — the zero function is the hardest instance
   with a hint (a corollary of Theorems 11.54 and 11.58); is there an adaptive algorithm
   without a hint that matches the hinted cost at *every* instance up to `e^{o(n)}`, cheap
   instances included?  (iv) **exponentially small accuracies** `ε = e^{-λn}`: the hinted
   exponents of rows 4–6 of Theorem 11.25(d) are not known to be attained without a hint.
   (v) **other spaces** — *a field as known part is done at the level of exponents* (§11.20,
   refereed: R9): the tail lemma is taken relative to a reference instance, the reference is
   the lower envelope of the additive instances, and the isoperimetric input is an
   asymptotic statement for that reference, not the isoperimetry of a fixed product measure
   (which gives the worse exponents of plain sampling from the Gibbs measure of the known
   part — the guess of the earlier checkpoints was wrong in this respect, D47).  Open there:
   a finite-`n` bound for the tail function of the reference with a usable error term (the
   proof gives `n^{-1/8}`; numerically it is `O(ln n/n)`, and on the 4-cube the exact maximisers
   are not always one-centre balls: ratio `2.08`) — a weighted Harper-type inequality; bounded
   accuracies; a proof that no single tilted product measure attains the non-adaptive
   exponent at extensive accuracies when `p ≠ ½` (numerical in three examples), and whether
   the product measure with the capacity-achieving marginal attains it on the whole class
   at bounded accuracy (it does at cone instances; Theorem 11.61); an end-to-end simulation of the
   nested algorithm with a field; instance-optimality beyond symmetric
   instances; larger alphabets and sites of several types — **§11.26: theorems by transfer,
   reviewed (SCI-REV-0005: proved; two gaps in the written proof of the adaptive upper
   bound closed)** (open there: a referee for Theorem 11.97(c) together with Theorem
   11.78(b); a finite-`n` form of Theorem 11.97(c) with a usable error term — exact tail
   functions of the reference on chains small enough for exhaustive search; a simulation
   of the nested algorithm; concavity of `F*` for two letters, that is, of `max_p E_0(ρ, p)`
   in `ρ` for binary-input binary-output channels; which site law
   and which pinned composition is the hardest; alphabets beyond four letters and more
   than two site types numerically; whether the channel-coding dictionary yields anything
   beyond names — bounds on `E_0`, algorithms for `C_t`, strong-converse analogues); **known parts with
   interactions** — for functions of the type (mean-field models) §11.23 settles the
   optimal non-adaptive sample (up to a polynomial factor) and characterises the hinted
   exponent of symmetric instances by a single-letter supremum for every rate
   function (refereed, R10); with two phases the value of that supremum, and with it the
   non-adaptive exponent, is known only in part; open there, in order of importance:
   (α) *the adaptive exponent
   without a hint* (conjecture: the single-letter value `R_H` of the flat-histogram
   instance; the nested algorithm fails because fibre averages are not Lipschitz relative
   to a reference.  §11.25 reduces the question to the uniform measure on one type class
   (Theorem 11.92), where the conjecture is that the proof of Theorem 11.56 goes through
   with random splits (Conjecture 11.94); that would give the uniform cube's exponent as
   an upper bound for *every* interaction and the exact exponent for interactions
   without a field.  **Two things are open: redoing the proof of Theorem 11.56 on
   products of type classes, and — when exits that change the type matter — the exact
   exponent between `R_H` and the bound from type classes**, which needs information
   across type classes; nesting by the type of the inner block leads to a recursion over
   rate functions that we could not close.  For ferromagnets the uniform cube's exponent
   is already an upper bound, through mixtures of fields: Proposition 11.81(c)); (β) the value
   of the single-letter supremum with two phases beyond the accuracy `e₀` at which sets
   around one centre stop being extremal, and a proof that they are extremal below it;
   (γ) without convexity: strict monotonicity of the shear and the witness condition for
   the pair identity, which fails for cones around profile classes near the threshold at
   which the top of the barrier leaves the contact set (there the non-adaptive exponent is
   proved to lie in `[0.00184, 0.00338]` only); (γ′) the junction with the uniform cube: a
   proof that it is at `min{βJ*, βJ_w}` — the smaller of the coupling at which the symmetric
   exit of the uniform cube's profile stops being a local minimum and the coupling at
   which a constant exit at a well becomes feasible — and that `R_H < R_unif` beyond it
   (Proposition 11.81(b); the second would follow from uniqueness of the uniform cube's
   optimal profile among laws of block types of type `½`); (δ) ~~whether an
   antiferromagnet without a field — in the limit a single slice — has exactly the
   uniform cube's exponents~~ **settled in §11.25 for two of the three exponents**, the
   hinted one of `H` and the non-adaptive one (Corollary 11.91: yes, and no function-of-type
   known part exceeds them; reviewed by the Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0001,
   whose finding M1 this restriction is — for adaptive algorithms without a hint an
   antiferromagnet is only known to lie between these two exponents:
   item (α)); (ε) mean-field Potts models and two
   order parameters (a sketch); (ζ) larger alphabets: the comparison
   with the uniform cube **fails** for three or more letters (§11.25, remark; Proposition
   11.103(d): at small slopes a known part that pins the composition onto two letters is
   harder than none, a field with one rare letter is harder still — by `0.03 %` at slope
   `0.5` — and near the threshold a field can be; Proposition 11.103(f) bounds every site
   law by the ceiling `u²/32`); open: *which* site law and
   which pinned composition is the hardest for a given envelope (for the Hamming envelope
   the evidence points to groupings of the letters into about `e^{u/2}` equally weighted
   classes at vanishing accuracy, Proposition 11.103(e), but not near the threshold, and a
   law with one rare letter can exceed every equal grouping by a small margin).  For known parts with *spatial* structure (short-range
   interactions; Markov chains along the sequence) nothing is proved; the natural next
   step is the method of types for Markov chains, where "uniform on type classes" still
   holds for pair types but the one-flip coupling of adjacent classes is no longer exact.
   The conjecture of the earlier checkpoints, that the minimax fixed sample is the
   normalised-maximum-likelihood mixture of the field-tilted Gibbs measures, is right
   about the ensemble only for convex rate functions (D49).  For Euclidean Lipschitz functions on Gaussian space
   the algorithm does not transfer (a fixed split of the coordinates gains nothing: Theorem
   11.120(b)), the hinted lower bound does, with ball-shaped dips in high dimension (Theorem
   11.120(c)), and the adaptive exponent between the two is open; (vi) **a machine-checked
   count** — the number of evaluations of the two-level algorithms (Theorems 11.52, 11.56) is
   a paper proof, in a part of the argument where five wrong versions preceded the right
   one; the Computational Research Division has been asked to attack it with real inner
   brackets and three nested levels (THY-REQ-0001).
   This is a tractability question for integrating `e^{−βg}` over a Lipschitz class in high
   dimension, and the natural bridge to the open lower bound of Holzmüller–Bach (2025) for
   stochastic log-partition estimation outside the optimisation regime;
   (e) for `f ≡ 0` in doubling spaces, does the resource-augmented bound of Theorem 11.11
   convert into `≤ K·N* + 1` without the `log(1/ε)` of Bachoc et al. (`prior_art/L4`, sketched,
   unverified)?  With a known part it does not (D30), and the search itself is unboundedly
   worse than the smallest certificate even on the line (§11.11, D39).  For asymmetric
   envelopes Theorem 11.11 needs a quasi-symmetry constant of the slack, which can be
   arbitrarily bad, and its constants `θ`, `ε/6` are probably not tight; the centre-form bound
   of Proposition 11.30 covers `κ = 1` but not dominated states.  Is there a search rule with a
   guarantee against the certificate size on product landscapes (the exponent of best-first
   search there is only bracketed, workstream C)?
3. **Complexity classification of the exact criteria** (referee, Q4.1(iv)).  For pairwise `E₀`
   and site-additive `d`, "is configuration `x` possibly optimal" is a pairwise minimisation;
   "is state `r` of site `i` possibly optimal" is an `∃∀` question — is it `Σ₂ᵖ`-hard, and
   polynomial on chains?  On succinct product spaces even *verifying* a certificate is
   coNP-hard in general (covering radius); the kernels avoid this only through explicit
   branch-and-bound certificates.
4. **Second-order classes.**  The question of the previous version — is the cost under dense
   constants exponential, as the covering radius `(2·gap/c)^{1/2}` suggests? — is answered in
   §11.12: yes, with a covering sandwich, and polynomially many evaluations suffice only when
   the excitation energy is at least a quarter of `c·n`.  Open: the simplex conjecture (is the
   three-legged spider the best `n+1` evaluations?); the window `n/4 ≲ e/c < n/3`; the cost for
   sparse constants beyond the clique bounds; re-centring with a termination guarantee; a
   box-restricted class; certified constants `c_ij` for one concrete residual — without which
   the interface is hypothetical.
5. **Dependent references.**  The exact worst-case free-energy gap for a Markov-chain
   reference: additivity fails in general (D25), and it fails for binary pairwise models and
   binary Markov trees as well (D41); for open binary chains without tilt no counterexample
   is known; a two-sided bracket from transfer matrices (best additive two-level residual
   below, Wasserstein-matrix bound above) is unwritten.
6. **Proof complexity of the extended kernels.**  Lower bounds for connected families
   (triangles coupled along a chain) for cut-free and for decomposition-aware certificates; an
   approximate version of the partition-kernel separation and a representation-independent
   notion of rigidity (§11.8); comparison with MICE/CPOG for model counting and with
   pseudo-Boolean proof logging.  *From the Scientific Discovery Division (SCI-RES-0014,
   its Propositions P7.3, P7.5; paper proofs of its workstream, not re-derived by us):*
   one `branch` on a site with pairwise leaves certifies exactly what the pairwise
   relaxation with the triplet constraints of all triples through that site certifies;
   and on a ring of `n` binary sites with attractive neighbours and repulsive other pairs
   (`F(S) = |S| − w·#{ring edges inside S} + R·#{other pairs inside S}`, `3/2 < w < 2`, `R ≥ 3`) every
   certified tree without `sum` has depth at least `⌈n/3⌉`, and one with `⌈n/3⌉ + 1` leaves
   exists — a connected family that needs linear depth and linearly many leaves.
   **Open (its question): a connected family with a unique minimiser whose `sum`-free
   certificates need exponentially many leaves.**  Every gap it met on real or random
   instances closed at depth one or two.
7. **Engineering** (referee, Q2): a certificate producer and experiments at realistic sizes; a
   compiled checker with a refinement proof (kernel evaluation of `verify` as written by
   `decide +kernel` does not scale; an integer checker of one leaf written for the kernel
   does, to `1.5·10⁵` table entries in seconds — measured, `experiments/coordinator_checks/kernel_eval/` —
   so the open step on that route is a proof, written once, that the integer checker
   implies `LeafOK` for the decoded instance, and an integer checker for whole trees);
   certified envelope constants for a real residual.

8. **Probabilistic certificates.**  A kernel that checks a spot-check transcript against
   verifier-side randomness, with `hedgedSpotCheck_correct` as its soundness theorem.  The
   detection probability `p` must itself be certified: for the minimum it is a minimum over
   closed slack balls and the set of near-minimisers (harness XII.4, XII.7); for free energies
   it is an isoperimetric quantity (item 2(b)) — at additive instances above the threshold the
   two-reference sandwich certifies it by a single-site computation.
9. **Envelopes for chains** (§§11.14, 11.17).  *Partly answered in cycle 10*: residual classes
   that are linear in pair-distance profiles have per-pair constants and, at extensive
   accuracy, certificates whose number of evaluations does not depend on the chain length —
   for a class that is much smaller than the RMSD-Lipschitz classes of §11.14, and with a
   bound that is numerically vacuous.  *Data received in cycle 10* (Computational Research
   Division): no saturation at any enumerated size — linear growth on the lattice through
   27 beads, geometric growth off-lattice through 15 beads (§11.17).  Open: (a) **a
   thermodynamic limit theorem for certificate sizes.**  For the zero residual and a known
   part that is a function of the gauche count, the cover problem depends on the chain only
   through the set of pairs (profile, fewest gauche torsions realising it); if that set,
   divided by `N`, converges, the certificate size at accuracy `ε₁N` should converge to a
   covering number of the limit with position-dependent radii (`ENG-REQ-0001`).  Is there a
   limit shape, is it convex (concatenation suggests it; the obstruction is a chain end
   buried in a compact piece), how large is the plateau, and at what chain length is it
   approached?  *Answered in part for the lattice chain in §11.22* (workstream S; reviewed by the
   Scientific Discovery Division, SCI-REV-0002, whose wording this is): a compact convex
   limit shape exists for bridges; the certificate sizes of bridges converge to its covering
   number off a countable, unidentified set of accuracies; for every limit point of the
   certificate sizes of all walks at `(L, ε₁) = (1, ½)`: between 116 and 3 627 **[P,
   computer-assisted]**; that the sizes of all walks converge is a conjecture **[C]**; our
   estimate of the limit is a few hundred and of the chain length at which it is approached
   `10³`–`10⁵` beads or more **[N]** — the shape has a surface correction of exact order `N^{-1/3}`
   at its compact end, but no theorem bounds that chain length in either direction (the
   first version said "for all walks the plateau is between 50 and 3 627 … and is approached
   at `10³`–`10⁵` beads").  **Still open:** (a0) whether `ε₁ = ½` or `¼` is a jump of the limiting
   covering number, and any rigorous statement about *when* the covering numbers are near
   their limit points;
   (a1) *Conjecture 11.75* — unrestricted walks have the same limit shape as bridges;
   equivalently, walks and bridges have the same ground-state energy per bead for every
   three-shell pair energy with a stiffness term; equivalently, every walk has the
   `(profile, #gauche)` of `o(N)` bridges up to `o(N)`.  Local surgery cannot prove it (a double
   strand is rigid); what is missing is a bound on the cost of a multi-scale decomposition.
   The free-energy analogue for self-attracting walks is a standing open problem; this
   question is weaker.  (a2) The exact body: seven vertices of the outer polytope are
   attained by no periodic chain system with at most 12 sites per cell — either a
   second-level cluster programme (two-shell cluster, six-ring) removes them or larger
   cells attain them (`THY-REQ-0008`); with it `N_∞` to better than a factor of ten.  (a3) The
   routing lemma that puts every periodic chain system into the limit set (a sketch).
   (a4) A rate for the whole body (the compact end is settled at `N^{-1/3}`; interior points
   are approached at rate `N^{-1/2}` uniformly, Proposition 11.69a, and at rate `1/N` with a
   universal constant in the limit, because bridges with clean ends form an exact
   semigroup that generates all of `ℤ⁵`, Proposition 11.69b; open: an effective threshold
   `M₀` in its part (f) — our elementary estimate is effective but has a constant of at
   least `3 132` and needs five clean bridges of one level around the point).
   (a5) Anything
   off-lattice: there the profile is a function, the plateau is exponential in
   `L·S_c·M/ε₁`, and only a heuristic estimate exists; a prediction of the measured growth
   rate per torsion needs the distance-entropy function of the profile classes.  The
   Computational Research Division has measured it up to 14 torsions (ENG-RES-0009): at
   `L = 1` the entropy per torsion of a profile ball of radius `N/2` is `0.33` and still rising
   by `0.013` per torsion — the value `0.39` that we had inferred from the growth of the
   covering numbers (THY-RES-0002) is a statement about a limit these sizes have not
   reached, neither established nor excluded; at `L = ⅕` it has nearly converged at `0.65`
   (inferred: `0.6`); and the number of pairs per bead within the cutoff is `3.1` at 17 beads
   against the bulk value of about `63` on which the heuristic plateau estimate rests —
   **every enumerable chain is at one twentieth of the bulk coordination**.  (a6) The
   abstract limit theorems are machine-checked (`CoverStability.lean`, `SetLimit.lean`); the
   two lattice lemmas that feed them — the site-set reduction and the concatenation of
   bridges — are not.  (b) an upper bound for the class
   "pair-additive plus a small first-order remainder" that matches the lower bound "the two
   slacks add", or a proof that the cost is a product; (c) randomised algorithms for linear
   classes — all lower bounds there are for deterministic schemes at the zero residual, and a
   generic evaluation sees every perturbation, so the dip construction has no analogue;
   (d) the cost of *checking* a certificate in the profile format over voxels of torsions,
   where the lever arm returns; (e) profiles for three-body terms; (f) whether a physically
   motivated residual has a useful Lipschitz constant in this format — the interface is
   hypothetical until one instance is certified.  Unchanged from cycle 9: close the bracket of
   Theorem 11.38 (constants two orders of magnitude apart; lower bound at the zero residual
   only; excluded volume ignored), prove the lower constant of the lever-arm law, and a lower
   bound for the RMSD format when its constant is extensive.
10. **Second-order classes at finite temperature** (Theorem 11.33): sharpen the polynomial
   bound below the Curie–Weiss coupling; a known part with interactions — what replaces the
   hypothesis "`f` additive" of (a) (the proof needs Dobrushin's condition for `f + g`), and
   where the boundary between polynomial and exponential then lies (it moves: remark after
   the theorem); non-homogeneous constants (Dobrushin's condition is
   then a row-sum condition); `k`-state sites; the continuous analogue and its relation to the
   smoothness classes of Holzmüller–Bach.  **Observables other than `ln Z`** (Theorem 11.35):
   close the interval between `H/√2` and `H` for the magnetisation at weak coupling.
   **Second and third order at zero temperature** (Theorem 11.18a, Propositions 11.18b,
   11.18c): (a) *certified* constants `c_ij`, `c_T` for a physical remainder — an interval
   evaluation of mixed differences from the functional form, in place of maxima over an
   enumerated domain (the Scientific Discovery Division's measurement shows such bounds
   would not be vacuous for neutral side chains in rotamer variables); (b) the best
   pairwise relaxation of the three-body envelope — the linear programme over the shares
   of Theorem 11.18a(d) — and how far it is from the envelope (measured by the division:
   the pair form loses a median factor of ten in `ln Z(model) − ln Z(E)` against the
   three-body envelope, the site form a further `6.8`); (c) *answered by the division,
   SCI-REV-0012:* the share certificate of Proposition 11.18b(d) certifies 11 of its 13
   instances in which the row-sum condition fails and the exact criterion holds, and
   state-dependent shares — the dual certificate of the pairwise linear relaxation,
   Proposition 11.18b(e) — all 13; open is a certificate beyond the relaxation, for the
   instances with an integrality gap (five of its analyses); (d) a machine-checked
   version of the remainder theorems on reset-closed domains (the Lean statements are
   for full products), where completeness of shares fails (Proposition 11.18c(a)) and the
   exact criterion is a minimisation over the domain; (e) covers of a domain with
   exclusions by reset-closed pieces: how many references are needed — the division's
   measurement says the reference should be chosen first (the minimiser of the
   clash-free domain) and the domain second; (f) **the Hamming ball for randomised
   algorithms** (Proposition 11.18e(b′)): for a bracket of prescribed width, is
   `sup_g E|Q(g)| ≥ (1 − δ)N_ball − o(1)`?  True on one site, instance by instance; false
   for a bracket of unspecified width on more than one site (the science division's
   counter-algorithm); a Gaussian prior does not decide it; for the cube at order two
   there is an outline that would give `(1 − 2δ)N_ball` — a prior with widely separated
   coefficient scales and a pairing of instances with the same transcript — whose
   combinatorial steps are verified and whose analytic steps are to be written.
11. **Observable free energies** (§11.28; the question of the Scientific Discovery
   Division that we rank first among the new ones).  The *range* of a ratio of two
   macrostate weights is settled as a duality; open are, in order: (a) **the number of
   evaluations** needed to certify `ln[Z(A)/Z(B)]` to a given accuracy — with a hint, the
   counterpart of Theorem 11.25; without one, of Theorems 11.45 and 11.54 — where the
   sensitive alternatives are no longer dips on small sets alone: a perturbation that
   moves weight between the two macrostates matters at first order, and the constraints
   from `B` to `A` couple the two partition functions (**settled for box classes**, where
   there is no geometry and nothing couples them: the larger of the two macrostates' own
   distances to the floor, Corollary 11.114); (b) the exact range for a pairwise
   known part (on a tree by dynamic programming?) and for macrostates defined by a
   counting statistic; (c) the range and the cost for chains with geometric envelopes
   (§11.17), where macrostates are sets of conformations and the envelope is a profile
   distance; (d) prior art — *answered at summary level by the Scientific Discovery
   Division (SCI-RES-0005)*: for a separable envelope Theorem 11.105 is the closed form
   of the density-ratio class; the general duality was not found; two leads are
   unresolved (credal sets from comparative probabilities; cones of the
   Birkhoff–Hilbert-metric method); (e) soft macrostates (weight functions) and more than
   two of them; (f) a common generalisation of Theorems 11.106 and 11.106a — a condition
   under which the maximal field is the optimal closed pair.
12. **Local data with a field** (§11.29).  The class exponents are settled (Theorem
   11.109a).  Open: (a) the exact exponent *at an instance* with a one-body oracle — the
   bracket `V ≤ R^{orc} ≤ U` of Proposition 11.109b; the division conjectures the lower end,
   and what is missing is an isoperimetric upper bound that knows the window of one-body
   marginals (a type-resolved Theorem 11.63); (b) marginals of order `k ≥ 3` with a field
   (the division's conjecture); (c) *done by the division:* the compensation lemma, the
   excess of a dip and the lower bound for adaptive algorithms are machine-checked
   (its files, adopted at the eighteenth checkpoint); parts (d), (e) of Theorem 11.109a
   and Proposition 11.109b are not.
13. **Remainders that are small in a typical norm** (§11.30).  For box classes the cost
   is settled up to constants: the Boltzmann factor of the free-energy distance to the
   floor, which is extensive for a remainder that is a sum over the system, plus a term
   from the ceiling.  Open, in the order of their value for applications: (a) **a
   certified floor in compact geometries.**  The science division has shown
   (SCI-MSG-0020) that for a solvent term on an extended backbone a floor and a ceiling
   that are *functions* — two banded pairwise models from evaluations on a Hamming ball
   and certified constants of order `m` (Theorem 11.18d) — bracket `ln Z` of a system far
   beyond enumeration, and that the same recipe fails on a helix and for charged side
   chains, where the certified constants fall too slowly with the order.  Its bound by
   analysis alone loses a factor of hundreds because it treats atom pairs one at a time
   and cannot see the cancellation between self and cross terms of a neutral molecule.
   **Is that loss intrinsic to bounds that are sums of absolute values of pair terms —
   a lower bound of that kind — or is there a signed bound that escapes it?**
   *Answered by the division (SCI-MSG-0024, its workstream P5; its numbers and paper
   proofs, model-relative, not checked by us beyond the two lemmas of Theorem 11.18d(a′),
   (b′) that we machine-checked): the loss is intrinsic, and the helix is certified all the
   same.*  A bound that uses the charges only through their magnitudes must hold for
   every sign pattern (Born radii do not depend on the charges); reversing signs on its
   enumerated helix instances makes the order-`m` remainder 16 to 153 times the truth at
   `m = 3, 4, 5` for leucine — a lower bound for every sign-blind bound, by exact
   evaluation, with an explicit family on which the loss grows linearly in the number of
   partners in range; sums kept signed on one side stay 6–53 times above the truth; and
   a term kept signed at the reference is the next order in disguise (Theorem 11.18d(b′)).
   Yet with the floor as a function, order 6 and site penalties bracket `ln Z` of a
   thirty-residue leucine helix within `0.73` nats without sampling, and pair shares
   (Theorem 11.18d(c′)) give `0.016` nats at twenty residues and `0.033` at thirty from the
   same evaluations (SCI-RES-0013):
   that ensemble keeps fewer than one side chain off its anchor, and a penalty of level
   `k` costs the `k`-th power of that probability (Proposition 11.18f(a)).  **On the helix
   the certificate works through its form, not through a better bound.**  And where the
   ensemble is not frozen it stops: for serine on the helix (more than half of the side
   chains off the anchor) the division finds that at order 4 even the envelope — the
   limit of every allocation of shares — gives `0.27` nats at six residues, fourfold more
   with each residue (its addendum A17 (15)).  Open: order 6
   (the least sign-blind bound is between 3.8 and 36 times the truth); polar and charged
   side chains; compact ensembles with real side-chain entropy, where a sampled bracket
   at the price of the envelope (Proposition 11.113a) is untried; and whether a bound
   that sees the signs can be uniform over contexts by a mechanism other than evaluation
   — the division found no candidate.  In our terms a sign-blind bound is a certificate
   *without evaluations* for the class of all sign patterns of a known kernel — a class in
   which one generic evaluation identifies the member, since the values `sᵀA(x)s` of a
   generic symmetric matrix separate the sign patterns up to a global sign — so the
   obstruction is one of analysis and computation, not of information, and our query
   bounds have nothing to say about it (an answer to its question P5-T1(ii)).
   *For a cluster with a net charge the loss is bounded, by the square of
   `R = Σ|q|/|Σq|`* **[P, elementary; harness XI.25]** (an answer to the division's question
   P8-T2, SCI-MSG-0027: "is there a statement `SB ≤ C·(Σ|q|/|Σq|)²·truth` for charges
   dominated by one sign?").  Let the remainder be a quadratic form `t = qᵀMq` in the
   charges (`M` a mixed difference of the kernel), `w = |q|`, and `SB = max_s |(s∘w)ᵀM(s∘w)|`
   over all sign patterns — the least bound that sees the charges through their
   magnitudes only.  For any reference value `m̄ ≠ 0` put `e = max_{ij}|M_ij − m̄|` and
   `ρ = e/|m̄|`.  Then `SB ≤ (|m̄| + e)(Σw)²` and `|t| ≥ |m̄|(Σq)² − e(Σw)²`, hence

       SB  ≤  (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρR²) · R² · |t|          whenever ρR² < 1,

   with equality `SB = R²|t|` for a constant kernel — the square cannot be improved — and
   for two clusters and a bilinear form the factor `(1 + ρ)/(1 − ρR_aR_b)·R_aR_b`.  A neutral
   cluster has `R = ∞`: the division's unbounded loss.  **Without a bound on the variation
   of the kernel there is no such statement, even for charges of one sign**:
   `M = [[1, −1], [−1, 1]]`, `q = (1, 1)` has `t = 0` and `SB = 4` — and a mixed difference of a
   positive kernel does change sign in general.  So the answer is yes exactly where the
   remainder kernel is nearly constant over the atoms in range, relative to its mean
   and to `1/R²` — two compact charged groups far apart compared with their size.  The
   division's validation case (five lysine residues, order 4: truth `0.0250`, all charges
   positive `0.111`, best sign pattern found `0.127` kcal/mol) has a loss of `5.1`, and "all
   positive" within 13 per cent of the best pattern, as for a kernel of nearly one sign;
   for an ammonium head group with force-field charges of about `−0.39` and `3 × 0.34` the
   ratio is `R² ≈ 4.9` (charges quoted from memory, not checked) — the same size.
   **Measured by the division since (SCI-RES-0021, its script `kernel_spread.py`; [M],
   theirs): the charges are as quoted (`R² = 4.905`), but the regime of the lemma is
   reached by none of the fifty blocks between ammonium groups of that case** — `ρ` lies
   between `0.95` and `2.1`, the sixteen entries of a block being of one sign and spanning
   a factor of forty to `10⁵` (the fourth mixed difference of the kernel is carried by the
   nearest atom pairs), so `ρR² ≥ 4.67`; the blocks that carry the remainder lose `2.6`–`4.3`,
   below `R²`, for a reason that is not the lemma's (a one-signed block concentrated on few
   atom pairs), and for such blocks there is no bound in terms of `R` alone.  The
   agreement of `5.1` with `R² ≈ 4.9` is a coincidence.  The lemma states the price for
   groups that act as a whole; it does not explain the slack on the division's instance,
   and no statement that does is known.  And the
   machine-checked part of its certificate ends at Theorem 11.18d:
   its chain rule for mixed differences, its term-by-term bound and its banding are paper
   proofs with unreviewed code; (b) classes between the box and the first-order
   classes — a box *with* geometry (the intersection is treated in Corollary 11.111);
   exponential-moment constraints under `π` are the Rényi family of Proposition 11.112,
   settled up to constants with a hint and open at the level of the instance-optimal
   sampler and of the exact constants without a hint (an earlier version of this item
   said that without a floor "a single hidden state defeats every sampler" under such a
   constraint: that is true of polynomial moments of the remainder and false of
   exponential ones — `DEAD_ENDS.md` D57 item 6); (c) the cost of a *ratio* of macrostate weights in a box
   class is settled (Corollary 11.114); open is the same in a class *with* geometry —
   item 11(a) — and in a box known only up to a common shift of the remainder, which is
   the natural class for a difference; (d) known parts that can only be sampled
   approximately (a Markov chain with a certified mixing time); (e) the exact hinted cost
   on a finite space with heavy states — a covering programme, of which the dip- and
   bump-weighted sampler is a feasible point (the science division's remark); (f) *closed
   at the nineteenth checkpoint:* a bracket for sandwiches that uses more than the
   range — Proposition 11.113(c′), the empirical Bernstein bound of Maurer and Pontil;
   (g) the nested sampler of Proposition 11.113a on a real sandwich (not run), and an
   inner bracket for the envelope that is certified *without* free sampling — a
   deterministic bound on `Z(e_∓)` between the share models; (h) the lower bound without
   a hint for a sandwich (`sinh²(Δ/2)/ε²`) is proved on paper for fine-grained samplers
   (Proposition 11.113(d), a two-point argument); open are the constant — the exact
   two-point number is three times the Pinsker bound and a third of the sufficient
   count — and a machine check (the library has packing bounds for hinted verification
   only).
14. **Known parts with interactions** (§11.32).  For a nearest-neighbour chain the game
   function is known in brackets, and the direction of the effect of the coupling turns
   with the envelope.  Open: (a) **the crossover** — the slope at which `a_∞` and `h_∞` pass
   below the uniform cube's; the Markov recursion with blocks of four and five sites
   would decide it at `u = 1.5, 2, 2.5` (the Scientific Discovery Division's request
   R10-T2, with the vertex enumeration asked of the engineering division, R10-E1), and a
   proof of its first-order expansion at large slopes,
   `F_∞(t) = (1−t)ln 2 − e^{−tu}cosh²(Kt) + o(e^{−tu})`, would settle all large slopes at once;
   (b) the lower side of the small-slope law for the limit `F_∞` (the division's
   Conjecture R10.3: `lim_{u→0}F_∞(t; u)/u² = (t(1−t)/2)·lim V_n/n` for homogeneous
   finite-range chains); (c) the threshold: is `E_n = ln[Z_n(u/2)/Z_n(0)]` for every `n` and
   `p`, or does it fail at strong coupling, where the relaxation with the chain as
   reference has a value well above `E_F` (R10-T5)?  (d) **upper bounds on costs at bounded
   accuracy** — the analogue of Theorem 11.58 for block landscapes — and anything uniform
   in the block length; (e) an optimal fixed sample for chains: the stratified
   construction of §11.26 fails because class-wise quantile truncations leave the class;
   (f) a field, more states, site-dependent couplings (the reductions hold verbatim; the
   brackets become sub- and super-additive processes), strips and `ℤ^d` (sketches);
   (g) a machine check of Theorem 11.116(a), (b) — finite algebra, like (c), which is
   machine-checked (`SoftMinLowerBound.lean`) — and of the one-sided recursion (d).

As it stands, the second phase contains one cluster with the shape of a research contribution —
*the query complexity of certifying ground states and free energies under envelope
uncertainty*: an exact covering characterisation (certificate size = instance-wise deterministic
complexity), a dichotomy and exponents at zero and finite temperature with one variational
formula and three budgets, lower bounds for every randomised algorithm with a hedged converse,
an accuracy threshold and the complete accuracy diagram on the cube, hardness, a
resource-augmented guarantee for best-first search, and second-order classes — with every
one-shot lower bound machine-checked.

*The second referee's assessment* of this cluster without §11.10 (`reviews/R2`, §4), which we
accept: "a coherent note, not a theorem-driven paper".  It is not publishable as mathematics or
information theory, because after the reformulation each step is a short application of a
standard tool (type covering, Merhav's theorem, Chernoff and Hölder, the dominating-set
reduction, a packing argument, a discrete Taylor remainder); it could be a short note for the
certified-optimisation audience, or a formalisation paper.  Of the seven things the referee
found missing, this revision supplies four: the corrected statement of Theorem 11.15 and the
missing step of Theorem 11.9; the positioning (the exponents are corollaries); an algorithmic
statement (lower bounds for all algorithms; learn-then-cover on additive instances); and a
probabilistic notion with matching limits (spot-checked hints; Theorems 11.24–11.25).  Still
missing: a step beyond product landscapes (a pairwise chain as known part — **since the
eighteenth checkpoint there is one, §11.32: a nearest-neighbour chain as known part, with
exponents that differ from the cube's in both directions; known in brackets only**); a regime in which
best-first search is provably within a constant of `N_cov`, or tight constants; a lower bound
and one certified instance for second-order classes; and, new, the exact randomised exponent
(item 2(b)).

*The fifth and sixth referees' assessments* of §§11.16–11.17 (`reviews/R5`, `reviews/R6`), which
we accept.  §11.16: Lemma 11.43(a) is elementary and (b) a routine corollary of Harper's
theorem; Theorem 11.44 was not found in print and is a routine combination of truncation at a
quantile, an isoperimetric tail bound, Chernoff and Markov; the method of Theorem 11.45 is
known, its hard family is that of Mathé–Novak (2007) moved to the cube, and the exact
non-adaptive exponent on the cube for `ln Z` is apparently new.  §11.17: the linear theory is
known (optimal recovery, set-membership estimation, robust linear programming), the profile
distance is known as a descriptor distance, the entropy bound is the classical one for
monotone functions, and what was not found — the profile distance as the exact envelope of a
residual class next to a known part, with the count of evaluations — is immediate once
named.  Neither section changes the verdict of the earlier referees; §11.17 answers the
question of §11.14 for a narrower class than the one that was asked about.

*The third referee's assessment* of §11.10 (`reviews/R3`, §4), which we accept: the section does
not change the verdict.  Theorem 11.22 is the indistinguishability argument with a union bound
— fractional block sensitivity transplanted to real-valued classes; Theorem 11.23(a) is the
definition of a certificate read as instance complexity; Theorems 11.23(b) and 11.24 insert one
explicit family of alternatives.  The section makes the note more complete, and "randomisation
is worth at most the integrality gap for the minimum but has a threshold for `ln Z`" is a clean
message for the certified-optimisation audience, where the randomised case is named as open.
Theorem 11.25 was, as submitted, too thin (one class, one instance, part (c) wrong at one end
and unproved at the other); the referee named five ways to make it a contribution.  This
revision carries out the first — the complete accuracy diagram at the zero residual with a
hedged converse, lower bounds machine-checked.  Workstreams A and B address the third and the
fourth (Theorems 11.27–11.28: the conjecture refuted, the right family of perturbations, the
instance-wise threshold for every alphabet, the hint-free threshold of two-state classes;
verified here except for the matching upper bound of the exponent, which is not yet
refereed).  The second (hint-free
algorithms) and the fifth (the bridge to smoothness classes) are open (item 2(d)).  The referee
also found the same error for the second time — an asymptotic statement claimed for all
`ε = o(n)` although it fails for exponentially small accuracies (R2-C1 in Theorem 11.15, R3-C1 in
Theorem 11.25(c)) — and four overstatements of scope ("the sandwich", "the cube class", "the best
algorithm"); the corrections are in §11.10, in the README and in `DEAD_ENDS.md` D35–D37.
